en: (no. 2651 ka) (Title: Gautamatantra) (Extent: 80 folios)
(Year— 1948) (Subject— Tantra) Oṃ, salutation to Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Having prostrated before the Lord of Dvārakā, who enchants the hearts of the cowherd women,
this Gautama-tantra— the most excellent among all tantras— is now being written.
Once, while dwelling in Siddhāśrama, the wise sage Gautama was devoted to austerity and sacred study; he was full of devotion and dedicated to the Supreme Person.
Bowing his head to Viṣṇu, praising Janārdana with his speech,
worshipping the Lord of Sacrifice with his two hands, and intent upon the study of the heart-mantra,
he was a knower of the truth of all the Vedas and a master of the Itihāsas and Purāṇas.
An expert in the principles of mantras, medicinal herbs, rituals, subjugation, yoga,
and established doctrines, and seeking the goals of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa, that best of the twice-born prostrated before Nārada; bowing low with humility, he questioned him.
"O Blessed One, mantras that grant desires are authorized for Śūdras and women;
yet they yield diverse fruits and are not known to bestow a single uniform fruit.
It has not been heard that all these mantras yield equal results."

O Blessed One, tell me that mantra which brings about the attainment of all fruits, which is indeed a kinsman to all, which grants authority to all castes, and which is truly suitable for women, so that all my purposes may be accomplished.
"Nothing whatsoever remains unknown to him in this world of moving and unmoving beings.
Having heard this, the best of sages bowed to Viṣṇu and spoke:
"Well asked! I too once questioned the Lotus-born (Brahmā), and he replied:"
I shall tell you that which was spoken by the Self-Existent One:
O twice-born one, all desires are accomplished through the recitation of the mantra of Kṛṣṇa;
among all classes of mantras, the Vaiṣṇava is said to be the most excellent.
O observer of noble vows, in all the Gāṇapatya, Śaiva, Śākta,
and Vaiṣṇava traditions, the mantras of Kṛṣṇa lead to the attainment of fruits;
specifically, this ten-syllable mantra grants perfection through mere recitation.
By the mere knowledge of this mantra, one shall obtain the fourfold liberation.
O Lord of Sages, it is a conflagration for the entire mass of sins;
a mantra equal to this does not exist even in the entire world.
Kṛṣṇa, being propitiated by him, becomes pleased at that very moment.
I shall describe everything to you in brief; listen well to it yourself.
The Lord of Śacī [Indra] obtained the supreme sovereignty over the gods from the lotus-born [Brahmā].
The gods attained heaven; Bṛhaspati attained the lordship of speech;
and even Garuḍa, O best of the twice-born, became the sovereign of birds.
Someone, having propitiated Kṛṣṇa, attained the status of the Lord of Wealth (Kubera).

By propitiating Kṛṣṇa with this mantra, Candra became beloved by all people; and Kāma brought all desires under his control through it. This is the supreme mantra among mantras, the highest secret among secrets.
Having understood this king of mantras, a person becomes one who has achieved his purpose;
he shall possess sons, wealth, fame, prosperity, and cattle;
he shall be fortunate, respected, praiseworthy, illustrious, and renowned.
A person shall become beloved by all the worlds and shall become omniscient;
through this mantra, seekers of liberation have attained release in the three worlds.
By means of this mantra, the knower of mantras shall possess devotion characterized by love.
Purified by all sacred fords (*tīrtha*), he is the sanctifier of all holy fields (*kṣetra*);
as unassailable as the Sun, he is ever pure like the Moon;
like Śaṅkara, he is the Lord of Siddhis; and like Viṣṇu, he is the refuge of the virtuous.
What is the use of speaking much here? Listen to the secret, O Gautama:
this mantra bestows the fruit of nirvāṇa; what is the point of other extensive prattlings?
[Thus ends the chapter on the fruits of the ten-syllable mantra in the glorious Gaudapāda’s Great King of Tantras, the most excellent among all tantras. || 1 ||
Gautama said:
O Knower of the essence of all the Vedas, O Expert in all the Agamas,
O Brahmin, tell me now the ten-syllabled king of mantras.
Nārada said:
Now I shall fully describe the procedure established by the sages,
including the mantras, seers, meters, deities, and so forth, in their proper order.
Having extracted the syllable ending in *kha* (khaṃ), joined with the thirteenth vowel (*au*),
and conjoined with the final vowel of the fourth group (*u*), one likewise takes the two syllables ending in *cha* and *dha*.
Then, having extracted the syllable of nectar (*amṛta*, *ha*), one places the pair of *ma*s together on one side.

The ten-syllable mantra, beginning with *patūryyaṃ*, followed by *mukhavṛttena* and joined with *svāhā*, is declared to bestow both seen and unseen fruits. By that [mantra]: *gopījanavallabhāya svāhā*.
I shall now declare the seed-syllable (bīja) and its power (śakti); it is the Brahman-consciousness, higher than the highest.
Together with Māyā and Brahmā, it consists of the syllable *māṃ* (ma-aṃ), endowed with the nasal resonance (*nāda*) and the point (*bindu*).
This is declared to be the seed-syllable, the reality of Kṛṣṇa, higher than the highest.
The ocean of semen (ŚU) joined with the ocean of nectar (KHA),
combined with the circle of the void (GA) and the circle of the mouth (MA)— this is declared to be the Śakti higher than the highest.
This Śakti is supreme, subtle, eternal, and the bestower of consciousness.

One should contemplate the fourfold seed and power within all mantras: Īśvara as the seed of the worlds, Śakti consisting of the qualities (guṇas), the Paramātman, and likewise the intellect (buddhi), Vāyu, and Kuṇḍalinī.
The triad therein is common; that is now being defined.
Īśvara is the seed of the worlds; He is called the primordial Brahman. His power (śakti) is likewise declared to be Māyā, consisting of the guṇas.
O best of beings, primordial nature (prakṛti), the person (puruṣa), eternal time (kāla),

the principles (tattvas), and the Lord (īśvara)— these are remembered as the five, with Brahman being the fifth. The end of creation is the person, while the supreme primordial nature is called the Fourth (turyā).
The elements take the form of flesh, and Time takes the form of the principles (tattvas).
That which is called Īśvara is Nāda; Bindu is consciousness, consisting of pure spirit.
Merely by knowing this, one wanders the earth as one liberated while living (jīvanmukta).
The words of the Śruti declare that from the syllable *klīm* he created the universe— his knowledge, sacred fords, and sanctuaries; from the letter *l*,
the earth was born, and from the letter *k*, the origin of water.
From the vowel *ī* fire was produced; from the *nāda*, wind was born;
from the *bindu*, the origin of space (*ākāśa*) arose—such is the mantra whose meaning corresponds to the elements.
By the word *sva* is meant the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*), and *ha* is the supreme consciousness (*cit-prakṛti*).
The one who performs the binding of the mouth through the arising of the unity of those two is indeed the one in whom the dissolution of the universe occurs within his own syllable.
One should know "gopī" as *prakṛti* (primordial nature), and "jana" as the collection of the [twenty-four] principles (*tattva*).
The substratum of these two is Īśvara, who, as the cause, is described by Valabha as the supreme light of intense bliss. Thus they say: "The Puruṣa rose up three-quarters above."
The first utterance:
by the mere pronunciation of the seed-syllable (*bīja*), the nature of consciousness (*citsvabhāva*) arises;
and through identity with the Beloved (*vallabha*) and Svāhā, it bestows knowledge.
Thus has this truth been told, O Sage, which is indeed well-esteemed by Brahmā:
alternatively, the Gopīs are Prakṛti and the people (Janas) are the circle of her portions;
the beloved master of these two is remembered as the Lord named Kṛṣṇa.
He is celebrated by the Vedas as the Lord of cause and effect;
indeed, he is the husband of the gopīs who have attained perfection through many births.
Thus addressed as "Nanda’s son," he who increases the joy of the three worlds was praised.
The stainless mantra-practitioner should contemplate [this] for the sake of attaining all prosperity;
it is the witness and knower of even the ten principles, and is imperishable. Known as the "Ten-Syllabled," this king of mantras is higher than the highest.
Because its nature consists of the seed-syllable (bīja) [which has been] dissolved, it is called "Daśārṇa" (the ten-syllabled).
O Sage, the recitation preceded by the seed-syllable is declared to be its secret.
Nārada is said to be its sage (ṛṣi), and Virāj is remembered as its meter (chandas).
Śrī Kṛṣṇa is its presiding deity, and Durgā is the presiding deity of the site;
he who, having learned this directly from the mouth of Maheśvara through austerity,
accomplishes it with a purified soul— he is declared to be its seer (ṛṣi).

One should place [the mantra] upon one's head with a sense of reverence; otherwise, regarding the four goals of human life (puruṣārtha), a mantra will not yield its fruit due to ignorance of the seer (ṛṣi) and the meter (chandas).
The power of mantras diminishes for those who do not know their ritual application (viniyoga).
Now I shall describe the mantra-nyāsa, which bestows both seen and unseen fruits.
Having encased the ten syllables with the *praṇava* (oṃ) at the beginning and end, and ending each with *namaḥ*,
the nyāsa from the right thumb to the left [thumb] is declared to be the "creation" (*sṛṣṭi*) method.

The sequence from the left thumb to the right [thumb] is proclaimed as *saṃhṛti* (dissolution). When the sequence beginning with the *jyeṣṭhā* (thumb) is applied to both hands, it is called *sthiti* (maintenance);
this is proclaimed as *saṃhṛti*.
The position of both hands with the *jyeṣṭhā* [thumb] foremost is called the *sthiti* (stability). It is proclaimed as the *saṃhṛti* (withdrawal) of the hosts of gods, the *hāriṇī* (attracting),
the bestower of knowledge (*vidyā*), and the end of creation for those of pure mind.
For those who have not taken up household life, the three [stages] remain until the end of the stage of stability, according to their inclination toward desire.
Some desire that [these stages] exist until the end of stability for the *vānaprastha* (forest-dweller) as well.
For the sages (*muni*) and for the solitary ascetic (*vivikta*), they all end with the stage of withdrawal (*saṃhāra*).

The three types of nyāsa should always be performed; however, if one is unable, only one may be done. Furthermore, the practitioner should perform the varṇanyāsa upon the body, [placing them] at the base of the hand, the elbow, the wrist, and the base of the fingers.

Having placed [the hand] on the tips of the fingers, one should place it over the feet. One should remember that emanation (sṛṣṭi) begins from the base of the hands, persistence (sthiti) from the wrist, and withdrawal (saṃhṛti) from the tips of the fingers; thus, one should perform the placement of this triad ending with persistence.
Then, the nyāsa on the hands and limbs is proclaimed in the same manner:
one should say "ācakrāya hā" with the two thumbs,
and likewise utter "vicakrāya svāhā" with the two index fingers.
One should likewise utter "svāhā" for the *Sucakra* with the two middle fingers;
"trailokyarakṣaṇacakrāya svāhā" for the ring fingers; and "asurāntacakrāya svāhā" with the name of the two little fingers.

Rukmiṇī is the left-hand *prakṛti*, the manifest embodiment of nectar; the right hand is declared to be *puruṣa*, the light whose form is poison. From the union of these two hands, the supreme reality (*parātattva*) is thus produced.
In this very way, the purification of all objects is prescribed;
thereafter, the preceptor should perform the *pañcagavya* rite with the limb-mantras (*aṅgamantra*).
Wherever there are five limbs of the mantra, one should exclude the "eye" (*netra*) limb.
One should say "Ācakrāya tathā svāhā" and "Hṛdayāya namaḥ";
with the fingertips, excluding the thumb, one should touch the heart.
One should likewise say "Vicakrāya tathā svāhā" and "Śirase svāhā."
In the same manner, one should place [the mantra] on the head with the fingers of the hand;
likewise, one should utter "Śūcakra-ya svāhā" for the crest-lock (śikhā).
Similarly, with the fist having the thumb pointing downward, one should place it around the crest-lock.
"To the wheel for protecting the three worlds, svāhā!"—with "huṃ" for the armor.
Having touched his head with both hands, the ascetic should touch down to the ends of his feet.
"To the wheel that is the end-maker of the asuras, svāhā! Svāhā! Phaṭ!"—thus he should utter.
O tiger among sages, one should bind the sixteen directions with three upward-spread palm-claps; this is declared to be the daily ritual placement (nyāsa).
When perceived by the heart, it becomes the conscious self within the hearts of all beings.
The preceptor performs that [rite] for the Supreme Self with the Heart-mantra;
and into the Supreme Self, which is of the nature of consciousness and possesses qualities such as omniscience,
the wise one effects the intake of sense-objects with the Śiras-mantra.

The state of being composed of the name of one's own deity is established with reverence within the heart, chest, and limbs by means of the head-mantra (śiromantra) of that deity who is identical with the mantra;
[this is done] through the splendor expressed by the mantra of the deity whose essence is the mantra.
The armor-mantra (varma-mantra) is performed on all sides, for which no other preparation is required;
it bestows supreme knowledge within the Supreme Self in the form of pure consciousness. This splendor, consisting of the heart and other centers, is known as the "eye" (netra).
That mantra which destroys whatever internal or external form may cause the practitioner's ruin, yet is itself beyond ignorance— that is declared to be the supreme abode. Gautama said:
O Brahmin, best among the knowers of Brahman, devoted to the welfare of all beings,
you alone are the stainless inner controller of Lord Kṛṣṇa;
you are liberated from the defects of ignorance, well-restrained by your vows, and firm in your sacred observances.
The sole path for all the world, the sole knower of the reality of all the world,
the witness of all experience, you who are saluted by all the gods—
I now desire to hear the King of Mantras, which is higher than the highest.
The eighteen-syllable mantra is remembered as more secret than the secret itself.
O best of beings, if I am worthy, I desire to hear that mantra;
you ought to rescue me here, for I am submerged in the ocean of worldly existence.
Having praised him with these and other hymns of praise, and having bowed down again and again, the lord of sages approached his side; with his mind fixed upon his face, Nārada spoke: Nārada said:
"Excellent, O Brahmin, you have asked well! This king of mantras, which conforms to all the Vedas and Āgamas, was also remembered by me from Brahmā, O best of sages.
From that time forward, O eminent Brāhmaṇa, I have attained the state of being free from the stain of sin."
Out of affection for you, I shall speak, since you are dear to me, O Puruṣa:
having first uttered the syllable *klīṃ*, one should then utter *Kṛṣṇa* joined with the fourth case-ending (*-āya*),
and likewise having spoken *Govinda*, one should then recite the ten-syllabled mantra.
Out of devotion and having prostrated before you, this leader of mantras has been told;
for it is more secret than the secret, remembered as the wish-fulfilling gem (cintāmaṇi) for all desires.
O Śaunaka and other sages, and whatever other chief deities are performing austerities—
Through the thorough knowledge of the King of Mantras, they immediately attain that state of equality.
The word *kṛṣṇa* has the meaning of "existence" (*sattā*), and *na* is of the nature of "bliss" (*nanda*).
Consequently, the Self becomes the form of bliss, consisting of the joy of being.
Through the word "go" (cow), one should obtain knowledge and liberation, and thereby that Lord;
from the word "go," the Veda is said to arise, and thus men attain the All-pervading One.
In this way, O best of sages, the latent impression (*vāsanā*) regarding mantras has been explained to you.

By the power of this knowledge, Kṛṣṇa lives and not otherwise. What is the use of much further talk? By remembering him, the knower of mantras is undoubtedly liberated while living; he is indeed Viṣṇu himself—of this there is no doubt.
Nārada is declared to be its sage (ṛṣi), and Gāyatrī is said to be its meter (chandas).
Kṛṣṇa is its material nature (prakṛti), and Durgā is the presiding deity (adhiṣṭhātṛ-devatā).
Vāsudeva, Saṃkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha [are the deities].
The supreme one, known as Nārāyaṇa, consists of five words;
the meaning of the syllables has been explained, and thus the name of the word is proclaimed.
Therefore, having understood this, the practitioner of mantra attains the four aims of human life.
One obtains this; there is no doubt here—this is the truth, the very truth, O Gautama.
The seed-syllables and their powers have been declared previously, and the ritual application (viniyoga) is as before. By joining the five parts of the mantra with the five words,
[they are placed] in the aperture of Brahmā (the crown of the head), between the eyebrows, and likewise in the hollow of the tongue.

One should perform the placement (nyāsa) in the region of the throat, the heart, the navel, the penis, and the root [perineum], as well as in the two nostrils, the two eyes, and the two ears; furthermore,
one should perform the three pervasive [placements] in the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra).
Having performed the placement (nyāsa) of the five feet in the head, mouth, heart, navel, and the base,
in both ascending and descending order, one should then place Keśava and the others.
Having again performed the placement of the syllables (varṇanyāsa), one should then place Keśava and the others.

He who performs worship without the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) and the placement of the letters (lipinyāsa) shall receive contrary results; likewise, worship performed without devotion yields no fruit. Mātṛkā is said to be of two kinds: the supreme (parā) and the non-supreme (aparā).

The *parā* [vowels] are to be placed within the *suṣumnā*, and the *aparā* [consonants] in the external region. Now follows the internal *mātṛkā-nyāsa*: on the four-petalled *mūlādhāra*, which is adorned with the four letters *va*, *śa*, *ṣa*, and *sa* located at the navel.
In the Svādhiṣṭhāna, which has six petals, resembles lightning, and possesses the luster of fire,
there are the letters va, bha, ma, ya, ra, and la, their heads illuminated by the bindu. In the twelve-petaled Anāhata, which resembles the brilliance of coral, [the same letters are situated].

In the Viśuddha [cakra], which is endowed with the sixteen petals beginning with *ka* and ending with *ṭha*, which is heart-pleasing to yogins, smoke-colored, adorned with vowels, and on the sixteenth day; and in the Ājñācakra,
which is moon-like, two-petaled, and adorned with the letters *ha* and *kṣa*.

In the thousand-spoked [cakra], resembling a jewel and adorned with all colors, which is itself adorned by the three hundred million worlds consisting of the three lines beginning with 'A', 'Ka', and so forth; in its center is the supreme bindu, which consists of emanation, maintenance, and dissolution.
With the mind thus concentrated, one should perform this internal renunciation;
one should meditate upon Viṣṇu, whose nature is consciousness, from the *mūlādhāra* to the *brahmarandhra*.
One should satisfy the *mātṛkā* with the streams of nectar dripping from the *bindu* and then perform the placement (*nyāsa*).
Having uttered each syllable individually from the *mūlādhāra* up to the eyebrows with the mantra "Obeisance to the Infinite" (*namo'nantam*), this is proclaimed as the *ācānta* placement (*nyāsa*).
Now listen attentively to me regarding the external *mātṛkā-nyāsa*.
On the forehead, face, round eyes, ears, nose, and cheeks;
on the lips, teeth, head, mouth, arms, joints, fingers, and toes;
on the sides, back, navel, belly, heart, and shoulders.

One should likewise first remove [the vowels] from the portion of the *kakudya* (the palate), as well as from the pair of hands and feet, and from the belly and face; one should insert the letters of the Mātṛkā in their proper order.
The Mātṛkā is said to be fourfold: the simple [vowels], those joined with the nasal drop (*bindu*), [those joined with the visarga], and [those joined with the half-moon].
Listen, the secret is being told: [the mantra] with the visarga is both [vidyā and karī];
the solitary one is the bestower of knowledge; the one with both [bindu and visarga] bestows devotion;
the one with the visarga bestows sons; and the one with the bindu bestows wealth.
Then the best of practitioners should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) beginning with Keśava.
Prajāpati is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Gāyatrī is the meter (*chanda*), and Lord Hari, who is Ardha-lakṣmī, is the deity. The six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) are performed with the *śrī*-seed syllable.
Having performed the ritual for the purification of the hands, one should practice meditation upon the Supreme beyond the supreme,
who resembles the rising sun and possesses the luster of molten gold,
with his two sides graced by Kamalā and Vasudhā.
Having meditated upon him thus— adorned with various ornaments fashioned from diverse jewels,
clothed in yellow garments, and holding the conch and the Kaumodakī mace in his hands,
with the discus and lotus in his left hands— one should then perform the ritual placement (nyāsa).
Having first uttered the *praṇava* (oṃ), and immediately thereafter the *śrībīja*, one should then place the letters of the *mātṛkā*. I shall explain that method:
one should assign Keśava with Kīrti, and one should assign Nārāyaṇa with Kānti.
One should install Mādhava together with Tuṣṭi, Govinda together with Puṣṭi,
Viṣṇu together with Dhṛti, and Madhusūdana together with Śānti; likewise,
one should install Trivikrama with Kriyā and Vāmana with Dayā.
One should place Śrīdhara together with Medhā, and Hṛṣīkeśa together with Harṣā;
then Aṃbujanābha with Śraddhā, and thereafter Dāmodara with Lajjā.
Then one should place Vāsudeva, and after that Saṃkarṣaṇa along with Lakṣmī.

Then, out of affection, one should place Sarasvatī upon Pradyumna; Rati upon Aniruddha; Durgā upon the wielder of the discus (Cakrin); Jayā upon the wielder of the mace (Gadin); Prabhā upon the wielder of the Śārṅga bow (Śārṅgin); Khaḍgi upon Satya; Caṇḍā upon the wielder of the conch (Śaṅkhin); and Vāṇī upon Halin.
One should place Mūṣalin with Vilāsinī, Śūlin with Vijayā, Pāśin with Virajā, and Aṅkuśin with Viśvā. One should also place Mukunda with Vinadā, and Nandaja with Sunandā.
Through mindfulness, Nandin; through supernatural power, Nara, the conqueror of hell;

through prosperity, Hariśuddhi; through devotion to Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇabhakti; through intellect, Satya; and likewise Sātvata; through my noose, Īśakṣama; through heroism, Śūrarāma; and likewise Umā and Janārdana.
One should then install Kledinī upon Bhūdhara Viśvamūrti, followed by Klinnā;
then Vaikuṇṭha and Vasudhā, as well as Vasudhā and Puruṣottama; and Balī joined with Parā, along with Balānuja and Parāyaṇa.
Bāla is joined with Sūkṣmā; Vṛṣaghna is united with Saṃdhyā;
Vṛṣa is joined with Prajñā; Haṃsa is endowed with Prabhā;
Varāha is joined with Niśā; and Vimala is united with Amodā.
The powers of Śiva (Śiva-śaktis) have been described by Narasiṃha Vidyutā.
Having thus performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) upon the limbs and meditated with a concentrated mind,
one who worships the God with devotion shall obtain his desired fruit.

This Nyāsa beginning with Keśava bestows the state of Acyuta upon embodied beings merely by its application; this is the truth, the truth—there is no doubt. All these [deities] beginning with Keśava are dark-complexioned and are traditionally known as Nārāyaṇas.
With four resplendent arms holding a conch, a discus, a mace, and a lotus; [the mantras] are:
śacegīpīśagīpīcaśapacaṃgaṃśapāṃga ca, śaṃgaṃ camyaṃ śapaṃgaṃ ca, [assigned] to the right hands in order, starting from the upper right.
Having fully uttered "namontāḥ," one should recite the mantra of Nārāyaṇa;
likewise, having uttered "prāṇātmānaṃ," one should remember "keśavāya. Then, joined with the mind, one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) beginning with "kītyai" and so forth.
Those seeking liberation and ascetics should resort to this supreme renunciation (nyāsa).
Alternatively, one should perform the nyāsa preceded by the seed-syllable of Lakṣmī;
through mindfulness and fortitude, having attained Mahālakṣmī, one shall go to the state of Hari at the end.
One should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) beginning with the Vāgbhava syllable; thereby one attains the state of the Lord of Speech (Vāgīśvara).
Whichever [seed-syllable] is placed first in the ritual placement, the assignment of the limbs (aṅgakalpanā) should be performed with those seed-syllables.
Thereafter, the practitioner (sādhaka) should perform the placement of the principles (tattvanyāsa) for the sake of attaining spiritual success (siddhi).
Having performed that by which he attains the very form of the illustrious Devarūpa,
one should recite the letters beginning with *mā* and ending with *kā*, as well as the seed-syllables (*bīja*) one by one;
then, having uttered "Obeisance to the Supreme" (*namaḥ parāya*), one should thereafter say "Obeisance to the Self of Reality" (*tatvātmane namaḥ*).
Having recited the *jīva* and the two *prāṇas*, one should place them upon all the limbs;
then, one should place the three *tattvas* within the center of the heart:
the seed-syllable *vaṃ*, the *matitattva*, and *ahaṃkāra* as *phaṃ*.

One should place the triad consisting of the seed-syllable *paṃ*, the principle of mind (*manastattva*), and likewise [the letter *yaṃ*]. Then, one should place the seed-syllable *naṃ* and the principle of sound (*śabdatattva*) upon the crown of the head. Thereafter, the wise practitioner should place the seed-syllable *vaṃ* and the principle of touch (*sparśatattva*) in the mouth.

Then one should place the seed-syllable *daṃ* and the element of form (*rūpatattva*) in the heart; next, one should place the seed-syllable *thaṃ* and the element of taste (*rasatattva*) in the secret place;
and then one should place the seed-syllable *taṃ* and the element of smell (*gandhatattva*) in the two feet.
The practitioner should place the seed-syllable *ṇaṃ* and the principle of *śrotra* (hearing) upon the two ears.
He should place the seed-syllable *ṭaṃ* and the principle of *tvak* (skin) upon the skin.
He should place the seed-syllable *ḍaṃ* and the principle of *netra* (eye) upon the two eyes.
The practitioner should place the seed-syllable *ṭhaṃ*, the principle of taste, upon the tongue;
then he should place the seed-syllable *ḍhaṃ*, the principle of smell, upon the nose; and the practitioner should place the seed-syllable *ñaṃ*, the principle of speech, upon the mouth.
One should duly assign the seed-syllable *jhaṃ* and the principle of breath (*prāṇitatva*) to the two hands;
one should assign the seed-syllable *jaṃ* and the principle of the feet (*pādatatva*) to the two feet;
and, being composed, one should assign the seed-syllable *chaṃ* and the principle of the anus (*pāyutatva*) to the anus.
Then one should place the seed-syllable *caṃ* and the principle (*tatva*) of the *liṅga* upon the penis;
then one should place the seed-syllable *ṅaṃ* and the principle of space (*ākāśa*) upon the crown of the head;
and again, one should place the seed-syllable *ghaṃ* and the principle of air (*vāyu*) upon the mouth.
The wise practitioner should place the seed-syllable *gaṃ*, the fire principle (*tejas-tattva*), in the heart;
then he should place the seed-syllable *khaṃ*, the water principle (*jala-tattva*), in the penis;
and again, he should place the seed-syllable *kaṃ*, the earth principle (*pṛthivī-tattva*), in the feet.
One should place the seed-syllable *śam*, the principle of the heart-lotus, in the heart;
one should place the seed-syllable *ham*, the principle of the solar orb, in the heart;
and one should place the seed-syllable *sam*, the principle of the lunar orb, there in that same place.

One should place the seed-syllable *vaṃ*, the principle of the fire-mandala (*vahnimaṇḍala-tattva*), right there; and the seed-syllable *ṣaṃ*, the principle of the Supreme Lord (*parameṣṭhī-tattva*) and Vāsudeva, on the head.
Then the seed-syllable *yaṃ*, the principle of the individual soul (*puṃs-tattva*) and Saṃkarṣaṇa, on the mouth.
One should place the seed-syllable *laṃ*, the principle of *viśva*, and Pradyumna in the heart;
the seed-syllable *vaṃ*, the principle of *nivṛtti*, and Aniruddha in the generative organ;
and the seed-syllable *laṃ*, the principle of *sarva*, and Nārāyaṇa in the feet.

Having thus performed the placement of the principles (*tattva*)— the seed-syllable *kṣrauṃ*, the principle of wrath (*kopatattva*), and Nṛsiṃha— upon all the limbs, one should perform breath control (*prāṇāyāma*). If using the ten-syllable mantra, one should exhale twenty-eight times.
In the same manner, one should fill [the breath] with the left [nostril] and likewise restrain it according to that measure.
One complete *prāṇāyāma* consists of exhalation (*recaka*), inhalation (*pūraka*), and retention (*kumbhaka*).
If the mantra consists of eighteen syllables, one should perform it in this way accordingly.
One should exhale with the seed-syllable of desire (KĀM) alone, separately for each;
one should fill [with breath] using that syllable recited seven times, and retain it with it twenty times.
One should perform this practice with this very seed-syllable for all the Kṛṣṇa mantras.

Alternatively, while reciting all mantras according to the sequence of their syllables, the practitioner of mantra should perform breath control (prāṇāyāma) through exhalation (recaka), inhalation (pūraka), and retention (kuṃbhaka). This is declared to be the "mantric breath control"; now I shall describe the "yogic" [breath control].

The wise man should exhale with sixteen measures and fill [the breath] with thirty-two measures; he should then retain it for sixty-four measures. One breath constitutes one measure; such is the rule regarding the measure.
The time required for the hand to rotate once around the left forearm is to be known as one *mātrā* by the sages who have reached the further shore of the Vedas.
Prāṇāyāma is said to be of two kinds: *sagarbha* (with seed) and *nigarbhaka* (seedless).
The mantra becomes endowed with potency through recitation according to its measure and number.
Higher than breath control (prāṇāyāma) is the supreme reality; higher than breath control is austerity;
higher than breath control is knowledge; higher than breath control is the supreme state.

There is no yoga superior to *prāṇāyāma*, and there is no wealth superior to *prāṇāyāma*; this has been told to you again and again, O observer of noble vows. Through the practice of yoga for two years, the direct realization of Brahman will certainly be attained.
Whatever obscuration of consciousness is dissolved herein, there is no doubt;
without prāṇāyāma, there is no path to liberation, as I have declared.
And whatever practice is undertaken without prāṇāyāma, that shall be fruitless.
Through breath control (prāṇāyāma), the sages attained perfection, and not otherwise. The yogi who is devoted to breath control is no mere yogi; he is Śiva himself.
Such is the retention of the movement and return of the vital breath (prāṇa).
That which is proclaimed as *prāṇāyāma* is known by those expert in the Yoga-śāstras. *Prāṇa* is renowned as the vital air (*vāyu*), and *āyāma* is its restraint.
Thus, *prāṇāyāma* is declared to be the means for accomplishing yoga for practitioners of yoga.
The movements within the nostrils are prescribed for the first two [prāṇāyāmas].
One should exhale through the right nostril and then fill [the lungs] from the left;
practicing the mantra thirty-two times, that is called prāṇāyāma.

O twice-born one, indeed, by means of *prāṇāyāma* (breath control), the killing of a Brahmin, the drinking of liquor, and likewise sexual intercourse with an *agamyā* (unapproachable woman)— all these are destroyed instantly;
even sins such as the destruction of an embryo (*bhrūṇahatyā*) it shall destroy within a single month.
Every morning and evening, one should constantly perform sixteen breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas).
This destroys all sins just as fire consumes a heap of cotton.
This is remembered as the expiation for all sins whatsoever.

Just as one who is free from disease casts off the armor situated within his own body, so too, through breath control (prāṇāyāma), does one burn away the ignorance born of desire and action. Or rather, what is the use of much speaking? Listen to my words, O Gautama.
Indeed, for yogins seeking the perfection of liberation, there is nothing superior to *prāṇāyāma*.
Having performed *prāṇāyāma*, one should then assign the sacred seats (*pīṭhas*) within the body:
Ādhāraśakti, Prakṛti, Kūrma, and Śūkara.
The earth, the ocean of milk, and Śvetadvīpa are situated in the center;
in the middle of that is a palace of jewels which bestows all desired fruits. Within the palace is the Kalpavṛkṣa tree, resplendent with all kinds of gems.
One should likewise place Dharma, Jñāna, Vairāgya, and Aiśvarya on the right side of the hip, as well as on the two left sides.
One should then place the letters beginning with *na* and *ña* on the sides of the mouth and the sides of the navel.
Having performed the placement in this manner, one should again place upon the heart a lotus consisting of the universe:
having eight petals shining with the nature (*prakṛti*) and filaments consisting of the transformations (*vikāra*).
In its center, the practitioner of mantra should place the pericarp consisting of the fifty letters.
One should arrange the three mandalas with the three mantras of the Praṇava,
likewise accompanied by their digits (kalās) numbering ten, twelve, and sixteen.
These letters, which arise from the components of the Praṇava, are the syllables Ā, U, and Ma.

Those known as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa are the forms of the collective (samaṣṭi) and the individual (vyaṣṭi). Through the collective alone is Brahman, characterized by existence, consciousness, and bliss. Therein, one should then place Sattva and the other qualities preceded by their respective seed-syllables.
In that portion, one should not thus place the fourfold self (ātmacatuṣṭaya);
they are considered to be the Self (Ātman), the Inner Self (Antarātman), the Supreme Self (Paramātman), and the Knowledge-Self (Jñānātman).
This Self is the support of the world, the Soul of the Universe (Viśvātman), and possesses the form of the universe (Viśvarūpaka).
Accompanied by the seed-syllables of the name and others, it is established in the center of the heart;
therefore, one should place [the mantra] in the heart, for the activity of speech resides in the heart.
And because of its inner nature, this inner self (antarātman) is within the heart.
Consisting of mind and known as taijasa, it sustains the functions of the internal senses;
for this reason, O Sage, it is celebrated as the "inner self" (antarātman). The syllable *aṃ* is declared to be its seed-syllable (*bīja*); therefore, the wise one should first place that there.
Known as the deep sleep (suṣupti) whose essence is Ramā and the rest, it removes the distractions of the mind;
when the senses have dissolved therein, one remains in the auspicious and solitary state.
One should worship that Supreme Self, who is the seed, for the attainment of all goals.
Saṃkarṣaṇa, Aniruddha, and Pradyumna—this triad is consciousness;
that Vāsudeva is the self of knowledge, the self-existent one whose form is wisdom. When the three functions have dissolved, he remains as pure bliss and consciousness alone.

This Vāsudeva is the self of bliss; primordial nature (prakṛti) is a mere fraction of his consciousness. I shall proclaim his seed-syllable, which consists solely of bliss and consciousness, the essence extracted from the three Vedas, and the cause of all causes.
She who possesses the form of the eightfold nature consists of Keśaveṣṭā and Pṛśaktī;
she is the central power known as Parā, whose essential nature is consciousness and bliss.
The powers are Vimalā, Utkarṣiṇī, Jñānā, Kriyā, and Yogā.
Prahvī, Satyā, and likewise Īśānānugrahā are recorded as the ninth;
having duly assigned the nine Śaktis, one should then assign the Great Mantra there:
"Obeisance to the Blessed One," it is declared, followed by the word "to the Self of all beings."
The word *vāsudeva* ending in the suffix *ṅe* (dative), conjoined with *sarvātmayoga*, is to be known; thereafter, the mantra for the Yoga-pīṭha is: "Obeisance to the Self of the Lotus-Pīṭha.
This is declared to be the Pīṭha-mantra, which is supreme and the self of all beings.
One should meditate upon that dark and tender radiance above that.
[Thus ends the second chapter in the Śrīgautamīyatantra, the most excellent among all tantras. || 2 ||
Now, O Nandī, listen attentively to the entire system of Nyāsa.
The daily Nyāsas have been previously described; without them, all [practices], even when performed in every manner according to the nature of Mantra and Tantra, become fruitless.

O best of Brahmins, listen as I shall describe other arrangements that grant all human goals (puruṣārtha) for the sake of desiring superior results; by doing so, one becomes identical with Viṣṇu. One should place the six vowels as before, and afterwards the subsequent group of six vowels.
Likewise, one should place the twelve forms together with Vāsudeva on the head-dress (kalāpa). With a well-composed mind, the donor should place Keśava on the head;
and Nārāyaṇa, together with Aryaman, on the belly.
One should place Mādhava in the heart together with the mantra; Govinda in the hollow of the throat with the Varuṇa mantra;
and one should place Madhusūdana on the right end of the arm with the Bharga mantra.
The wise practitioner should place Padmanābha on the right side of the throat together with the daughter of the Vindhya mountains; he should place Dāmodara on the left side together with Akhendrā;
and he should place Vāsudeva at the end of the arms together with Puṣṭi.
One should place Saṃkarṣaṇa on the belly together with Paryanya;
one should place Pradyumna on the region of the back together with Tvaṣṭṛ;
and one should place Aniruddha in the region of the armpits together with Viṣṇu.
One should place the excellent twelve-syllable mantra at the aperture of Brahmā (the *brahmarandhra*);
through its pervasion and its splendor, one becomes Vāsudeva himself.
Having extracted the three measures (*trimātrika*), one should write "namo bhagavate."
With "Vāsudevāya" in the dative case, this mantra is for the consumption of wine and other [intoxicants].
Merely by knowing this, one becomes Vāsudeva. One should install the Mātṛkā [alphabet] encapsulated by the Manu [seed-syllable], which is the Mother of the Universe.
By that very mantra, success shall be attained through the destruction of the multitude of defects.
I shall now describe the placement (*nyāsa*) of the ten-syllable *golaka*, which bestows prosperity;
it consists of ten repetitions of the mantra and must be kept secret.
In the foundation, the banner, the navel, the heart, the throat, and the region of the mouth;
in the two thighs, the neck, the navel, the belly, and the two breasts;
likewise in the two sides, the two hips, the head, the face, and the two eyes.

In the same manner, one should respectfully place [the mantra] on the ears and nose, on the cheeks and the joints of the arms, at the tips of those [limbs], on the joints of the feet, and at the tips of those as well; then on the head, and pervasively in the directions beginning with the west.
The practitioner should diligently place [the syllables] on the two arms, the two thighs, the head, the eyes, the mouth,
the region of the throat, the eyes, the heart, the teeth, the left knee,
the ears, the cheeks, the shoulders, the breasts, the sides, and the hips.
One should duly assign the phonemes to the pair of knees, shanks, and feet;
this is the Vibhūti-pañjara-nyāsa, which brings about all prosperity. Then, for the sake of swift accomplishment, one should assign the ten principles (daśatattva) and the [twelve] darśanas.
Earth, water, fire, air, ether, the two [mind and intellect], the five elements, ego,
the principle of the Great One (mahat), as well as primordial nature (prakṛti) and the individual soul (puruṣa)—
these are the principles; listen attentively as they are described.
Then, one should place [the syllables] on the feet, the anus, the heart, the mouth, and the head;
the wise person should place two at the heart, three at the navel, and [the remainder] on all the limbs.
Then one should perform the placement (nyāsa) starting from the head down to the feet;
this placement bestows swift accomplishment for the most secret mantras.
A person of great intelligence may also perform it for other mantras of Gopāla.

One should place the syllables of the ten-syllable mantra according to the order of withdrawal (saṃhāra). In the placement of emanation (sṛṣṭi), one should place the syllables of this mantra in reverse order.
Having uttered each individual syllable, one should then recite "namo 'nantāya."
O Sage, one should perform the ritual placements (nyāsa) of the principles (tattvas), ending with *parāya* and accompanied by the word *namaḥ*,
either mentally or upon a flower;
otherwise, it becomes fruitless, [if performed] with the thumb and ring finger.
[Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Application for Desired Aims," in the glorious *Gautamīya Mahātantra*, which is the most excellent among all tantras. || 3 ||
Then one should meditate upon Vṛndāvana, which is saluted by all the gods,
endowed with the flowers of every season, made resonant by the songs of flocks of birds, and whose quarters are made vocal by the humming of wandering bees.
It was served by breezes cooled by the waves of the Yamunā's waters,
adorned with groves of trees entwined with various flowering creepers,
and illuminated by the radiance of the rising sun and moon as if by lamps.
Its interior was dusted with the pollen of lotuses, blue water-lilies, and white lilies;
it was crowded with troops of monkeys and frequented by various wild animals.
Surrounded by thirty-two forests, it bestowed even greater happiness than Vaikuṇṭha.
It was presided over on all sides by the gods, headed by Purandara;
in its center was a ground of jewels possessing a radiance equal to ten thousand suns,
where there was a garden of Kalpa-trees that constantly showered down precious gems.
In its center was a jeweled pavilion, shining upon a peak of rubies;
it was variegated with clusters of various gems, resplendent with all splendors,
and adorned with wonderful canopies shimmering with fruits.
Adorned with jeweled arches and gate-towers, and encircled by a platform of rubies; endowed with divine bells and resplendent with rows of pearls and gems;
possessing a brilliance equal to ten million suns, it was completely free from the six defects.
Hunger and thirst, as well as those of the vital breath and the mind,
grief and delusion, and the decay and death of the body— these are the six waves.
It is endowed with four gates and adorned with eight panels.
There, one should meditate upon the most magnificent wish-fulfilling tree (kalpataru), raining down jewels,
served by all the seasons, showering sprays of nectar,
with leaves shining like emeralds and sprouts made of coral and gems.

At its base, the practitioner of mantra should visualize a beautiful and auspicious jewel-lion throne, spread with pearls and gems, radiant with rubies, providing wonderful and virtuous shade that cuts through the torments of saṃsāra.
There, one should meditate upon the Lord of the World, who consists of all principles (*sarvatattvamaya*), as having the brilliance of the sun and seated upon an eight-petalled lotus;
he has crossed over the ocean of worldly existence for the sake of accomplishing virtue, desire, and wealth.
Kṛṣṇa, wearing yellow garments, with eyes like lotuses,
with red eyes, lips, and beautiful hands and soles of the feet;
his chest illuminated by the Kaustubha gem and adorned with various jewels.
Adorned with necklaces of pearls and gems shining intensely,
he wore a crown of blazing splendor emitting the luster of various jewels;
he was further graced by necklaces, armlets, bracelets, and earrings.
With the Śrīvatsa mark upon his chest, he was beautiful and adorned with anklets and other ornaments;
he was endowed with various kinds of jewels, including necklaces and finger-rings,
and his forehead was marked with a tilaka made of gorocanā and saffron.
Adorned with the beauty of Alakā, clothed in a pair of yellow garments,
shining with the bimba-like lips of his consort, filled with the nectar-essence of the flute,
wearing a crest-ornament fashioned from peacock feathers, and decorated with wild flowers.
Resplendent with a beautiful garland resembling *kadamba* flowers,
possessing the loveliness of ten million Cupids, and with a shimmering, charming belly;
holding a flute with both hands and applying it to his mouth as he plays.
Hari had gone to Vṛndāvana, singing with divine melodies,
adorned by hundreds of maidens from heaven and other realms,
surrounded by herds of cows and calves, and graced by vast groves.
The omnipresent Lord, the sole teacher of the three worlds, was worshipped with lotus-petal-like glances and flowers of devotion by thousands of cowherd girls;
and likewise by Tumburu, Nārada, Hāhā, and Hūhū.
And the couple of Kinnaras, having likewise heard the song of Hari,
abandoned their instruments such as the lute; overcome with wonder,
they remained standing and singing praises of the Great-Souled One without ceasing.
Beheld with great wonder by Siddhas, Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Apsarases, birds, immobile beings, serpents, as well as Siddhas, Vidyādharas, monkeys, and humans.
Endowed with all auspicious marks and resplendent with beauty,
the infatuator of all the gopīs, the imperishable Lord of the worlds—
[he was praised] by the perfected Nārada and the wise Viśvāmitra.
By Parāśara, Vyāsa, Bhṛgu, Aṅgiras, Dakṣa, Sanaka and the others, by the Siddha Kapila, and by Vasiṣṭha, Vāgīśa, Hārīta, Yājñavalkya, Uśanas, and Kratu;
He was being praised by Mārkaṇḍeya, Bharadvāja, Pulastya, Pulaha, and others, as well as by eminent sages such as Vasiṣṭha, and by gods and demons who had gone to the world of Brahmā,
as well as by the Siddhas who had gone to the world of the Nāgas.
One should remember the All-pervading Lord being praised even by other foremost gods;
the practitioner who thus contemplates the imperishable Kṛṣṇa with his mind makes even the terrible ocean of worldly existence appear as small as the footprint of a calf.
[Thus ends the fourth chapter in the glorious Gaudapāda-mahātantra, the most excellent among all tantras. || 4 ||
Gautama said:
"O Brahmin, everything that has been spoken by you has been heard by me in its true essence. Now I ask: who here is authorized [to receive this]?"
Nārada said:
A servant of the guru attains eligibility for initiation;
likewise, among the twice-born, those who have not been initiated [attain eligibility] for their own duties, such as teaching and so forth.
Just as there is no entitlement here to the rites of twilight worship for those who have not been initiated,
so too there is no entitlement to the recitation of mantras, the practice of tantras, worship, and the like; therefore, one should make oneself consecrated by Śiva.
Therefore, for the sake of initiation, one should take refuge in an omniscient guru who is handsome,
pleasant-faced, pure, easy to approach, and well-versed in many tantras;
such a guru is considered to be free from doubt, a cutter of doubts, and independent.

One who has reached the further shore of knowledge regarding the Vedas, the Vedāṅgas, and the established doctrines of Vedānta; one who is devoted to the excellent service of Viṣṇu through speech, mind, body, and heart;
one who contemplates the Tantras of Viṣṇu and is a knower of the wisdom concerning Viṣṇu.

One who properly dedicates [the fruit] to Viṣṇu regarding the three types of sinful actions is considered by the wise to be truly well-restrained and one who has reached the further shore of knowledge regarding the meaning of mantras;
he is skilled in piercing the six cakras and has reached the further shore of knowledge regarding the six dhvajas.
One who discriminates between the aggregate, the word, form, and that which transcends form;
who knows the distinctions of the three junctions (saṃdhyās) and purifies the six paths (adhvan);
and who realizes the consciousness of mantra—such a person is declared a Guru by Svayambhū.

Salutations be to that Guru who is directly manifest; by whose command clay, ashes, wood, stone, and fruits become fruitful or fruitless. He is the knower of the distinctions of the five traditions (pañcāmnāya) and is capable of both restraint and grace.
The guru is the one who cuts through the disciple's doubts, and no other;
he is like another Cintāmaṇi jewel for the established doctrines of the Vaiṣṇava lineage.
Only one who belongs to an āśrama and is skilled in knowledge becomes a guru, and no other.

One who knows the meaning of mantra and tantra, the consciousness, and the movement of Kuṇḍalinī, and who understands the established conclusions of mantra according to the rules, is a Guru; no other is so. Even if he resides far away, one must go to him, just as the wise who know the tradition have declared.
These too should be praised, saluted, and served by one who desires his own welfare.
Such a teacher is to be known; otherwise, he brings suffering to the disciple.
The disciple should be of noble birth, pure in soul, and devoted to the goals of human existence (puruṣārtha).
One who is proficient in the studied Vedas, devoted to the welfare of his father and mother,
a knower of dharma and a performer of dharma, intent on service to his guru,
always knowing the true meaning of the scriptures, firm of body and firm of resolve.
Always seeking the welfare of living beings, he performs actions for the sake of the next world;
devoted to serving his guru with speech, mind, body,
and wealth, he abandons transient activities and is intent upon the performance of eternal duties.
One who has conquered the senses, conquered laziness, conquered delusion, and is free from envy;
who possesses devotion toward the sons of the guru and their wives just as toward the guru himself—
such a person should be a disciple, for any other brings suffering to the guru.
Within one year, a Brahmin endowed with all virtues becomes fit;
a Kṣatriya within two years, a Vaiśya within three years,
and a Śūdra within four years— thus has the fitness of a disciple been described.
When the disciple becomes worthy, then the true guru, out of compassion,
should perform the ritual of initiation perfectly with supreme grace.
The commencement of the mantra should take place in the month of Caitra, as it bestows all human goals.

In Vaiśākha there shall be the acquisition of jewels; in Jyeṣṭha, however, death is certain. In Āṣāḍha there shall be the loss of kinsmen; in Śrāvaṇa, one shall have a full lifespan. In Bhādrapada there shall be the destruction of offspring; in Āśvina, there shall be a collection of jewels.
In Kārttika, there shall be mastery of mantras; likewise, it shall be so in Mārgaśīrṣa.

In Pauṣa, however, there will be affliction from enemies; in Māgha, there is an increase in intelligence. In Phālguna, all desires shall be fulfilled; one should avoid the intercalary month (mala-māsa).

The consecration of mantras is commended on days when the five limbs are pure, during the rising of the moon and the sun, and specifically during the rising of Jupiter and Venus; it should be performed on Sundays,
Thursdays, Fridays, Mondays, as well as on Wednesdays and Fridays.
In the bright fortnight, initiation is auspicious; in the dark fortnight, it may be performed until the fifth day.
On the twelfth day, which is entirely pure and on an auspicious day, it should by all means be performed.
That twelfth day is dear to Kṛṣṇa, and it initiates the Kṛṣṇa-initiation.
The three Uttaras, Rohiṇī, Revatī,
and Puṣya; Dhaniṣṭhā, Vāyu (Svātī), Mitra (Anurādhā), Aśvinī, Pitrya (Maghā), Tvaṣṭṛ (Citrā), Nairṛta (Mūla), Aiśa (Jyeṣṭhā), Vaiṣṇava (Śravaṇa), and Hasta— these are auspicious for initiation.

One should perform the consecration with mantras under the asterisms of Āśvinī, Rohiṇī, Svātī, Viśākhā, and Hasta, as well as under the three Uttara asterisms and Kṛttikā. Initiation performed during all auspicious yogas bestows every kind of prosperity.
They say that auspicious *karana*s are favorable, especially during initiation (*dīkṣā*);

however, one should specifically avoid *śakuni* and the others, as well as *viṣṭi*. A *karaṇa* that is mobile (*cara*) is unfavorable in all respects, whereas one situated in fixed (*sthira*) zodiac signs bestows happiness.

The malefic planets situated in the third, sixth, and eleventh houses, and the benefic planets situated in the quadrants (kendras) and trines (trikoṇas), are auspicious for initiation (dīkṣā). All [planets] situated in the eighth house cause total destruction.
This applies to the disciple’s birth, the solar transits (saṃkrānti), the equinoxes (viṣuva), and likewise the solstices (ayana).
In other meritorious conjunctions, during the eclipses of the moon and sun,
or at a time favorable to the disciple, initiation brings all that is auspicious. At the times of a solar eclipse, there is nothing else more excellent.
In that place, whatever is performed shall all yield infinite fruit;
the accomplishment of the mantra occurs without effort, and not otherwise.
One should perform the consecration of the ground for as far as the sanctuary extends.
The ground that is white clay is proclaimed to be Brāhmaṇī;
the red clay is Kṣatriyā, and the yellow is proclaimed to be Vaiśyā;
the black ground is Śūdrā—thus it is proclaimed as fourfold.
The Brāhmī [lineage] brings success in all matters; the Kṣatriyā is considered to bestow sovereignty;
the Vaiśyā produces wealth and grain; but the Śūdrā, O Sage, is censured.
Thereafter, one who is expert in the knowledge of architecture should examine the ground.
One should perform the purification of the grain and the like, removing the husks, charcoal, and other such impurities;
for if this is not done, the practitioner shall obtain no fruit whatsoever. This should be preceded by the benedictions of Brahmins, the chanting of the Vedas, and auspicious rites.

One should construct the mandala of Vāstu according to the prescribed rules and as it appears beautiful. One should lay down a cord extending from east to west measuring one cubit. In its center, having marked a point, one should draw two fish-shaped figures on either side.
One should lay down a thread situated between those two, running from south to north.
Likewise, one should draw crocodiles (*makara*) in the corners using two [threads] each.
There, one should drop threads whose tips are situated in the middles of the fish.
There, it should be square, provided with four compartments,
extending from the northeast (Īśāna) to the southwest (Rākṣasa), and as far as the east (Prabhañjana);
thus, being composed, one should lay down two threads as the diagonal lines (karṇasūtra).
One should first honor a Brāhmaṇa in the four central squares; then, the most excellent practitioner, having invoked them, should worship in the four directions starting from the east:
Vivasvat, then Mitra, and immediately after Mahīdhara.
Furthermore, in the pairs of half-cells at the corners, one should place Vahni and the others around [the center]:
the wise man should place Sāvitra and Savitṛ, Śakra and Indrajaya,
Rudra and Rudrajaya, Āpa and Aparājita.
Then, at the two pairs of jackals on either side of the ear-threads, the preceptor should worship,
in sequence: Śarva, Guha, Ārpyamaṇa, Jātaka, Pilipicchaka, Carakī, Vidārī, and Pūtanā.
The best of preceptors should worship the eight deities in the directions starting from the east within the seven-and-a-half square grids,
according to the division of eight:
in order, Īśāna, Parjanya, Jaya, Indra, and Bhāskara.
Immediately [beyond], Vṛṣa and Antarikṣa are situated in the eastern direction;
Agni, Puṣan, Vitatha, Yama, and Gṛharakṣaka;
and Gandharva, Bhṛṅgarāja, and Mṛga are those belonging to the southern direction.
Nirṛti, Dhauvārika, Sugrīva, Varuṇa,
the two gods Puṣpadanta and Śoṣa, and Yoga are situated in the western direction;
as are Vāyu, Nāga, Kṛkara, Soma, and Bhallāṭa.
Those known as Akula, Ākhyoda, Iti, and Aditi are situated in the direction of Kubera;
having filled their feet with five-colored powders for the sake of the devotees and the gods,
one should then offer them an oblation of milk-rice (pāyasa).
One should worship all [the planets] with sweet milk-rice (pāyasa) combined with sweet substances;
or, for the pacification of the afflictions, the wise man should worship them with their respective materials.
One should offer incense consisting of milk-rice, parched grain (lāja), and the roots of the dūrvā grass.

O Brahman, accept this offering (bali) adorned with black gram rice (māṣabhakta) and other foods, though not yet joined with [other] grains; destroy the defects of the site (vāstu-doṣa). [Accept] the perfumes and other items, preceded by sugar and combined with milk-rice (pāyasa) on top.
O you named Āryyaka, accept this; destroy every defect!
O Vivasvat, accept this, which is honored with sandalwood and the like, and adorned with camphor and agallochum;
destroy every defect!

O Lord, accept this pleasing oblation consisting of milk-rice with jaggery, accompanied by flowers and other offerings; grant me perpetual peace. [I offer] rice mixed with black gram and meat, along with perfumes and other items combined with milk.
"Accept this [offering] and destroy all defects, O Upholder of the Earth!
Having thus worshipped in the center, one should offer the *bali* starting from the northeast (Īśāna),
consisting of milk mixed with sugar-candy and adorned with flowers and other offerings.
Accept this pleasing offering; grant me peace from calamities.
Accept this offering—this curd mixed with jaggery and well-consecrated with perfumes and other substances—and utterly destroy the obstacle that is my calf.

O Lord Savitṛ, accept these flowers and the like, the water with *kuśa* grass, the sugar, the heavy [substance], and the fragrant [incense]; grant me peace here. O Protector, accept this flour-cake with molasses, adorned with red perfumes and other offerings.
O Sūrya, accept this offering and destroy all obstacles here.
O Śakra-deva, accept this pleasing offering, along with sharp-edged weapons, flowers, and saffron and other substances; salutations to you.
"Accept this delightful offering of rice mixed with ghee and adorned with garments, perfumes, and the like; O Indra, be victorious! Homage to you!
Accept this meat, both cooked and raw, combined with garments, flowers, and other offerings."
Accept this pleasing offering, O God Rudra; salutations to you!
Accept this offering, O Rudra—consisting of meat cooked with ghee and combined with perfumes, flowers, and mountains; be victorious and grant me well-being.
O Rakṣas, accept this red flower along with meat; destroy this obstacle!
O Putana, accept this which is joined with bile, blood, and bone, and adorned with red perfumes and the like; destroy this obstacle!
O Śarva, accept this bali-offering consisting of meat and rice, adorned with garments, perfumes, and other ornaments; destroy this obstacle caused by the Rākṣasa!
[Accept] this offering combined with meat, flowers, and so forth, placed upon a base of black-gram rice.
Accept this offering, O Skanda; destroy the Rākṣasas and obstacles! Accept this arghya, consisting of meat, flour-mixtures, and cooked meat with water; destroy the Rākṣasas and obstacles!
O Rakṣasa, accept this blood, flesh, rice, fish, along with perfumes and incense; take this Jambhakatva and destroy all obstacles.
[I offer] unbroken rice with clarified butter, eyes, cloth, and perfumes, well-adorned.
"O Skanda, accept this offering; destroy the Rākṣasa obstacle!
This [offering] consists of meat together with flour-cakes, accompanied by cooked meat and water.
O Lord, accept this Arghya, which destroys the Rākṣasa obstacle and the defects of the Vāstu."
Accept this pleasing oblation, consisting of an *utpala* flower joined with betel-leaf and accompanied by garments and other offerings; salutations to you, O Bhāskara!
[I offer] a canopy of smoke-colored luster, beautifully adorned with perfumes and other articles.

Accept this offering (bali) endowed with the site-essence (vāstu); salutations to you immediately! And this, consisting of black gram rice (māṣabhakta), honored with garments, perfumes, and so forth—accept this bull-offering (vṛṣabali) and utterly destroy the defects of the site.
But take this tiger meat, together with offerings such as *naivedya*;
accept this pleasing *bali* and grant me peace from the sky (*vyomaśānti*).
[I offer] gold, flour-cakes, and garments, along with perfumes and other articles.
O Seven-Tongued One, accept this [oblation] mixed with clarified butter; salutations to you!
O God Pūṣan, accept this pleasing offering consisting of milk joined with parched grain (lājā), along with red flowers and other [ingredients]; salutations to you!
"O Soma, accept this offering endowed with the fragrance of curd and other qualities, accompanied by yellow flowers; destroy all defects!
[Accept] this rice mixed with ghee, accompanied by fragrances and flowers."
Accept this pleasing offering, O Bhallāṭaka; salutations to you!
Accept this pleasing offering—black gram rice smeared with ghee and adorned with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings—O you named Argala; salutations to you!

"Accept this delightful offering, O Goddess, Mother, consisting of sweetmeats mixed with honey and accompanied by garments, perfumes, and other articles; accept this milk combined with sugar and adorned with various flowers. Salutations to you!"
O Mother of the Daityas, accept this and destroy every defect!
O deities who are the guardians of the site (vāstudevatās) throughout heaven, the netherworld, and the middle realm, accept this pleasing offering; being satisfied, return to your own abodes.
The Mothers, the Bhūtas, the Vetālas, and others who desire offerings,
as well as those who are the attendants of Viṣṇu— they too should accept this offering.
Having given the offering to the ancestors and to the guardians of the field (Kṣetrapālas) according to one's desire, [one should proceed].
In its absence, one should worship with red threads, kusha grass, flowers, and so forth.
[Thus ends the fifth chapter in the Gautamīyatantra, the most excellent among all tantras. || 5 ||
Bowing down, one should draw that [line] so that it becomes a square of four compartments, exceedingly beautiful;
one should apply two diagonal threads and preserve the proportions by means of them.
The sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) should be square, endowed with all the required characteristics,
and practiced by Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras alike;
it is declared to accomplish all rites within the six types of ritual actions, beginning with pacification (śānti).
By this, the supreme mantra should generate all the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas);
thereafter, the practitioner (mantrī), knowing the ritual procedure, should dig the pit according to the scripture,
carefully avoiding the body and the head region of the serpent.

If the blow falls on the head, death occurs; if it falls on the body (piṇḍa), it results in the destruction of the sacrificial cakes (piṇḍa). If it falls on the tail, there arises suffering; if on the chest, it accomplishes all goals.
The depth of the excavation is said to be equal to the width of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
Leaving one finger-measure at the neck, there should indeed be three girdles;
according to the measurement of the pit in finger-units,
they should be four, three, and two fingers respectively, and in a square [pit], they should be square and very beautiful.
The fire-pan (agniyoni) for the Hotṛ priest should resemble the lower lip of an elephant;
it should possess a length of six and a width and height of four finger-breadths.
It should be six finger-breadths long and four finger-breadths wide.
The womb (yoni) should be elevated by two finger-breadths and marked with the [proper] characteristics;
from the base, there should be a stalk (nāla) with an opening in the middle of the womb.
This stalk is desired to have a fine tip, a thick root, and to be perforated.
One should fashion a cavity in the center of the *yoni*; that indeed is known as the *agrāhi*.
In the middle of the *kuṇḍa*, there should be a navel, either lotus-shaped or square;
it should be two finger-breadths high and four finger-breadths wide.

One should make the tip of the yoni half a finger-breadth in width and slightly downward-facing. In this manner, one should increase the dimensions by two [fingers] in other types of sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas).
The neck (kaṇṭha) there should be two fingers wide, and it should be increased according to the measurement of the pit.
From a square pit measuring one cubit,
one should construct a pit of two cubits according to the measurement of the diagonal cord; by this method, the dimensions should be increased in all pits everywhere.

The subtle *prakṛti* is indeed the *kuṇḍa*, characterized by all defining marks. Its two feet and two hands constitute the four corners; the belly is called the *kuṇḍa*, and the womb (*yoni*) is its causal form.
Therefore, let the offerings be deposited right there; then, being composed of that [deity], they properly yield fruit, whereas otherwise they become fruitless.
Having made it a perfect square, one should extend one-fifth of its total length forward from the centerline; then,
having drawn a cord from corner to corner, [one obtains] four parts.
Having established [the mark] at one part in the middle of the corner, one should then rotate it;
from the central thread to the center, one should then lay down a pair of threads. Measuring that distance up to the hip (hṛddhi), it will thus become shaped like a yoni.
When the field has been made square and likewise divided into four parts,
one should place one part in the east and one part in the west; then,
taking a cord in the middle, one should draw a circle from that measurement.
By means of the southern half, it should likewise be a beautiful half-moon.

On both sides of the lower thread of the square diagram, one should add three finger-breadths; above, one should add six finger-breadths. Then, one should lay down two threads equal in length to the central thread.
This triangular pit is declared to be facing eastward and bestows all that is desired.
Having conceptually divided the field into eight equal parts,
one should arrange each part on both sides of the center.
Having fixed a string in the middle, one should then rotate it from that measurement.
The circular pit (kuṇḍa) shall be exceedingly beautiful. Having divided the area of the five-cornered pit into seven parts,
one should place the tip of the cord outside that single part of the four-cornered [pit] and extend it as before.
From that measurement, one should rotate a circle and again form a square.

Having divided the circle into four parts and the square into five parts from the beginning, the wise practitioner should mark it fivefold; then, from each mark, [the lines] should be drawn by the expert.
Furthermore, one should properly strike five lines in sequence;
this shall be a five-cornered sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), which is here called the seven-angled one.
When the field has been divided into eight parts along the central line,
the wise one should increase each part by one in the four directions;
he should then place [the measurement] fourteen finger-breadths below and above according to that measure.
Just as there would be a middle [line] in the center, the cord should be thirty finger-breadths long;
from the marking of six lines there, a hexagon is produced.
Upon the highest rim of the previously described circular kuṇḍa,
one should draw sixteen very beautiful lotus petals;
this is known as the *abjakuṇḍa* by those who have reached the further shore of the Vedas and Vedāntas.
Now, regarding the seven-cornered pit (saptāsrakuṇḍa):
having divided the square [pit] into ten parts,
the preceptor should extend the central eastward line toward the east by one part on the exterior.
From that measurement, one should draw a circle and again a square;
having divided it into sixty-four parts, the wise man should mark the line seven times with twenty parts and three joined together.
From the mark to the next mark, one should drop seven long lines;
in this way, the pit (kuṇḍa), consisting of seven corners, becomes truly beautiful.
In a square and level field, having marked the corners,
the preceptor should take the central thread and demarcate half of the field.
Having fixed the thread in the center, the wise one should establish the half-measure toward the corner.

Then, one should increase by half the amount that exceeds [the side] at the corner toward the cardinal direction; the other [side] should likewise be increased by that same measure, so that an outer square is formed. From the measurement of twelve finger-breadths (aṅgulas) of this outer square—
One should cast the thread in the eight directions; this is the excellent eight-cornered sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
The sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) should be circular, square, or octagonal according to the teacher;
having thus prepared such pits on all sides.

The first girdle is said to be *sāttvika*, the second *rājasa*, and the third should be known as *tāmasa*; thus has the description of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) been stated. On the northern side of the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*), one should construct a hall extending from east to west.
One should construct the hidden foundation so that it is beautiful and captivating to the sight of all;
there, one should cast five lines extending from east to west,
and by erasing them at their respective centers, twelve squares are formed therein.
One should fill those squares with powders of five colors;
one should place the *pālikās*, the five principal ones, and the *sarāvas*,
numbering twelve, sixteen, eight, and twenty-four respectively.
One should fashion their faces with that same measure and their feet pointing upwards;
one should arrange them so they are spread out with mouths measuring three parts of a finger-breadth.
And those are the forms of Nārāyaṇa, Maheśāna, and Brahmā.
Then, the *pālikās*, the five-faced vessels (*pañcamukhī*), and the *sarāvaṇis*—
all these meritorious items having been cleansed with mantras—
are indeed to be completely encircled on all sides with threefold auspicious threads.
They are filled on all sides with soft sand and husks; having worshipped one's own deity, one should place the *pālikās* in sequence starting from the west,
containing *śyāmāka*, *priyaṅgu*, fruits, and mustard seeds.
Then, having washed mung beans, black gram, sesame, horse-gram,
and chickpeas with pure water,
they should indeed be worshipped with their respective deities and consecrated with the root mantra.
Then, let the Brahmins be led out together with the five kinds of sounds;
having sprinkled them with turmeric water and bowed down to them again and again,
one should thereafter cover them with a new garment.
Then, having sprinkled [the seeds] repeatedly with pure water every morning and evening,
one should cause them to remain or be sown for either seven nights or nine nights;
and at the end of the night, one should offer an oblation (bali) during the night.
On the first night, one should offer an oblation (bali) to the spirits (bhūtas) consisting of parched grain, sesame, beans, flour, and curd.
On the second night, one should cast an offering of sesame and rice to the ancestors (pitṛs).
On the third day, one should offer bali to the yakṣas with flour mixed with water and a sense of shame; on the fourth night, one should again offer bali to the nāgas,
consisting of charming flour-dust mixed with coconut water.

On the fifth day, one should offer a bali-oblation of lotus seeds along with unbroken rice grains to the Brāhmaṇas; then on the sixth day, one should likewise present food together with cakes to Bhaga;
and on the seventh day, one should distribute a bali-oblation of molasses-rice to Viṣṇu.
On the eighth day, one should offer an excellent bali to the Mātṛkās with goat meat, birds, fish,
and honey.
And on the ninth day, one should offer a bali of sesame-rice to Viṣṇu.
One's own name, preceded by the *praṇava* (Om) and ending in the dative case followed by *namaḥ*, should likewise be the mantra for the *bali* offering;
this applies equally to the invocation (*āvāhana*) and the dismissal (*visarjana*).
Furthermore, [the offerings] should be placed outside, all around the various leaves.
And one should diligently offer [oblations] to the world-protectors (lokapālas) in the eight directions. When those vessels have been joined, one should worship Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and Hara.
Vāyu and Agni, however, are dear to Mudga and Niṣāda, as well as to Kulaptyaka.
O Sage, Āvārakī is considered the deity of the *rakṣasas*; Śeṣa is likewise in Siddhāntaka;
Prāṇapati in Śālirāja; the god Vaivasvata in Tila;
Indra in Śyāma; and Varuṇa in Rājamāsa.
Having firmly tied a small portion of grain in a piece of cloth, one should cast it [into the water];
after two watches (yāmas) have passed, one should extract it and sow it.
Soma is the deity of seeds, for he is radiant during the night.
Therefore, having brought forth the seeds, one should sow them only at night;
once they have sprouted, one should never look upon them [with ordinary sight].
Only the preceptor or his disciple, by his command, may enter there.
One should indicate the auspicious or inauspicious results for the agent by means of the fully grown sprouts:
with dark or black sprouts, there is loss of wealth and suffering;
with copper-colored sprouts that have grown on the Brahman [portion], death occurs, without a doubt.
The preceptor, having carefully observed [the omens], should indeed cause [the rite] to be performed;
he should perform the propitiatory rite (śāntika) in every way for the sake of accomplishing the desires of the performer.
[Thus ends the sixth chapter in the glorious Gautamīya, the most excellent among great tantras. || 6 ||
Now I shall proclaim the initiation (dīkṣā) which brings about all accomplishments;
without which there would be no success even for a mantra after hundreds of years.
Its ancillary parts were previously described; now they are being told—listen.
"If I grant divine status, may the succession of sins be destroyed. Then the disciple, having bathed, being well-attired and endowed with all necessary materials,
should choose the preceptor with devotion, honoring him with garments, ornaments, and decorations.
One should perform the Nāndīmukha Śrāddha and satisfy the Brāhmaṇas; one should gratify one’s own preceptor with gifts of cows, land, gold, clothing, and so forth,
so that being satisfied and with a cheerful countenance, he may impart the mantra.
Now, in this context, I shall describe the preliminary rites which,
when performed, lead to eligibility for the practice of mantras, yantras, worship, and so forth;
without which there can be no accomplishment and one will instead incur hell.
Having risen during the *muhūrta* of Brahmā, one should meditate upon the Guru and the Deity within one's own head,
in the thousand-petaled lotus known as Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Father,
who resembles ten thousand moons and whose hands shine with the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.

One should meditate with the intellect upon the Supreme Guru— known as Kṛṣṇa, the imperishable— who wears white garments, is adorned with white garlands and unguents, is joined by his many Śaktis on his left thigh, and who has been elevated into unity with Śiva.
Having gratified [the deity] mentally with mental offerings, the wise one,
having praised him with hymns, should bow down and worship the Lord of Mantras.
With the collyrium-stick of knowledge, for one blinded by the darkness of ignorance—
Salutation to that one's own guru by whom the eye was opened;
salutation to that one's own guru who revealed that state which is of the nature of an unbroken circle and by whom the moving and the unmoving are pervaded.
In the Mūlādhāra, known as the triangle and possessing a splendor equal to ten million suns,
one should meditate upon the eternal Kuṇḍalinī, situated above the seed-syllable of desire (Kāma-bīja),
dark-hued, subtle, and the essence of the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the universe.
One should meditate upon her who transcends the universe, whose form is knowledge, and who flows upwards; having pierced through the six wheels and brought her to the supreme Śiva,
one should, with an undisturbed mind, remember her as having attained union with Him.
Having first brought [the nectar] to the *sudhā* [cakra], one should flood the *śākta-maṇḍala*. By that very same sequence of cakras, one should conclude at the *mūlādhāra*.
Through this yoga of meditation, mantras are perfected; not otherwise.
Those who stand on the side of the enemy, those who are old yet arrogant with youth,
and those who are corrupted by other servants— these indeed attain success and not otherwise.
One should contemplate one's own self as being identical with the other, known as Kṛṣṇa.
I am Kṛṣṇa and none other; I am Brahman alone, not subject to sorrow. I am of the nature of existence, consciousness, and bliss; I am eternally liberated and possessed of my own inherent nature.
You are indeed I, and I am you; you are one whose body is pure existence and consciousness.
O Kṛṣṇa, by the power of Your command, the interval between us two has vanished;
I have crossed over the terrible ocean of worldly existence, and indeed I have no further task remaining.
Nevertheless, O Lord, grant me Your command so that I may serve You.

"I know what is Dharma, yet I have no inclination toward it; I know what is Adharma, yet I have no aversion toward it—this is because You, O Hṛṣīkeśa, reside within my heart. Having thus prayed in his mind, he should perform the morning rites according to the rules for one who is initiated (*dīkṣita*), as well as for those living as celibate students (*brahmacārin*) or forest-dwellers (*vānaprastha*). For those observing purity and other such duties, the performance of the rites is twofold; however, for those performing the *sandhyā* prayers, the duty becomes specifically fourfold.
Having performed the ritual of *ācamana* and being seated in a clean place,
the practitioner who serves his guru should likewise perform the morning *saṃdhyā*.
