Having worshipped the sacred waters (*tīrthas*) three times in the water with the root mantra (*mūlamantra*), he should proceed.

Having cast [the water] upon the ground with the tip of a blade of *kuśa* grass, one should sprinkle it seven times upon the head. Holding water in the left hand, one should consecrate it with the mantra while using the right;
then, having thrown that [water] again with the left, one should sprinkle the head in two directions.
And by means of the instruction of the Guru and the divine designation of the Mudrā,
having drawn that water through the Iḍā and washed away the internal impurities once more,
one should sprinkle it upon the Vajra-stone situated on the right side.
One should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) again according to the rules with the Astra-mantra;
for this is indeed the "Today's Expiation" (adyamarṣaṇa), which cuts asunder all sins.
Then, having again cast a handful of water toward the center of the solar disc—
One should meditate upon the goddess Gāyatrī, who is seated upon the sun;
one should remember her as resembling the sun, holding a book and a rosary in her hands,
clad in black antelope skin, the Brāhmī goddess, the supreme mistress of the stars.
Having risen, one should recite the Gāyatrī of Kṛṣṇa one hundred times, which is non-different from that [original Gāyatrī]. It is proclaimed as follows:
"We know Kṛṣṇa; we meditate upon Dāmodara; may that Viṣṇu inspire us. This is declared to be the Gāyatrī of Kṛṣṇa. Therefore, "we know Kṛṣṇa" and "upon Dāmodara... [is the mantra].
We meditate upon Him; may that Viṣṇu inspire us.
She consists of all the gods, she is the purifier of all, and the bestower of boons.
There is also a reading: "She consists of all the Vedas."

That which begins with *praṇava* (oṃ) bestows liberation; that which begins with the *śrībīja* (śrīṃ) grants enjoyment; that which begins with *hṛllekhā* (hrīṃ) brings about the great *siddhis*; and that which begins with *vāgbhava* (aiṃ) makes all beings submissive. That which begins with *kāma* (klīṃ) delights the people.
Thus have the *sandhyā-mantras* been described to you for the attainment of the fruits of mantra.
If one should fail to perform [the rites] out of delusion, one would not obtain the fruit of initiation.
Alternatively, if due to incapacity, the practitioner of mantra (mantrī) should perform a concise twilight worship (saṃkṣepasandhyā);
having meditated upon Kṛṣṇa in the evening, morning, and at midday, he should recite the mantra.

Thus the three twilight prayers (sandhyās) have been declared, which bestow success upon ritual actions. If the twilight prayer is missed, or if it has been omitted, one should recite the Gāyatrī ten times.
One should perform this according to one's vitality and according to one's knowledge, remaining unwearied.
Whatever rite is intended for the sake of auspiciousness, one should perform it accordingly;
one should gaze upon a mirror, touch clarified butter, and look at collyrium.
For the sake of nourishing those whom I support, one should contemplate security and well-being.
One should bathe in pure water, such as that of a river, for the sake of worshipping Kṛṣṇa.
Worship is said to be fivefold; hear from me their distinctions:
*abhigamana*, *upādāna*, *yoga*, and *svādhyāya*.
I shall now describe in sequence the fivefold worship known as *ijyā*.
Among these, *abhigamana* consists of the sweeping of the deity’s abode,
its smearing with unguents, and the removal of faded floral offerings (*nirmālya*).
"Upādāna" means the gathering of perfumes, flowers, and so forth;
"ijyā" is, in its true sense, the worship of one's chosen deity;
and "svādhyāya" is the recitation of the Self, beginning with the name Kṛṣṇa, in due order.

The recitation of hymns, praises, and the like, as well as the chanting of the names of Hari, and the study of scriptures such as those concerning the ultimate reality (tattva), are proclaimed to be *svādhyāya*. Yoga is defined as the contemplation of one's own deity through one's own self.
Thus, O observer of noble vows, the fivefold mode of worship has been described to you;
it bestows, respectively, the fruits of proximity (sāmīpya), similarity of form (sārūpya), likeness (sādṛśya), and union (sāyujya).
At either morning or midday, one should resort to a sacred bathing place for the purpose of ritual ablution.

Bathing is said to be of two kinds, distinguished as internal and external. [One should meditate upon] Vāsudeva, who resembles infinite suns, four-armed, bearing the conch, discus, mace, and lotus, wearing a crown and a garland of forest flowers.

With that stream born from the water of His feet, one should constantly wash one's own body; by that, one should cleanse all impurity situated within the interior of the body. At that very moment, the internal garment becomes free of dust, surpassing hundreds of millions of sacred bathing places.
This most wonderful bath for yogis has indeed been described;
one who knows the ritual procedure should likewise perform the external bath according to the scriptures,
practicing the bath that cleanses impurities as prescribed in one's own Vedic branch.
Then, for the sake of accomplishing all rites, one should perform the mantra-bath;
having sprinkled the water with the Astra-mantra, one should divide it into three parts:
casting one portion into the water while reciting the Astra-mantra, and [placing the other two] upon the two feet.

Reciting the root mantra from the beginning to the end once, one should smear [the forehead] starting from the head; likewise, reciting the remainder from the beginning to the end, one should smear [the body] starting from the feet.
"O Gaṅgā, O Yamunā, O Godāvarī, O Sarasvatī!"
O Narmadā, Sindhu, and Kāverī, establish your presence in these waters!
O beautiful Goddess, I invoke you here for the purpose of bathing. Come, O Gaṅgā, salutations to you who are endowed with all sacred fords (tīrthas)!

Having thus invoked [the deity] according to the rule, one should consecrate it with the root mantra. Having addressed [it], one should join it with water, contemplate the orbs of the Moon, Sun, and Fire within that [water], and the practitioner, reciting the root mantra, should immerse himself in its midst.
Having risen and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), he should thereafter perform the six-limbed placement (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa).
He should sprinkle himself ten times with the mudrā known as the "water-pot" (kalaśamudrā),
or alternatively, he should consecrate himself seven times with waters empowered by the mantra.
Forming a fist with the left hand, one should encircle it with the right;
this is the auspicious mudrā called Kalasa, which removes all sins.
[One should offer] water from a Śālagrāma stone mixed with Tulasī leaves.
Having placed [the water] in a conch shell and whirling it three times, one should pour it over the head of the devotee.
He who, without drinking the water from the Śālagrāma stone, merely pours it upon his own head,
is declared to be a slayer of a Brāhmaṇa.

One should first drink the water from the feet of Viṣṇu, and then the water from the feet of a Brahmin; by practicing what is contrary [to this] out of delusion, one is called a destroyer of the self. Whatever holy places exist on earth, all those holy places are present in the ocean.
"Whatever holy places exist in the ocean are contained within the footprint of the Brahmin on the right;
the excellent oceans and holy places are within the footprint of the Brahmin on the right"—
thus is the reading.
Then, in brief, he should satiate the gods, humans, and ancestors.
Having squeezed out the water from his garment, washed it, and sipped water while remaining silent,
he should put on two pure garments as an undergarment and an upper cloth.
When the similar white [thread] has been cut, one should sip water while seated upon a seat;
having made an upright *puṇḍra* mark with sandalwood paste, one should perform the twilight devotion (*saṃdhyā*).
The twilight devotion previously described should be performed, and with a concentrated mind, one should meditate upon the Goddess.
Having meditated upon the Goddess, who is dark-complexioned, four-armed, with hands shining with the conch and discus,
holding a mace and a lotus, and seated upon a solar throne,
one should offer a handful of water and perform the libation (tarpaṇa) for the destruction of worms.
Having first gratified the lineage of gurus, one should gratify one’s chosen deity;
then one should daily gratify Nārada, Parvata, Jiṣṇu, Niśaṭha, Udbhava, Dāruka, Viśvakasena, Śaileya, and the gurus.
Whether numbering twenty-five, or tenfold, or even in other ways.

Having fully recited the root mantra, "I satisfy Śrī Kṛṣṇa," this mantra ending in "namaḥ" is declared by those intent on the ritual for libation (tarpaṇa). At sunset, one should recite: *klīṃ śrīkṛṣṇaṃ tarpayāmi namaḥ*. Then the ascetic should meditate upon the boon-granting Goddess Gāyatrī.
Meditating upon Gāyatrī— white in complexion, clad in white garments,
seated upon the bull, presiding over the eyes, bestowing boons, and holding a noose, a trident, and a human skull-cup,
and stationed in the midst of the solar orb— one should practice her recitation.
A mace should be depicted on the forehead, and likewise a bow and arrow on the head;
Nandaka [the sword] in the middle of the heart, and the conch and discus on the two arms.
Even if a Brahmin marked with the conch and discus dies in a cremation ground, [he attains liberation].
O Gautama, the destination that is proclaimed for Prayāga is his destination as well.
Having taken water for the purpose of worship, he should unite the sacred waters with the Sun,
while mentally recollecting Viṣṇu, who consists of the light of Brahman, and the Gāyatrī.
One should recite that [mantra] one hundred times for the attainment of dharma, kāma, and artha;
all sins are destroyed and knowledge arises before long.
Recalling the root mantra in the heart, one should indeed protect the sacrificial pavilion.

Having washed his hands and feet and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), the wise ascetic, being initiated for a special purpose, should then perform the worship of the Sun while remaining silent. Having again washed his hands and feet according to the prescribed rule, the ascetic—
Thereafter, one should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), especially according to the Vaiṣṇava tradition:
having drunk [water] with the three [mantras] beginning with Keśava, one should wash the hands with two;
having wiped the lips with two, one should then cleanse the mouth with two.
Having washed both hands with one [portion of water] and likewise the feet with another, he should sprinkle his head with the third; then, with the [mantras of] Saṃkarṣaṇa and the others,
[he should sprinkle] the mouth, nose, eyes, ears, navel, belly, and arms.
Having performed the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*) in this manner, one becomes Nārāyaṇa himself.
Keśava and the others were mentioned previously; now I shall describe Saṃkarṣaṇa and the rest:
Saṃkarṣaṇa, Vāsudeva, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha.
Puruṣottama, Adhokṣaja, Nṛsiṃha, as well as Acyuta,
Janārdana, Upendra, Hari, and Viṣṇu— these twelve are proclaimed.
[Thus ends the seventh chapter in the glorious Gautamīyatantra, the most excellent among all tantras. || 7 ||
Now, the twelvefold purification of the Vaiṣṇavas is described here:
approaching the temple, following after Hari,
circumambulating with devotion, and again, the cleansing of the feet.
The lifting up of leaves and flowers for the purpose of worship with devotion alone is considered the most distinguished purification of the hands among all purifications;
therein lies the chanting of the Name and the celebration of the Lord's qualities as well.
Through devotion to the Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the purification of speech is desired; likewise,
listening to His stories and witnessing His festivals are said here to be the complete purification of the ears and the eyes.

O Gautama, the wearing of the water used for washing the feet (pādodaka) and even the wearing of garlands is declared to be the purification of the head; furthermore, O Hari, [this applies to] prostration,
as well as the smelling of fragrant flowers and other offerings from the remains of worship (nirmālya).
Purification shall belong to Ananta; it is likewise ordained for the sense of smell.
Whatever leaves, flowers, and so forth are offered at the pair of Kṛṣṇa’s feet, that alone is purifying in the world; it shall cleanse everything.
Then one should meditate upon Vṛndāvana by the very path previously described;
in its center, one should meditate upon the golden ground and then upon the ninefold abode (navagṛha).
Then, having gone to the eastern gate, one should purify the general water offering (sāmānyārghya).
Having washed the conch with the Astra-mantra, one should fill it with the Kṛṣṇa-mantra;
one should consecrate it with the Praṇava alone—this is remembered as the general rule.
There, at the entrance, one should worship Āvāhya for the pacification of all obstacles.
Nanda, Sunanda, Caṇḍa, Pracaṇḍa, Bala, Prabala,
the one named Bhadra, and Subhadra are the Vaiṣṇava Vighnas;
two Vighnas are stationed at each door, and Vinatāsuta is in front.
One should worship with the name-mantra beginning with *praṇava* (Om) and ending with *namaḥ*.
Then, taking unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*) in the right hand with the *nārāca-mudrā*,
one should scatter them within the house with the weapon-mantra (*astra-mantra*) for the pacification of obstacles.
May those beings depart who reside upon the earth;
may those beings who create obstacles perish by the command of Śiva.
Having invoked the hosts of beings, [he should step] with the right foot foremost.
One should meditate here within the interior of the house, entering with the neck slightly bowed;
one should worship Brahmā right there for the pacification of defects in the site (vāstu).
Facing the east and with a restrained mind, one should sit upon the prescribed seat.
Likewise, the practitioner should sit on a seat of clay, or one covered with cloth, skins, or *kuśa* grass.
If one sits on a wooden seat, disease will arise; on a bamboo seat, there will be the destruction of one's lineage.
On a stone seat, there is obstruction of speech; on a seat of leaves, there is confusion of the mind.
On the earth there arises suffering, and in the royal [quarter] there shall be oppression.
Viṣṇu is the self whose nature is Time; therefore, he should face the east. One should place perfumes, flowers, leaves, and so forth on one’s own right side.
One should place a lamp, an offering (bali), and food oblation (naivedya) before [the deity], along with camphor. To the left, one should set a beautiful jar filled with well-scented water.
Behind, one should set a single vessel for washing the hands.
Having entered according to the prescribed rule, one should assume either the lotus posture (padmāsana) or the auspicious posture (svastika). Placing both soles of the feet properly upon the thighs—
this is declared to be the lotus posture, which is dear to the hearts of yogins.

Placing both soles of the feet properly between the knees and with the body straight, the yogin should enter [the posture]; that is called Svastika. One should place vessels containing auspicious sprouts in the four directions.
Having received the benedictions of the twice-born, one should commence the Vaiṣṇava sacrifice.
And the disciple, intent on devotion, should choose a preceptor with devotion,
free from stinginess regarding wealth, by offering garments, ornaments, and riches.
There, one should choose fifteen, ten, or three officiating priests (ṛtvij).
Having caused the proclamation of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) to be made, preceded by the five sounds,
one should then perform the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) for the sake of the complete purity of all purposes.
Having become one with palms joined in reverence, one should worship the three Gurus on the left:
the Guru, the Paramādi, and likewise the Parāparaguru.
On the right side, one should worship Gaṇeśa, and one should visualize the Lord upon the head.

Then, having sat down according to the rule upon a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) in the middle of the pavilion, which has been smeared with cow-dung and water, one should cause a thread to be laid across its center,
with its ends pointing east and west, accompanied by the recitation of blessings by Brahmins.
Having multiplied [the measurement], one should lay out the fish-mark starting from the center.
One should then place a thread situated in the middle of that, with its ends pointing south and north. Then, from the center, one should mark out a space measuring one cubit in each direction.
In the sacrificial enclosures (*satras*), another person should place crocodiles or fish;
from the tips of the threads, he should place fish in the corners.
One should drop threads in the cardinal directions so that their tips rest upon the fish situated in the corners.

From that, one should fashion a four-cornered, square mandala. Therein, one should cast the thread from the southeast to the northwest, and from the southwest to the northeast; likewise, the tips of the threads should extend toward the east, south, west, and north.
One should lay down four lines, beginning with the eastern line and the central thread;
these shall constitute the "made-hands. Fishes shall appear in the corner cells. One should then draw the lines toward the east and west, as well as toward the south and north.
When there are fifty-six additional squares beyond two hundred,
then the wise man should divide the squares in sequence:
in the center, with sixteen squares, there is a lotus measuring three circles.

With forty-eight squares, it should be adorned with lamps; with twelve hundred squares, there are those called "ornaments" (*śobhā*) consisting of four squares each. There should be ornaments of four squares, and the corner should consist of six squares.
Alternatively, one who is skilled in the traditional methods should draw four lines in the center—
east, south, west, and north— and that shall become the mandala of the zodiac signs.
[One should then mark] the pericarp, the filaments, and the half-petals of each petal.

One should clearly designate the circular and square locations for the petals, the tips of the petals, the circles, the squares, the rows, and the two beauties (the side-ornaments). The central mark of the mandala should be one cubit and four finger-breadths.
The filaments should be two finger-breadths (aṅgula) long, and their tips four finger-breadths.
Likewise, according to the measurement of the petals, their tips should not be less than two finger-breadths.
It is said that the interval between each of the three circles should be two finger-breadths.
Then, there should be a zodiacal wheel (rāśicakra) adorned with its respective colors.
To the left, one should construct a mandala measuring either six or eight [units];
this is indeed thirty-two finger-breadths (aṅgulas), or even more than that, as desired.
Some authorities maintain that the zodiacal circle is circular, while those who know it well say it is square; or else, the twelve signs may even be circular,
resembling an ant’s waist or like a citron fruit.
If the circle and the square consist of three and twelve divisions respectively,
they should be made resembling lotus petals, as described by the wise;
outside of that, one should fashion four beautiful wish-fulfilling trees.
It was filled with water-born and land-born flowers pleasing to the mind, and its spreading branches were perched upon by swans,
cranes, kāraṇḍava ducks, parrots, bees, cuckoos, peacocks,
ruddy geese, and other birds.
In all [the directions], one should place those which cause cessation and are pleasing to the eye; outside of that, one who knows the reality should construct an earthly mandala with black corners,
and he should likewise have the zodiacal signs (rāśis) made as mandalas.
If one were to fashion another mandala here using a different list of names,
and having invoked the deities therein, were to worship other deities instead—
then that practitioner of mantra, being of fickle intellect, would obtain the fruit of both.
If one who considers himself wise fails to understand the pervasion of the zodiacal signs by the God whose nature is Time,
everything he performs will be in vain due to his disregard for the sacred command;
therefore, with every effort, [one should meditate] upon all the signs in their proper order together with their presiding deities.
Having understood the appropriate mandalas and being single-minded,
one should proceed to worship or offer oblations to all the deities.
The colored powders (rajas) consist of five colors and are composed of five substances.
On this earth, these [substances] are yellow, white, reddish, dark, and black;
likewise, haridra is yellow, while tāṇḍūla is white. Furthermore, when combined with alkali (vakṣāra), it is said to be red, which leads to defects.
The wise practitioner should draw the boundary line with white powder, using charcoal from burnt grain husks, black soil, and so forth;
it should have a thickness and width of one finger-breadth, which is recommended for all ritual activities.
The pericarp (karṇikā) should be yellow, and the filaments (keśara) white, yellow, and red;
one should fill the space between the petals of the lotus with dark powder. Three circles are said to be made with white, red, and black colors.
The pathways should be variegated with various colors and diverse forms;
the primary and secondary door-decorations should be white, red, and yellow.
The corners remaining from the circle of the zodiac should indeed extend toward the intermediate directions.
The feet of the pedestal should be either black or reddish;
likewise, the petals should be reddish, while the joints between the petals are black. Others, however, state that both the black and the reddish parts are produced by the *rajas* quality.
[Thus ends the eighth chapter in the glorious Gaudapādīya Mahātantra, the most excellent among all tantras. || 8 ||
One should purify that house and the maṇḍala with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
One pala of milk is prescribed as the portion, and the cow urine is desired to be of the same measure. The ghee should be one pala, and the cow dung two tolakas.
The curd should be the measure of one handful; this is remembered as the *pañcagavya*.
Alternatively, equal portions of the five products of the cow are prescribed.
Having consecrated it with the root mantra, one should purify it with the tip of a *kuśa* blade.
By that, there shall be complete purification and the eradication of all sins.
Even after committing great transgressions, if one drinks the products of the cow (*gavya*),
those who know the Vedas declare that it destroys them by the mere act of drinking.
Thereafter, one should perform the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) by which one may obtain the full fruit.
Having uttered "Oṃ namaḥ sudarśanāya," the preceptor,
being composed, should perform three claps (tāla), each higher than the last.
The wise practitioner should perform the binding of the directions with ten snaps of the fingers;
then he should contemplate that the splendor generated by that very act shall provide protection.
Placing his hands palms-upward upon his lap, he should meditate.
Having raised the Śakti by means of the syllable *Hūṃ*, one should contemplate her as established in her own support:
the Mūlādhāra, the Svādhiṣṭhāna, the Maṇipūraka,
the Anāhata, the Viśuddha, and the Ājñā-cakra.
One should recollect the mantra in sequence at the anus, the base of the penis, the navel, the heart,
the throat, and likewise between the eyebrows.
One should then contemplate the foundational support as a four-petaled golden lotus.

In the center of that, one should contemplate the Yoni, possessing the brilliance of the moon, sun, and fire. Within that, the practitioner, composed in meditation, should contemplate the individual soul (jīvātman),
resembling the hibiscus and bandhūka flowers, like ten million lightning flashes, and as cooling as ten million moons.
The preceptor should likewise join [the soul], which has the form of a lamp-flame and resides on the seat of Kuṇḍalinī,
with the Supreme Self at the station of Śiva in the Sahasrāra, by means of the path of the Suṣumṇā and the mantra "So'ham."
In the same manner, the sequence of dissolution for the five gross elements is likewise.
Furthermore, [the faculties of] speech, feet, hands, anus, and genitals; as well as speaking, grasping, movement, excretion, and pleasure; and again, hearing, touch, sight, and taste.
The nose, sound, touch, form, taste, and smell—
these are the twenty-five principles (tattvas), which one should join with the Puruṣa.
One should likewise join ego (ahaṃkāra), mind (manas), intellect (buddhi), and consciousness (citta) to that very same [Puruṣa].

One should contemplate that all [elements] are dissolved into the state of the individual soul (jīva). Then, the wise one should fill the vital air through the left nostril (iḍā) with sixteen measures (mātrās), using the seed-syllable of Vāyu, which is smoke-colored (dhūmravarṇa) and marked with six dots (bindus).
One should fill [the breath] through the *suṣumṇā* with sixty-four measures;
the practitioner of mantra should exhale through the path of the *piṅgalā* with thirty-two measures.
One should fill [it] again by this same [path], while contemplating the blue wind.
The seed-syllable of fire is red in color, triangular in shape, and marked with a svastika. By means of that, through the practice of inhalation (pūraka) with sixteen counts,
and by holding the breath (kumbhaka) for sixty-four counts, one should burn it away.
On the left side stands the personification of sin, blazing with radiance;
he has the murder of a Brahmin for his head, the theft of gold for his two arms,
the drinking of intoxicants for his heart, and violating the teacher’s bed for his two hips.

One should meditate upon that cruel being, angry, holding a sword and shield, with blood-red hair, beard, and eyes, whose pair of feet are associated with that [demon], whose limbs and minor members are the great sins (pātaka), whose body hairs are the secondary sins (upapātaka), and who is situated within the belly.
One should burn it with the fire arisen from the *mūlādhāra*.
Having thus burned it all around for thirty-two *mātrās*,
the practitioner of mantra should exhale it along with the ashes through the path of the *piṅgalā*.
In the left channel (vāmanāḍī), one should join the lunar seed-syllable (candrabīja), which possesses a luster like that of the kunda flower and the moon,
with the seed-syllable of the crescent moon;
then, by means of the suṣumnā, one should [join] the lunar seed-syllable for sixty-four measures (mātrā).
Having meditated upon a rain consisting of the dead, appearing in the form of fifty syllables,
and having thus contemplated the body with the mind through the path of the Kula,
the practitioner of mantra should firmly lead [the consciousness] by means of the seed-syllable *laṃ* for thirty-two measures.
Then, having brought the *jīva* and the *tattvas* back by that same path to their own place with the *haṃsa-mantra*, one should establish them in their respective locations.
Having thus performed the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*), one should perform the ritual placement of the *mātṛkās* (*mātṛkānyāsa*).
Gautama said:
"O Brahmin, tell me, by means of the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi), whose purification is produced?
It is not that of the Self; rather, it is said to be the cause of all purifications."
There is no eternal oneness of the individual soul with Brahman;
nor is the eternity of the body asserted from its very inception. Consider this: to what could such eternity belong—neither to the mind nor to the intellect? Perform your investigation!
"Cut through such doubts, for you are remembered as equal to Brahmā.
Nārada said:
"That which is the purification of beings who have assumed the form of bodies—"
This purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) is considered to arise from union with the imperishable Brahman.
Within the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), the light-self (jyotirātman) manifests;
yogis who know the reality call that the subtle body (liṅgadeha).
By the mere purification of that [element], the purification of all things arises;
that alone is the cause of the birth of the universe and the cause of individual birth.
Upon separation from it, death occurs; otherwise, there is no liberation even through millions of births.
Thus has everything been declared regarding the attainment of the goals of human life in this scripture.
One should destroy [the impurities] through the practice of yoga and the like, and by the practice of mantra.
Having performed the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi), the best of teachers becomes fit for his task.
One should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) and the armor (sannāha) of the body in due order.
O Lord of the Mātṛkā-cakra, that [placement] begins with the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi).
Likewise, one should perform the placement of the principles (tattvanyāsa), and after that, the breath control (prāṇāyāma).
The soul (jīva) can never be identical with Brahman;
nor can the body, from its very inception, be said to possess permanence.
Furthermore, whose vision could it be—of the mind or of the intellect? O descendant of Kuru, consider this.
"Cut through such doubts, for you are remembered as equal to Brahmā.
Nārada said:
"Having performed the placement of the syllables (varṇanyāsa) in that manner, one should likewise perform the placement of the ten tattvas."
Thus has been declared the compendium of the sequence known as the Viṣṇu-pañjara.
One should then perform the placement of the arghya offering correctly and in due order:
one should visualize a square mandala in front of one's left side.
Having worshipped that support with flowers, the practitioner of mantra should install it;
"Maṃ, obeisance to the fire-maṇḍala"—this is the mantra prescribed for it. There, within that very circle, one should worship the ten kalās of fire.
In that very place, one should worship the twelve Kalās in a circular form:
having uttered "kaṃ bhaṃ" for Tāpinī, and likewise "khaṃ vaṃ" for Tāpinikā;
then, having pronounced "gaṃ phaṃ," one should worship Dhāriṇī and Dhūmrā.

Having worshipped Dyaṃ Paṃ Marīci, as well as Ṅaṃ Neṃ Jvalinikā, the Guru should worship Caṃ Dhaṃ Ruci and Chaṃ Daṃ Suṣumnā. The practitioner of mantra (maṃtrī) should worship Jaṃ Thaṃ Bhogadā with flowers and unbroken rice grains (akṣata).
Having worshipped Jhaṃ Taṃ as Viśvā, one should place Aṃ Ṇaṃ as Bodhinī;
likewise, one should worship Ṭhaṃ Ṭaṃ as Dhāriṇī and Ṭhaṃ Ḍaṃ as Kṣamā,
using the mantra "Namo" [annenaiva] accompanied by the dative case ending.
Having thus duly worshipped the syllables *śaṃ* and *khaṃ*, which are the wealth-bestowing feet of the Sun of Kalās,
and having recited the Mātṛkā in reverse order as well as his own chosen mantra, the wise practitioner should fill that very sacred site (*tīrtha*) with pure water.
One should worship the Moon there with the mantra *Uṃ* alone:
Amṛtā, Mānadā, Pūṣā, Puṣṭi, Puṣṭiratī,
Dhṛti, Śaśinī, Candrikā, Kānti, Jyotsnā, Śrī, Prīti, and Vṛddhidā.

One should worship with the sixteen-syllable mantra ending in "namaḥ," namely: *pūrṇā*, *apūrṇā*, and *amṛtā*. Therein, one should scatter auspicious unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*) along with *dūrvā* grass.

Covering [the face] with the left hand, one should recite the root mantra ten times over the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) from the right hand; then, one should place the Gālinī mudrā on the crest-lock (śikhā). Extending both hands and joining them together in the manner of a hollowed casket (saṃpuṭa), according to the prescribed sequence—
Having engaged the right thumb with the left little finger,
and the right thumb with the left [hand], this mudrā is considered Gālinī;
it is declared to bestow the fruit of the *argha* offering when moved over the top of the conch.

Having worshipped [the deity] named Kṛṣṇa with perfumes and other offerings, the yogin should perform the recitation (japa) while united with the light [of the deity]. Having well protected [the vessel] with the weapon-mantra (astra) and others, he should display the cow-seal (dhenu-mudrā).
To its right, however, he should place a conch, or one made of copper, or likewise one made of earth.
Then, having set down a single vessel, one should likewise fill it with water;
O brahmin sage, a copper vessel is considered dear to Viṣṇu’s pleasure,
and likewise, the conch is proclaimed to be the foremost among all vessels.
Likewise, an earthen vessel, or one of gold or silver, is prescribed;
these five vessels for Hari must be pure, and no other should be employed therein.
By that nectar, everything everywhere becomes fluid and composed of mantra.
Then, with perfumes and other offerings, the mantra-practitioner should assign the seats (pīṭhas) upon the body using fragrant unbroken rice, flowers, and pure, blazing lamps.
Having thus worshipped the seat, he should meditate upon the deity who is one with the mantra.
From the base to the aperture of Brahma (brahmarandhra), one should contemplate the threefold Kuṇḍalinī, whose nature is like a thread of poison;
likewise, there the seed-syllable (bījākṣara) is threefold.
One should place the fourth Kuṇḍalinī at the crown of the head and Vāsudeva as the fourth.
One should meditate on the syllable Oṃ at the root-center as liquid and resembling molten gold;
likewise, from the root up to the heart, one should meditate on the fire-cuṇḍalinī.
And in the heart, one should meditate on the Kāma-bīja, possessing a radiance equal to ten thousand suns.
There, the wise and undisturbed practitioner should meditate upon Sūryakuṇḍalinī, whose radiance is equal to ten million suns, extending from the heart up to the *kula* [the crown of the head].
From the center of the eyebrows to the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*), one should meditate on Māyā, possessing the luster of the moon joined with lightning.

In the same way, one should meditate upon Candra-kuṇḍalinī, whose form consists of the nectar of one's own Veda; and within the Bindu, one should remember Vāsudeva, who consists of Bindu and Nāda, who is the fourth state (turīya),
unconditioned by space or time, and composed of all splendor.
In that same way, having meditated upon the fourth Kuṇḍalinī as consisting solely of the form of pure knowledge,
the Guru should then mentally contemplate the complete seed-syllable as being composed of consciousness and bliss,
transparent, and unified in its singular oneness.
One should satisfy the Supreme Deity with a falling rain of nectar,
meditating again and again; being the embodiment of innate bliss,
one should satisfy [the deity] repeatedly with the nectars flowing from the [five] voids.
This is declared to be the internal sacrifice (antaryāga), which bestows liberation upon the living;
herein, the authority belongs solely to sages and those seeking liberation.
Alternatively, one may worship with mental offerings or even with manifest [external] materials.
Having meditated upon Vāsudeva as described within the center of the heart-lotus,
one should honor Him with welcoming words and the like, and with offerings such as water for the feet, bathing materials, ornaments,
perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, and the ritual of food offerings.
Then one should offer handfuls of flowers and present many garlands;
or else, one should worship the Lord with lamps produced from ghee.
One should perform the worship according to one's own capacity, beginning with words of welcome and concluding with the offering of food.
The Guru himself, his limbs anointed with the flowing paste of sandalwood and agallochum,
being skilled in the ritual procedure, should with devotion apply a tilaka at that spot using the Viṣṇupañjara mantra, resembling the flame of a lamp.
The preceptor should duly perform five offerings of handfuls of flowers (puṣpāñjali).
He should place a pair of tulasī leaves on the left foot and likewise on the right;
and on both sides, a pair of basil leaves (hayāri) accompanied by two scents.
One should place a pair of lotuses on the region of the head with the root mantra,
on the right and left with six [mantras], and again over the entire body with all [the mantras] everywhere.
Thus is described the handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) which brings about the presence of Hari.
One should offer sandalwood (*śrīkhaṇḍa*) on the right, combined with white flowers;
and on the left, one should offer sandalwood (*candana*), likewise combined with red flowers.
One should offer all flowers in the *añjali*, accompanied by all fragrances.
On the right is the one named Vāsudeva, the imperishable and pure consciousness;
on the left is the eternal Rukmiṇī, red in color and endowed with the quality of rajas. Therefore, the Guru should meditate upon himself as having the nature of both sattva and rajas.
Muttering the root mantra with the intellect at the base of the *suṣumnā*,
one should repeatedly meditate upon the meaning of that mantra, its consciousness, and its seed-syllable; thus,
one should practice the mantra alone from its arising until its dissolution.
Arising as both sound and form, the Self is proclaimed to be speech;

O Gautama, become absorbed in that which consists of the distinction between knowledge and ignorance. The mind, along with the senses, is purity; the bow is the contemplation of the meaning of the mantra.
Now, the excellence of the recitation (japa) has been described; it is the very essence of the present [teaching]. Thus, the threefold sequence of worship has been correctly explained to you;
by performing these according to the traditional transmission (sampradāya), the practitioner of mantra (mantrī) attains his desired goal.
Then, in the center of the mandala, one should begin the external worship with manifest substances, most extensive and of various flavors.
The vessels for the water for the feet (pādya), the respectful offering (arghya), and the water for sipping (ācamanīya) should be placed to one's own right.
Having arranged them, the preceptor should fill each with their respective substances:
there shall be three vessels for the *arghya*, three for the *pādya*,
and likewise three vessels for the *ācamanīya*, each according to its division.
Because performing [all] in that manner is difficult, it is recommended to do them one by one.
The practitioner of mantra should properly fill the auspicious mandala with pure rice grains and, likewise,
with seeds, up to the lotus mandala.
Having spread kuśa grass there itself, along with a lotus and a seat,
and having scattered flowers, one should then perform the installation of the water-pot (kumbha).
It may be made of gold, silver, copper, or clay, according to one's capacity.
One should not practice stinginess regarding wealth, for by doing so one incurs misfortune.
The water-pot (kumbha) should measure thirty-two finger-breadths in both width and height;
it should be sixteen or twelve finger-breadths [in diameter], but one should not make it smaller than that.
Having wound it all around with threads spun by virtuous women and properly tripled according to the rules, so that it does not fray anywhere—
should it break, death comes to the practitioner; should it fray, it becomes the seat of calamities.
Therefore, having recognized even the defects, one should act with total vigilance;
having washed the interior with a mantra and rendered it fragrant with perfumes,
one should install [the image] while reciting the *Āra* mantra, together with twice-born brahmins who are learned in the Vedas.

One should fill [the vessel] with the bark of the *samī* tree and water, or with sugarcane and medicinal herbs, or with the eight fragrances of Viṣṇu, or with water from sacred fords (*tīrtha*). [The eight fragrances are:
sandalwood, agallochum, *hnīvera*, costus, saffron, and yellow pigment (*rocanā*).
Jaṭāmāṃsī and Murāmāṃsī are known as the eight fragrances of Viṣṇu.
This pleasing set of eight aromatics brings about the presence of Viṣṇu. One should worship the fire-form, which is the support, together with its constituent parts.
Likewise, one should worship a pitcher consisting of the sun with its constituent digits (kalās);
similarly, one should worship water consisting of the moon with its digits.
This is declared to be the triad of luminaries, and water is remembered as being composed of that very essence.
It is taught that the filling should be performed everywhere with the letters of the Mātṛkā in reverse order;
likewise, having recited the root mantra, one who is free from affliction should fill [the vessel].
One should join the sacred waters (tīrthas) from the solar orb using the Tīrtha-mantra.
Having likewise placed a large conch shell in front of his own portion in the city,
he should install the support there and worship the fire-mandala.
Then, having installed the conch shell, he should worship it as being of the nature of the Sun.
One should perform the worship of all the *kalās* everywhere according to the sequence of circumambulation (*pradakṣiṇa*).
Having recited the *mātṛkā* in reverse order, one should likewise complete the mantra.
One should fill [the vessel] with decoction water, or with milk, or with those [substances] previously mentioned.

Having worshipped the digits (kalās) of the threefold fire and performed the ritual installation of the vital breath (prāṇasthāpana), the wise practitioner, for the sake of bringing about the presence of the deity, should perform the invocation (āvāhana) and other rites, worshipping each digit individually in due order according to the prescribed rule.
One should properly worship the Kalās arising from the components of the Praṇava there;
having performed the installation (sthāpana), one should join them and worship with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
Reciting a single Ṛg-verse at each respective place, one should cast the recitation (japa) therein.
The most excellent preceptor should apply the *pātha* consisting of splendor there:
first, "haṃsaḥ" in the *prakṛti*; immediately after, "pratadviṣṇuḥ";
"tryambakam" should be in the third; and "tadviprāsaḥ" constitutes the fourth.
Viṣṇu shall fashion the womb; this is proclaimed as the fifth [verse].
This group of five Ṛks is said to have the nature of the syllables of the Praṇava. Through the fivefold division of the Tāra (Om), there are fifty Kalās corresponding to the fifty letters.
Sṛṣṭi, Ṛddhi, Smṛti, Medhā, Kānti, Lakṣmī, Yuti, Sthirā, Sthiti, and Siddhi— these are said to belong to the *ka*-group in their respective order.
Born from Brahmā, who is the letter *a*, they possess the luster of molten gold.
These [deities]— Karadhatā, Akṣamālā, Paṅkajadvayā, Kuṇḍikā, Jarā, Capolinī, Śānti,
Īśvarī, Rati, Kāmikā, Varadā, Āhlādinī, and Prīti— are long and belong to the *tavarga* (the dental class of consonants).
From the syllable *U*, Viṣṇus were born, resembling the leaves of the *tāla* tree;
they are proclaimed to have four arms, displaying the gestures of fearlessness (*abhaya*) and granting boons (*vara*), and holding a discus and a conch.
Their intense gaze pierces through hundreds of fears, and their action is one of bestowing wealth.
The letters of the *pa* group are said to be the progenitors of death;
they are born from the letter *va* and possess a luster like the autumnal moon.
They carry in their excellent arms a trident, a skull-bowl, and the gesture of granting fearlessness.
These [syllables] were uttered by the Lord: yellow, white, reddish, and black;
the letter *aṃ* and those situated in the *ya*- and *ka*-groups are like the color of the hibiscus flower;
they hold the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*), a deer, an axe, and a boon-granting mudrā in their arms.
Nivṛtti, Saṃpratiṣṭhā, Vidyā, and immediately after that Śānti; then Ikṣikā, Dīpikā, Rocikā, Mocikā, and the supreme [Parā];
likewise Sūkṣmā, Sūkṣmāmṛtā, Jñānāmṛtā, and Āpyāyanī.
The internal powers of sound (svara-śaktis) are pervasive and of the nature of space; these, which are the source of all existence, were born from the Nāda by Sadāśiva.
[She holds] a rosary, a book, a string, a skull, and a threatening gesture.

Having invoked the *kalās* there and performed the restraint of the vital breath (*prāṇasaṃyama*), one should worship with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings; at its conclusion, one should offer water.
Then, having recited the twenty-eight [mantras] for the three-fold light (*tejastriya*) within the pitcher—

One should recite fifty *kalās* born from the *praṇava*, and again five *ṛks* should be recited; thereafter, one should recite the root mantra (*mūlamantra*). This mantra of ninety-four [syllables] brings about the presence of the deity.
In that same manner, while reciting the Mātṛkā-mantra, one should deposit the nine gems;
these consist of nine apertures and are composed of those very gems:
diamond, pearl, the one called flower (puṣpa), coral, and ruby.
Sapphire, emerald, ruby, and gold—
these are declared to be the nine gems (navaratna), the great abode of all the gods.
The practitioner of mantra should place a cup filled with fruit at its opening.
Having placed a seat before its mouth and having offered the five sprouts,
the practitioner of mantras should wrap it according to the prescribed rite with a pair of pure silken cloths or with a stainless garment, so that it becomes a source of all wonders.
Then one should offer many garlands and most enchanting fragrances;
there, in the shade of the wish-fulfilling tree, one should invoke Hari.
[Thus ends the ninth chapter in the glorious Śrīgautamīyamahāmantra. || 9 ||
Then, with hands joined in the *puṣpāñjali* gesture and the expanse of the sky [the heart] fully extended,
one should merge the radiance situated in the heart-lotus with the *kuṇḍalinī*,
while recollecting that which is pure, a mass of consciousness and bliss, consisting of all splendor.
One should indeed unite [the breath] with Unmanī during the piercing of the six cakras;
that state consists of the bliss of the individual soul (jīvānanda), is wondrous, and has attained sovereign power.
Having worshipped with mental offerings, one should gradually cause the breath to flow through the nostrils.
One should join that consciousness within the lotus of the *mātṛkā* held in the hand;
having invoked the mantra embodied within the center of the jar, one should worship it.
"O Kṛṣṇa, O Kṛṣṇa, O Great Yogin, all beings reside within your heart!"
"O Brahman, omnipresent and all-pervading, be present here out of compassion.
Having established [the deity] with this mantra, one should display the respective mudrās. One should lower the raised añjali; this shall be the āvāhanī (invocation) mudrā.
But this same [mudrā], when reversed, is for the rite of establishing [the deity];
the two outer thumbs joined in fists is praised as the *sannidhāpanī* (invoking) mudrā;
that same [mudrā] with the thumbs placed inside is the *sannirodhanī* (confining) mudrā.
The *Avaguṇṭhanī* [mudrā] is formed by the mutual intertwining of the index fingers;
having invoked [the deity] with the five *muṣṭi* [mudrās], one should perform the installation of the vital breaths (*prāṇasthāpana*).
Then, one should utter the *mantra*: "Śakti, encased by the noose and the goad, followed by *ahaṃ* and *saṃ*."

The life-breaths of Kṛṣṇa are here; the life-force of Kṛṣṇa is established here. May all his senses—speech, mind, and sight—having come here, remain for a long time in happiness, accompanied by Svāhā.

This *prāṇamantra* is proclaimed as the bestower of life to all living beings; by this alone, the mantras established by others are considered devoid of vitality. Its secret, according to the *tantra*, is to be learned from a guru through the majesty of knowledge.
O brahmin-sage, for the teacher there is nothing that cannot be accomplished, and not otherwise;
for by truly consigning the *mātṛkā* known as Keśava and the *tattva*,
and by the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the ten *tattvas* upon the hands and limbs, their presence (*sannidhi*) is attained.
The Lord, who is the self of all and omnipresent, is established as the substratum of the mandala;
worship of Hari should always be performed upon a Śālagrāma stone, a gem, a yantra, a mandala, or an image, but never on bare ground alone.
In a certain region of the Gaṇḍakī river, there is a great site known as Śālagrāma;
the stone produced there is remembered as Śālagrāma.
By the touch of a Śālagrāma stone, the sins of ten million births are destroyed.
What more need be said? Worship performed there brings about the presence of Hari.
By worshipping a single Śālagrāma, one obtains the fruit of worshipping a hundred lingas.
If, through the merits accumulated over many births, one should obtain a stone of Kṛṣṇa;
By that sign of the footprints of the Teacher, one's birth reaches its completion;
for, through the destruction of all suffering and the defects such as desire and anger,
they say that when he has thus attained [liberation], the Lord, being worshipped, is pleased.
A lotus with eight petals and a square base,
well-proportioned and endowed with four gates, its pericarp filled with the pride of desire—
this is declared to be the general yantra; now hear the eighteen-syllable mantra.

One should then draw a square with four doors, containing an eight-petalled lotus; in the center of the hexagon, one should write the six-syllabled supreme mantra, known as Kāma, surrounded by the seventeen vowels.
O illustrious one, this yantra has been told to you out of compassion.
Merely by knowing it, the practitioner becomes one whose very self is Kṛṣṇa.
Having pervaded the universe, it unfolds in the form of an unbroken circle.

Because it consists of all the gods, it is called a *maṇḍala*. A wise person should diligently have an image of Lord Kṛṣṇa fashioned by an artisan who is a devotee of Kṛṣṇa and who understands the work of Viśvakarman.

The best [measure] is ten and five fingers (fifteen), the middling is twelve fingers, and the lowest is eight fingers; one should not make it less or more. If a base man should do so, whether through ignorance or delusion, [he incurs fault].
The consecration of that [image] is fruitless, and no merit shall arise from its worship; wherever that image stands deficient in the measurement of finger-breadths (mānāṅgula),
it surely afflicts the king, and the householder shall go to hell.
O best of sages, it should be made according to the *māna-aṅgula* measurement and not otherwise.
A [liṅga] made of *kāśmarī* wood is said to bestow knowledge; one made of gold grants liberation;
one made of stone bestows prosperity; and one made of silver grants manifold liberation.
An image made of teja (metal) bestows splendor, one made of wood destroys enemies,
and one made of copper increases righteousness and grants great happiness.
An image made of clay is said to possess auspicious characteristics.
That image has been described to you as bestowing both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
it is proclaimed to be of two kinds: the portable (laṃpyā) and the stationary (sekhya).
It may be placed on a mountain peak, by a riverbank, at a crossroads, or in cow-pens.
Whether in a coastal region or elsewhere, there is no fault in one who is devoid of pride.
O Kṛṣṇa, one should fashion a divine image marked with the five auspicious signs;
the practitioner of mantras should then install it either in his home or in the midst of a cow-pen.
Then, being composed in meditation, the practitioner of mantras should worship with ritual offerings using the sixteen-fold service mantra known as Yama for the sake of accomplishment—
that [deity] whom even the gods, Brahmā, Hara, and others, long to behold.
"Out of compassion, O Lord of the gods, be present before me.
He replied, "O Supreme Lord, welcome; may you attain heaven.
I have achieved my purpose and am graced by you; my life has indeed become fruitful."
Since you have arrived, O Lord of Gods, imperishable and consisting of consciousness-bliss,
let there be no failure on the part of the practitioner due to ignorance or negligence;
therefore, remain present even for whatever task remains incomplete.

Water for the feet (pādya) is desired with śyāmāka grain, dūrvā grass, arka plant, and viṣṇukrāntā; O Supreme Lord, for You who are pure, this water for the feet— which brings about an immersion in supreme bliss through contact with even a mere fragment of devotion— is appropriate.
The wise man, having remembered his right hand, should offer water for sipping (ācamanīya) with nutmeg, cloves,
and kakkola, using the mantra "Svadhā," [addressing] the Veda of Vedas and the divine Self of the gods.
O Lord, I offer this vessel for the sake of purifying those who are already pure.
O God, one should place upon the head fragrant substances, flowers, unbroken rice, barley, tips of kuśa grass, sesame, mustard seeds, and dūrvā grass, using the *śiromantra*.
This is declared to be the *arghya* for the satisfaction of the wielder of the Śārṅga bow;
it is divine, the remover of the three-fold suffering, and characterized by supreme bliss.
For the sake of liberation from the three-fold suffering, I offer this *arghya* to you.
O Lord, for you who are free from all impurity, I prepare this complete *madhuparka*, consisting of clarified butter, curd, honey, and the essence of *svadhā*; be gracious to me.
And you should offer food into the mouth with pure water alone;
to you, by whose mere remembrance even one who is defiled by food remnants or impure attains purification, this water for sipping is offered once again.
O Lord, I perform this bath with water scented by camphor, sandalwood,
and saffron for Your own form, which is immersed in the ocean of supreme bliss and awakening;
I offer this bath along with its constituent parts and its limbs.
One should offer a pair of yellow garments, well-adorned according to one's ability.
For the sake of splendor, I offer you a garment of unobstructed wisdom— a parasol made of the variegated cloth of *māyā*— which is your own secret abode.
Then, one endowed with the observances should offer half of the garment as an upper cloth (uttarīya) to that Supreme Lord,
depending upon whom Mahāmāyā— she who eternally deludes the world with goodness— always exists; for him,
we prepare this upper garment.
Then one should offer a sacrificial thread (yajñasūtra), or else one made of gold—
to Him by whose three powers this entire world is woven together and remains unexhausted;
for that very Sacrifice, one should present this sacrificial thread.
One should offer ornaments such as necklaces, endowed with gold and gems,
to her whose limbs are naturally beautiful, who is truth itself, and who has truth as her refuge;
"O you worshipped by the immortals, I fashion these various ornaments for you."
One should offer water sprinkled with *arghya* between each successive service,
saying: "O Lord of all lords of gods, supreme cause of all vision,
completely filled with unbroken bliss, accept this excellent water."
The fragrance spoken of here is that which is blended with sandalwood, agallochum, and camphor.
One should smear it over the entire body for the pacification of the threefold suffering,
so that the quarters of space are filled with the fragrance of supreme bliss.
"Accept this supreme fragrance, O Supreme Lord.
One should offer five handfuls of flowers by the very path previously described,
as well as other suitable flowers for the Vaiṣṇava mantra.
The lotus, the oleander, the two types of basil, jasmine, the ketaki,

the kahlāra, the campaka, the blue lotus, the kunda, the mandāra, the nāgakeśara, the pārvatī, the nadyāvarta, the mallikā, the yūthī, the navamālikā, the saugandhika, the koraka, the koraṇḍa, the lokasarjjana, the bilva, the arjuna, the munipatraka,
the pure āmalaka leaf, and likewise the auspicious karṇikāra.
One should offer leaves such as those of the *palāśa* tree to Govinda according to what is available; however,
one should avoid flowers that are soiled, touched by the ground, defiled by worms or hair, or stale when performing the worship of the deity.
The lotus remains pure for three days, as does the āmalaka fruit;
the tulasī leaf is pure in every respect, as are the bilva leaves.
O ascetic, the karavīra flowers are fit for use for one day.
"Take this supreme flower, endowed with the four qualities, enchanting with its manifold attributes, and possessing the fragrance of bliss;
having placed the Mātṛkā, encapsulated by mantra, within the body of the God."
At each respective location of the nyāsa, one should worship them with perfumes, flowers, and unbroken grains (akṣata).
In the fivefold initiation (pañcātmikā-dīkṣā), one should worship Gaṇeśa and the others in sequence;
when Govinda is in the center, however, one should worship the Lord of the Ganas (Gaṇanāyaka) in the southwest.
Having worshipped Haṃ in the southeast, one should worship Śiva in the northeast;
one should worship the Goddess in the northwest for the attainment of the fruits of enjoyment and liberation.
Then, having worshipped with perfumes and other offerings, the worship of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) follows.
If one has the capacity, one should perform all these [rites] with their respective rays; otherwise, one should worship alone.
Having performed twenty recitations of the mantra and offered salutations, one should conclude.
Or, one may recite the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) upon the various parts of the body as they will be described hereafter.
One should worship the six limbs in the southeast, the northeast, the southwest,
and the northwest, as well as in the center and in the directions starting from the east.
[The goddesses] are the women of those who possess the luster of crystal, pearl, black collyrium, and fire.
The principal limb-deities are described as having their hands extended with the granting of fearlessness (*abhaya*) and the bestowing of boons (*varada*).
Having thus worshipped them, the wise one should worship this body according to its divisions. With a well-composed mind, he should worship the flute-instrument situated in the mouth.
This mantra, "varṇavāya namaḥ," is proclaimed for Him.
Upon His chest is the Kaustubha gem, possessing a splendor equal to ten thousand suns;
"kaustubhāya namaḥ" is declared as its mantra.
Below that is the *vanamālā* (forest-garland) mantra, possessing the luster of ten thousand moons.
Having first uttered the *praṇava* (oṃ), one should offer salutation to the *vanamālā*.
This is declared to be the *vanamālā* mantra, which destroys the entire flood of sins.
Above the Kaustubha gem is the Śrīvatsa mark, possessing a radiance equal to ten thousand moons;
its mantra is "Salutation to Śrīvatsa," as declared by the great sages.
On his two ears, which resemble a thousand suns, are crocodile-shaped earrings.
The mantra for "Salutation to Makarakuṇḍala" has been thus declared. One should say:
"Salutation to the crown, radiant on the head, possessing a splendor equal to ten thousand suns;
salutation to the crown, shining with a brilliance equal to ten thousand suns."
This [mantra] beginning with the *praṇava* has been declared by the great seers for the kirīṭa.
One should worship it starting from the eastern direction and proceeding in a clockwise sequence with the mantras of Dāma,
Sudāma, Vasudāma, and Kiṅkiṇī, using perfumes and flowers.
They are proclaimed to be the very forms of Kṛṣṇa’s internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa). They are to be worshipped as non-different from the Self; just as Kṛṣṇa is, so too are they.
One should worship them with mantras beginning with the Praṇava and ending with "namas te."

The nine limbs of the Lord have been described; now hear, O Gautama, about the limbs of His enjoyment (bhogāṅga). One should first worship the eight queens of the Lord in front of Him, beginning with Rukmiṇī and the others, in the order of circumambulation.
Rukmiṇī, Satyabhāmā, Lakṣaṇā, Sulakṣaṇā,
Kālindī, Ṛkṣajā, Anjanī, Sunandā, and Sunandakā—
each possessing a complexion like molten gold, Rukmiṇī was in the full bloom of her youth.
Clad in white garments and adorned with all ornaments,
her eyes meet the lotus-face of the Lord like honey-bees; holding the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness in her hands, she exists for the liberation of the virtuous who are devoted to her.
This Lakṣmī is the supreme power (parā-śakti), whose form consists of grace toward the universe;
she is dark as the *kalāya* flower, adorned with all ornaments,
wearing yellow garments, possessing full breasts, known by the name Satyā, and remembered as Dharaṇī.
Holding a jewel-filled vessel in her left hand and granting boons with her right,
the others are described in sequence as fair-complexioned and dark-complexioned;
they are clad in yellow garments and have faces as enchanting as those of celestial beings.
Outside of that, one should again worship Vasudeva and Yaśodā, as well as Devakī.
Vasudeva is golden-hued, standing with his hands in the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness;
Devakī is dark-complexioned, beautiful, and adorned with all ornaments.
Clad in a pair of white garments, she bestows all desired fruits;
Yaśodā, resembling a golden conch, is the giver of a pair of white garments.
She is radiant with all ornaments, her face illuminated by her earrings.
One should worship Rohiṇī there and honor Nanda, who is fair-complexioned,
endowed with the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and the bestower of all human goals;
likewise, one should worship Baladeva, who resembles a kunda flower.
One should likewise remember Hālālola, Kuṇḍalila, and Hemavanta;
then one should worship Subhadrā, who is dark-complexioned and in the full bloom of youth. Outside of that, one should worship all the Vṛṣṇis, as well as the cowherds and cowherdesses.
Outside of that, one should worship Indranīla, Mukunda, and the others; namely, Indranīla, Mukunda, Ānanda, Kacchapa,
Puṣkara, Śaṅkha, and Padma— these are proclaimed as the eight treasures (nidhis).
Outside of that, one should worship the Kalpa trees, and outside of those, Indra and the other [guardians].
One should fully worship Indra, who is dark-complexioned, mounted upon Airāvata, and likewise bearing the thunderbolt,
together with his presiding deity and his retinue, situated outside of that.
One should worship Agni, who has a luster like gold, who holds a spear and a javelin,
who is mounted upon a ram, who is endowed with power, and who is the lord of splendors. To the south, one should worship the deity of the ancestors (Pitṛdeva), seated upon a buffalo.
One should worship Yama, the wielder of the staff, as the deity presiding over the ancestors;
likewise, one should worship the lord of the Rākṣasas in the southwest, the god who holds a sword and is mounted upon a horse, together with his retinue.
In the west, one should worship Varuṇa, white and radiant, mounted upon a sea-monster (makara),
the lord of waters, holding a noose, together with his attendants. And in the northwest, one should worship the god Vāyu, known as the sovereign of the vital breaths (prāṇa).
One should worship the elephant-faced [Gaṇeśa] holding a goad in his right hand;
one should worship Soma, who possesses the luster of the autumnal moon, who bears the mark of the hare out of compassion,
the lord of the northern quarter, mounted upon a man.
One should worship Īśāna, who is mounted upon a bull, possesses a radiance equal to ten thousand moons,
is the lord of the Rudras, and holds a trident in his hand, with the finest perfumes.
In the region between Indra and Īśāna, one should worship Brahmā, whose vehicle is a swan.
One should worship the four-faced [Brahmā], who is golden-white and holds a lotus in his hand;
between the Rakṣas and Varuṇa, one should sacrifice to Viṣṇu, the wielder of the discus;
and one should worship the Lord of Serpents seated upon Suparṇa, as well as the attendants of Viṣṇu.
One should worship the auspicious weapons, such as the vajra and others, outside of them;
just as waves arising from the ocean return to their state of being broken [into the sea],
so too these [beings] born from Kṛṣṇa then returned to him as their source.
By meditating upon that, the practitioner should unite with auspiciousness;
thus, the teacher should worship Kṛṣṇa through seven repetitions.
It is certain that dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa will then be in his hand.
Alternatively, O dear one, one should worship him with the lords of the directions and their respective weapons.

Or, worshipping Kṛṣṇa in this manner, he becomes a worthy recipient of the fulfillment of desires and liberation. One who is unable to perform this sacrifice should worship with the eight names of Kṛṣṇa.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa, Vāsudeva, and he who is called Nārāyaṇa;
the preeminent Devakīnandana, and thereafter the Vārṣṇeya;
he is remembered as the destroyer of asuras, the remover of the earth's burden, and the establisher of dharma.
Or, by worshipping Kṛṣṇa according to one's means,
one enjoys excellent pleasures here in this world and, in the end, shall go to the abode of Hari.
[One should worship] with agallochum, ushira, guggulu, sugar, clarified butter, honey, and sandalwood.
O you who know the essence, this honey, offered by enemies, cannot be digested;
yet it is a supreme fragrance, rich in scent, produced from the lord of the forest.
May this incense, fit for all the gods, be accepted.
Then, having prepared a wick filled with camphor using either clarified butter or sesame oil, one should place it in a vessel or similar receptacle so that its flame blazes brightly.
Having consecrated it with the Adhyodaka water, one should offer it to Nandaja.
Having brought down the bell, which reaches the limit of the field of vision and is positioned to the left,
one should ring it with the left hand while sprinkling [water] with the right hand,
[reciting]: "O you of great splendor, well-illuminated, who removes the darkness everywhere!"

This lamp of light, possessing great brilliance, is to be accepted; it illuminates both the interior and the exterior, dispelling darkness everywhere. This lamp of light, which removes gloom from within and without, is to be accepted. [Offered] in a vessel of gold, copper, silver, or a lotus leaf, accompanied by white side-dishes, sugar, and honey.

Having brought curd, milk, ghee, and fruits such as plantains, one should place them before the deity with the *paṃ* seed-syllable; then, according to the rules, one should display the *dhenu-mudrā* while reciting the *astra-mantra*.
The seed-syllable of the Moon, situated in water, conjoined with the fourteenth vowel,
and endowed with the *nāda* and *bindu*, that seed-syllable is of the nature of nectar.
Having uttered "Parāya," one should then speak "Aniruddha."
Having said "So be it," one should say "I prepare the food offering; salutations.
This is the mantra for the food offering (naivedya); with this, one should present the offering.
One should then offer water with the mantra: "Thou art the under-layer of nectar; Svāhā!"

"Anvāhāryāya prāṇāya svāhā"—this is the first oblation. The mudrā known as Prāṇa is considered to be formed by the thumb, ring finger, and middle finger. "Āhavanīyāya apānāya svāhā"—this is the second [oblation].
The mudrā for that is proclaimed to be formed by the little finger, the thumb, and the nameless finger.
"To Gārhapatya, to Vyāna, Svāhā!"—this is the third oblation.
The mudrā for that is proclaimed to be formed by the index finger, the thumb, and the middle finger.

To Satya and Udāna, Svāhā; and the fourth [is offered] with the middle finger, the ring finger, the thumb, and the fourth [finger]. To Āvasatya and Samāna, Svāhā; and likewise the fifth [is offered] with the little finger.
That mudrā is proclaimed to be formed with all the fingers together.
With these very [mantras] beginning with the *praṇava*, the Guru should offer oblations into the mouth of the deity:
"Oṃ, I present this to you; accept it, O Hari, Hare!"
This mantra for the offering of the presentation (nivedyārpaṇa) has been well-proclaimed for the worship.

After reflecting for a moment, the wise one should then offer water for rinsing the mouth (gaṇḍūṣaka), offering the water with the mantra: "Thou art the spreading of nectar; Svāhā! (amṛtopastaraṇam asi svāhā).
One should indeed give the remaining excellent *naivedya* to Viśvaksena;
for these [deities] eat what is left over—keep this in mind regarding them.
To Śiva it is given with "To Caṇḍeśvara," and to Viṣṇu with "To Viśvaksena."
One should give the remnants of the offering (śaktyucchiṣṭa) to the Śoṣaka attendants; through such worship, the accomplishments (siddhis) are attained.
Otherwise, there will be no accomplishment at all, and the worshipper shall go to hell.
Having removed the entire collection of food offerings (naivedya) and having performed the purification of the site, [one should proceed].
One should offer water for rinsing the mouth as well as a tooth-cleansing stick;
then, having applied an ointment to the hands, one should again offer water.
Having given two fine garments, one should also present golden sandals.
Having brought the place of worship, one should likewise offer many garlands;
then one should present divine incense and betel-leaf mixed with camphor.
Having praised Hari with hymns according to the rules and having performed circumambulation, [one should proceed].
O great sage, the fruit that a man obtains by giving wealth to those who know the Vedas,
he obtains with devotion by performing a circumambulation of Kṛṣṇa;
even as one might obtain by giving the earth with its seven islands to those who know the Vedas.

One obtains that fruit through devotion by performing the circumambulation of the Kṛṣṇā. A prostration with the two feet, the two hands, the two knees, the chest, the head, the eyes, the speech, and the mind is declared to be the eight-limbed (aṣṭāṅga) salutation.
The wise person who, falling upon the ground before the dark [Lord], performs the eight-limbed prostration (aṣṭāṅga-namaskāra),
shall abandon the sins born of a thousand lifetimes and attain Vaikuṇṭha—
[the Lord] who is dark like a fresh rain-cloud and whose eyes are like blue lotuses.
I bow to Kṛṣṇa, the delight of the vine-grove, who has assumed the form of a cowherd;
whose dark, curly hair is adorned with shimmering peacock feathers,
and who is decorated with a forest garland resembling a cluster of kadamba flowers.
His cheeks were adorned with swinging golden earrings;
his chest was illuminated by a magnificent necklace of large pearls;
and his body was radiant with golden armlets, anklets, and a diadem.
He repeatedly enchanted the hearts of the cowherd girls with the sweet sounds of the flute placed between his lovely lips, while his gathered garments fluttered in the agitation of a gentle breeze.
He was a honey-bee drinking from the lotus-faces of the vine-like women,
agitating their minds with his smiling sidelong glances; while they,
their bodies transformed by youth, were closely clinging to one another.
Surrounded by cowherd women adorned with variegated garments and ornaments,
eager for the sport of playing in the waters of the Kālindī which are as dark as crushed collyrium, He was in one place making the herd of cows fight and in another place calling out to the cowherds.
Somewhere in Vṛndāvana, he was seated in the shade of a kadamba tree, cooled by the contact with the waters of the Kālindī and shaken by a gentle breeze;
he sat upon a jeweled throne resting against a mountain of gems.
Seated within a golden pavilion situated amidst wish-fulfilling trees,
on the delightful Govardhana mountain, he dwells, his face fragrant with the scent of spring blossoms and longing for the arrival of daybreak.
Holding the excellent mountain as a parasol upon the palm of his left hand—
a dense cloud of pearls released from the shattered fragments of the mountain—
He brings delight to the earth with the sounds of his flute-playing and the resonance of his "huṃ" chants.
It was constantly watched by cowherd boys with their calves looking up toward him; it was graced by cowherds who followed Kṛṣṇa alone, singing of his deeds and imitating his movements,
with sticks and nooses raised in their hands.

The Supreme Being, praised with very affectionate words by Nārada, Agastya, and other eminent sages who were masters of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences— the man who thus contemplates that God and praises Him with devotion, [attains his goal].
Being pleased with him at the three junctions of the day, he grants his desired boon; he becomes a favorite of the king, dear to all people,
attains stable prosperity, and certainly becomes eloquent.
Then, having displayed the mudrās, one should perform the consecration by fire (agnisaṃskāra).
Because they gladden all the deities and because they dissolve the succession of sins,
those mudrās have been described by the wise as bestowing the presence of the gods.
Gautama said:
"O Blessed One, you have indicated the mudrās to me, but you have not revealed them.
Out of compassion, O Guru, tell me how they are to be formed."
Nārada said:
"The little finger and the thumb of your two hands are capable;
the index, middle, and ring fingers should be joined together and free from curvature."
This is declared to be the Gālinī mudrā, which is praised for the worship of Gopāla.
With both hands positioned like a garland of forest flowers (vanamālā), reaching from the neck down to the knees— this is the Vanamālikā mudrā.
The thumb of the left hand is placed upon the lip;
its little finger is joined with the right thumb, while that [right] little finger is extended. The index, middle, and ring fingers are slightly contracted and moved.
The flute-mudrā, which is well-guarded and dear to Hari, is described here:
having joined the fingers of both the left and right hands together,
the little finger of the right hand is brought into contact with the left nostril.
The middle finger of the right hand should press upon the index finger of the left hand,
and the index finger of the right hand should be pressed by the middle finger of the left hand;
the wise one should then join the thumbs of both hands together.
The Dhenu-mudrā has been described and kept secret by the most excellent practitioners:
having joined the two hands together,
one should firmly press the little finger of the left hand with the fingers of the right hand.
Likewise, one should press [the thumbs] very firmly with the left fingers;
this is the Bilva-mudrā, which is highly praised for the worship of Kṛṣṇa.
Whatever has been done by body, mind, speech, or intellect—
Knowing this, one who understands the accumulation of sins committed in this life or in a previous one quickly abandons that [sin], without a doubt.
All the gods pay homage to such a person, and likewise, people bow down before them.
Having uttered the *kama* syllable according to the rules, one should place it upon the heart;
having placed the other hand on the left, with the fingers properly aligned,
one should interlace the middle and ring fingers of the two hands back-to-back.
Having pressed the right little finger with the left little finger,
one should press the right index finger with the left ring finger;
one should place the three fingers of the right hand over the three fingers of the left hand.
Having joined one [finger] with three [fingers], there shall be the mudrā consisting of the Kaustubha gem;
one should place the left thumb upon the right wrist.
This mudrā, called Kaustubha, has been described and should be displayed with effort.
Having placed the other hand on the left and having properly aligned the fingers,
one should then place the palm of the left hand over the index finger;
the two thumbs should be moved, and this is declared to be the Matsya-mudrā (the Fish Gesture).
Having joined the two hands together with the wrists well-aligned,
and having placed the thumbs and little fingers well-joined,
all the remaining fingers of both hands are bent toward the left.

One should cause them to be joined to one another with their centers empty; this is called the "Ocean of Vases," which is auspicious for the ritual of Gopālārcā. Having formed the other [mudrā] by joining the palms together with the fingers interlaced.

When the fingers are closely joined to one another and placed with the space between them equal to the width of a thumb, this is declared to be the Kūrma-mudrā, which is kept secret in all the tantras. Then, having bent the four fingers of the left hand...
Having extended the thumb, one should encircle it with the right hand;
extending the right index finger along with the thumb,
the knower of mantras forms the Śaṅkha-mudrā, which destroys sins by its mere sight.
[Thus ends the tenth chapter in the Great Tantra of Gautama. || 10 ||
Now, O Kṛṣṇa, I shall describe here the production of the sacred fire according to the mantras,
by performing which one enjoys the fruits of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa.
Having smeared the entire sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) with cow dung, the knower of mantras [should proceed].
Having prepared the general *arghya* offering, one should then sprinkle [the area] with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*).
One should fashion a triangle, outside of which is a hexagon, and a lotus;
or likewise, a square with four gates as the fire-mandala (*vahnimaṇḍala*).

On the northern side of the pit (kuṇḍa), one should draw three auspicious lines measuring one cubit (hasta) from south to north; likewise, one should draw another set of three lines. Having sprinkled everything with the water of the respectful offering (arghya), one should indeed perform the fivefold purification (pañcaśuddhi).
One should gaze upon it with the root mantra and then smear it with the armor mantra (kavaca). Having protected it with the weapon mantra (astra), one should perform the consecration of the fire.
This fire may be produced from stone or born from a womb (yoni).
One may take wealth produced in the house of those learned in the Vedas, or that found in the forest;
whatever is obtained by chance is suitable for the performance of the fire-sacrifice (homa).
Wealth acquired from a Brāhmaṇa who maintains no sacred fires shall indeed bring about gain.
The fire-god shall grant a fourth part of the fruit to one who is a mere nominal Kṣatriya;
from a Vaiśya or a Śūdra, the rite of oblation becomes fruitless.
Therefore, with every effort, one should properly prepare the sacrificial fire.
Having brought [the food] and placed it in a bronze vessel, one should set aside the portion for the flesh-eaters (kravyāda).
Having offered salutations to the flesh-eaters, there should be a mantra beginning with the syllable Om (praṇava).
For the lines drawn pointing toward the north, Brahmā, Vaivasvata, and Indu [are the presiding deities].
At the tips of the lines facing east are Mukunda, Īśa, and Purandara.
Then, one should worship the Yoga-pīṭha upon the pericarp (karṇikā) above the fire;
first, one should worship Dharma, Jñāna, Vairāgya, and Aiśvarya.
One who knows the ritual procedure should likewise worship the eastern and other directions, as well as the deities beginning with Dharma;
and in the center of the fire, one should worship the powers (Śaktis):
Pītā, Śvetā, Aruṇā, Kṛṣṇā, Dhūmrā, Tīvrā, and Sphuliṅginī.
Rucirā and Jvālinī are said to be the nine powers (śaktis) of the sun;
