having worshipped the solar orb (amarka-maṇḍala), one should worship the lunar orb (somamaṇḍala) with the syllable *uṃ*,
and likewise worship the fiery orb (vahni-maṇḍala) with the syllable *maṃ* using perfumes and flowers.
One should worship Vāgīśvarī— who has bathed away death and resembles a blue lotus—
together with Vāgīśvara, using the ritual services (upacāras).
Their worship is said to be performed by means of the two seed-syllables (bījas) of Śakti and Praṇava.
One should visualize Vāgīśvarī as being in her menses and presided over by the Puruṣa.
Having consecrated the fire placed in a vessel, one should empower it with the seed-syllable *raṃ*.
Joining consciousness to it by means of the *praṇava* (OM), one should worship it.
Facing himself toward the fire, with his knee on the ground and his back to the earth,
he should place this [fire] into the womb of the Goddess with the thought that it is the seed of Śiva.
Then, he should offer water for sipping (ācamanīya) to both the God and the Goddess.
The supreme guru should meditate on the form of fire sustained by the umbilical cord;
thereafter, for the protection of the unborn child, he should offer a blade of *darbha* grass and adorn the goddess Mātṛkā—
the mother of the origin of the three worlds— with ornaments.
Adorned with the letter *ra*, the vital breath (*vāyu*), the vowel *u*, and the *nāda* and *bindu*, these mantras of the tongues—
beginning with *sa* and ending with *ṣa*— are proclaimed. They are located in the anus,
the genitals, the navel, the heart, and at the base of the throat.
One should place the tongues Jvālā and Rucā in the *lambikā* (the uvula) and between the eyebrows;
Hiraṇyā, Kanakā, Raktā, the one called Kṛṣṇā, Suprabhā, Bahurūpā, Atiraktā, and the tongue named Kapīṭayoni are considered [to be there].
Sahasrārcis, Svasti, Pūrṇa, Utthita, Puruṣa,
Dhūmavyāpin, Saptajihva, and Dhanurdhara—
these are remembered as the six-limbed mantras of Agni, beginning with the *praṇava* (Oṃ) and ending with *namaḥ*.
The deities of the limbs (aṅgadevatā) should be installed in sequence, beginning with the heart:
on the head, the shoulders, the sides, the hips, and the sides of the hips;
having installed them on the shoulders and the head, one proceeds by way of circumambulation.
Jātavedas, Saptajihva, the one known as Havyavāhana,
another known as Aśvodaraja, and again the one called Vaiśvānara;
Kaumāratejas, Viśvāmukha, and likewise Devamukha at the end.
Having thus disposed the body [of the deity], one should kindle it with this mantra:
"O Citpiṅgala, burn that pair, and likewise that other;
O Omniscient One, make me know—svāhā! This is the mantra proclaimed.
I worship Agni, the blazing one, Jātavedas, the consumer of oblations—
pure, golden-hued, prosperous, and facing in all directions—
with the kindling mantra and with three mantras for the consumer of oblations.
The wise practitioner should kindle [the fire]; otherwise, it will be fruitless.
Then, the practitioner should strew [the sacrificial grass] according to the rule, moving clockwise, using pure *darbha* blades that are without pith and which cover the root, middle, and tip.
In this manner, one who is most skilled in the ritual procedure should perform the spreading of the grass, avoiding the direction presided over by Ananta (the North-East).
Likewise, he should fashion three enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) from wood produced from sacrificial trees.
Then, the expert in the ritual should spread the grass within the middle girdle (*mekhalā*).
Then, if the practitioner performs it on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) or upon the ground, he should spread everything [there] and,
having worshipped with perfumes and other offerings, he should visualize the deity of fire as three-eyed, red-hued, with his crown bound up, and holding a white lotus.

One should meditate upon Śaṅkara, who is like a parrot, red as a ruby, seated upon a lotus, possessing his desired power, and exalted by the auspicious Svastika; adorned with a garland of emerald lotuses, golden-hued and stainless,
wearing a shining golden sacred thread, four-armed, two-headed, and having two nostrils for the offerings to gods and ancestors.

The most excellent preceptor should thus meditate in his mind upon [the deity] holding a water-pot, a palm-leaf fan, a spear, and a swastika; possessing four ears, resounding with sound, and supreme— especially at the beginning of the propitiatory rite (śāntika).
In the rite of killing (māraṇa), one should meditate on Kṛṣṇa as having a black complexion. Having worshipped the eight forms facing forward, one should worship the six limbs in the hexagon;
in the center, one should worship the tongue of fire, and then worship the Fire-god with his mantra.
First the word *vaiśvānara*, then *jātavedas*, then *lohitākṣam*, then *ihāvaha* is uttered; thereafter,
"O best of all performers of rites, grant me [the fruit], svāhā!"— this is the mantra that bestows prosperity.
Having brought another vessel, one should wash it while reciting the *astu* mantra.
Having weighed out the medicinal ingredients (*kuṇṭha-aṅgaga*) into it, one should place them there with the appropriate limb-mantra (*aṅga-mantra*).
Having poured clarified butter (*ājya*) into that vessel, one should know that heating it is beneficial.
Having kindled a cluster of *kuśa* grass and cast it into the clarified butter (*ājya*), one should throw it into the fire;
this is called "illumination" (*abhidyotana*) and is prescribed for all rites in every context.
Again, having thoroughly ignited *kuśa* blades, one should cast them into the midst of the fuel to be burned.
The wise one declares that the consecration of the clarified butter (ājya) is performed with the root mantra;
having consecrated it with the root mantra, he should protect it while reciting the weapon-mantra (astra).
Then, having displayed the flute and the yoni-mudrās, that clarified butter becomes of the nature of nectar.
Having taken up the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, the preceptor prepared according to the rite;
he should heat them three times in the fire, then wash them again with water. Having heated them once more, the mantra-practitioner should place them to his right.
One should place a fist-sized bundle of darbha grass, together with its stalks, into clarified butter.
Having divided it into two parts corresponding to the bright and dark fortnights, one should then recollect the channels (nāḍīs),
such as Iḍā and the others, in the left, right, and middle portions respectively.
Taking ghee with the *śruva* ladle from the southern portion,
he should offer it into the right eye of the Fire with the mantra "To Agni, Svāhā!"; then, taking [ghee] from the left in the same manner, he should offer it to Soma with "To Soma, Svāhā!"
With this mantra, one should offer oblations into the left eye of the fire;
likewise, taking [the substance] from the middle, one should offer oblations into the forehead-eye of the fire with this mantra: "Svāhā to Agni and Soma."
Taking clarified butter from the southern portion with the *śruva* ladle while reciting the heart-mantra, the Guru should offer it into the mouth of the Fire with the mantra:
"Svāhā to Agni, the Creator of Emanation.
In this manner, the Guru should perform the rite of opening the eyes and the mouths of the Fire.
Having offered oblations with the *punarvyāhṛti* mantras, one should offer the tongue and the limbs according to their forms;
then, for the sake of consecration, the preceptor should offer oblations three times with the *vaiśvānara* mantra,
and subsequently offer twelve oblations into the fire.
The wise man, reciting [the mantra] beginning with the Praṇava and ending with Svāhā,
should perform the rites of conception (garbhādhāna), the rite for a male child (puṃsavana), the parting of the hair (sīmantonnayana),
as well as the birth-ceremony (jātakarman), the naming (nāma), and the first outing (upaniṣkramaṇa).
The tonsure ceremony (cūḍā), the initiation (upanayana), further study of the Vedas,
the gift of a cow (godāna), and marriage— these are the purificatory rites (saṃskāras) for auspicious acts;
those skilled in the Tantras prescribe them as ending with death for inauspicious acts.
Then, having worshipped the two parents of the fire, one should lead it into the heart;
with the fire-mantra, one should duly offer five oblations.
One should offer five fuel-sticks (samidhs) smeared with clarified butter at the tips of the impurities.
One should offer eleven oblations with the heart-mantra of the Guru according to the rules, excluding the word *svāhā*,
and with the mantra of Mahāgaṇeśa;
this is remembered as the common mouth of the fire for all the gods.

Having invoked the Supreme Lord upon the multiform tongue and worshipped Him thoroughly with perfumes and other offerings, one should offer sixteen oblations according to the prescribed rite using the root mantra; this is the unification with the faces.
Furthermore, one should offer twenty-five oblations with that same [mantra].
This is declared to be the junction of the channels (nāḍī-sandhāna) between the fire and the deity as well.
One should offer one oblation each for the limbs (aṅga) and the retinue (parivāra).
Having again offered oblations with the vyāhṛtis, one should perform the fire-sacrifice according to the rules;
one should offer sesame seeds and clarified butter by the thousands as prescribed. When no specific sacrificial substance is mentioned, sesame and clarified butter are said to be the oblation.
One should offer a red lotus combined with the three sweets,
or one should offer milk-rice (pāyasa) mixed with honey according to one's discretion. In all ritual acts, the wise practitioner should offer oblations into the mouth of the fire.
By offering oblations into the ears, one incurs deafness; by offering into the eyes, one attains blindness.
By offering into the nose, there is mental affliction; indeed, one who offers into the head brings about death.
For where there is wood, there is the ear; and where there is smoke, there is the nose.
Since the eye has but a slight flame, Śiva is present there; since there is ash, he is Śiva;
and since the fire blazes forth, that is the mouth of Jātavedas.
Having thus completed the *homa*, the wise one should then cook the *caru*.
In a pure vessel made of copper, one should not place milk from a Kapila cow;
rather, one should pour twenty handfuls of rice produced from pure grains.
Then, one should offer a stream of clarified butter until the sacrificial oblation (caru) becomes cooked.
Then, having drawn it out, the wise one should worship it by dividing it into three parts.
Then he should perform the ritual:
taking one part, he should perform the daily fire-oblation (nityahoma).
In a fire-pit, on a sacrificial mound, or likewise on a purified spot of ground measuring one cubit,
provided with kusha grass, flowers, and water, the practitioner,
having established the fire there through the recitation of the Jātavedas mantra, [should proceed].
One should mutter the *mantra*.
Then, having offered oblations with the *vyāhṛtis* and having invoked Kṛṣṇa with devotion,
one should worship Him thoroughly with perfumes and other offerings, [reciting] the root-mantra twenty-five times.

The practitioner of mantras should offer oblations and perform the six-limbed fire-sacrifice (ṣaḍaṅgahoma). Then, having prostrated with his body bowed and paid homage, the knower of mantras should dismiss [the deity] into the lunar abode; this is declared to be the daily fire-sacrifice (nityahoma).
One should then perform the *bali* offering for Viśva according to the procedure prescribed in one's own *Gṛhya-sūtra*.
Then, having prepared the sacrificial porridge (*caru*), one should offer two portions to Kṛṣṇa;
having eaten one portion oneself, one should present the remainder to the disciple.
The disciple, being self-controlled, should lie down upon a bed of *kambala*, *palāla*, or *kuśa* grass.
The preceptor should bind his own topknot with the mantra of Bhūteśvara.
Then he should sleep for that night; this is declared to be the *adhivāsa*.
[Thus ends the eleventh chapter in the Gautama-dharma-sūtra. || 11 ||
Then, having risen at dawn and performed his daily rites, the teacher— though his own duties were fulfilled— should sit in the presence of the disciple; the disciple, for his part,
should recount the events of the night, whether they be auspicious or inauspicious.
Eating together with women who are well-adorned,
climbing a mountain peak, riding elephants, horses, and chariots,
ascending a palace or mansion, and witnessing a festival for a deity.

O you of noble vows, the sight and touch of one's own left side are auspicious; these are declared to be the signs of one who has attained perfection through mantras. I shall describe them clearly; listen to all those things that are to be censured.
Being struck by black-clad soldiers in a dream, being smeared with oil,
speaking words of anger to Brahmins, consorting with the wives of others,
and other such censured acts are said to be obstacles to spiritual success (siddhi).
Having thus recognized the fault, the preceptor should remedy it instantly;

he should perform a fire sacrifice (homa) for a thousand times or more with substances indicated in the ritual manual (kalpa). Having offered oblations along with the ancillary rites and the retinue, he should then perform the bali offering.

Outside the perimeter of the maṇḍala, the knower of mantras should offer bali-offerings to Lokeśa and the others, as well as to the lunar mansions, the days of the week, and the zodiac signs in their proper order; having worshipped them correctly with perfumes and other offerings, he should do so there with their respective mantras.
One should respectfully offer a bali-oblation of pure food, along with perfumes, flowers, incense, and lamps,
to the stars beginning with Aśvinī. The zodiac signs, starting from Aries, are designated by the names of the preceding constellations, each consisting of two and one-quarter quarters (pādas).
One should utter "to the deities" for the *pada*; likewise, one should say "by day and by night.
Then, one should say "salutation to all moving beings and to all elemental spirits.
In this manner, when that zodiacal sign (*rāśi*) is complete, one should employ it accordingly.

Likewise, one should state the offerings for the planets that are the lords of the zodiac signs in their respective places; however, between Pisces and Aries, one should declare the offering for the Karaṇas.
Venus is the lord of Aries and Scorpio, and [Venus] is the lord of Taurus and Libra.
Mercury is the lord of Virgo, and the Moon is the lord of Cancer;
the Sun is the lord of Leo, and Jupiter is the lord of Sagittarius and Pisces;
these are the lords of the signs of Capricorn and Aquarius, as well as Mandi (Saturn).
One should likewise worship the attendants of Viṣṇu with the mantra "lāṃ indrāya" and so forth.
Then, according to the prescribed rite, the most excellent preceptor should offer the bali-oblation to the lords of the directions.

Oṃ, salutation to the deities of the Aśvinī constellation, to those who roam by day and night, and to all beings; salutation to the deities of the Bharaṇī and the first quarter of Kṛttikā constellations, to those who roam by day and night, and to all beings.

Salutation to the deities of Kṛttikā, Tripāda, and Rohiṇī; salutation to all beings who roam by day and by night! Salutation to the deities of Kṛttikā, Tripāda, and Rohiṇī; salutation to all beings who roam by day and by night! Salutation to the deities of Rohiṇī, Mṛgaśīrṣa, and half of Pūrvāṣāḍhā; salutation to all beings who roam by day and by night!

Homage to the deities of the latter half of Mṛgaśīrṣa, who roam by day and by night, and to all beings! Homage to the deities of Ārdrā and the three quarters of Punarvasu, who roam by day and by night, and to all beings!
Homage to the deities of the quarter of Punarvasu and Puṣya, who roam by day and by night, and to all beings!
Homage to the deities of Aśleṣā who wander by day and by night; homage to all beings! Homage to the deities of Maghā who wander by day and by night; homage to all beings!
Homage to the deities of the quarters of Pūrvaphalgunī and Uttaraphalgunī who wander by day and by night; homage to all beings!
To Uttarāphalgunī, to Dvipādahastā, to the deities who roam by day and by night, to all beings, homage!
To Hastā and half of Citrā, to the deities who roam by day and by night, to all beings, homage!
To Hastā and half of Citrā, to the deities who roam by day and by night, to all beings, homage!

Homage to the deities of the latter half of Citrā and Svātī, who roam by day and by night, and to all beings! Homage to the deities of the three quarters of Svātī and Viśākhā, who roam by day and by night, and to all beings!
Homage to the deities of the quarter of Viśākhā and the three quarters of Anurādhā, who roam by day and by night, and to all deities!
Salutation to the deities beginning with Jyeṣṭhā, who wander by day and night, and to all beings.

Salutation to the deities beginning with Mūla, who wander by day and night, and to all beings. Salutation to the deities of the quarters of Pūrvāṣāḍhā and Uttarāṣāḍhā, who wander by day and night, and to all beings.
Homage to the deities of Uttarāṣāḍhā and Śravaṇā who roam by day and night, and to all beings!

Homage to the deities of Śravaṇā and the half of Dhaniṣṭhā who roam by day and night, and to all beings! Homage to the deities of the half of Dhaniṣṭhā and Śatabhiṣaj who roam by day and night, and to all beings!

Homage to the deities of Śatabhiṣaj and Pūrvabhādrapada who roam by day and by night, and to all beings! Homage to the deities of Pūrvabhādrapada and Uttarabhādrapada who roam by day and by night, and to all beings!
Homage to the deities of Revatī who roam by day and by night, and to all beings!
Salutation to the deities of the Aries zodiac sign—Aśvinī, Bharaṇī, and the first quarter of Kṛttikā—to those who roam by day and night, and to all beings.
Salutation to the deities of the Taurus zodiac sign—the remaining three quarters of Kṛttikā, Rohiṇī, and the first half of Mṛgaśiras—to those who roam by day and night, and to all beings.
Salutation to the deities of the Gemini zodiac sign—Mṛgaśiras, Ārdrā, and the three quarters of Punarvasu—to those who roam by day and night, and to all beings.
Salutation to the deities of Karkaṭa, Punarvasu, Ekapāda, Puṣya, and Āśleṣā, who wander by day and by night; salutation to all beings!
Salutation to the deities of Siṃha, Maghā, Pūrvā, and one quarter of Uttarā, who wander by day and by night; salutation to all beings!
Salutation to the deities of Kanyā, the three quarters of Uttarā, Hasta, and half of Citrā, who wander by day and by night; salutation to all beings!
Salutation to the deities of the latter half of Citrā, Svātī, and three-quarters of Viśākhā, who roam by day and night, and to all beings: *namaḥ*.
Salutation to the deities of Scorpio, one quarter of Viśākhā, Anurādhā, and Jyeṣṭhā, who roam by day and night, and to all beings: *namaḥ*.
Salutation to the deities of Sagittarius, Mūla, Pūrvāṣāḍhā, and one quarter of Uttarāṣāḍhā, who roam by day and night, and to all beings: *namaḥ*.
Homage to the deities of the three quarters of Uttarāṣāḍhā, Śravaṇā, and half of Dhaniṣṭhā, who roam by day and by night; homage to all beings!
Homage to the deities of Kumbha, the latter half of Dhaniṣṭhā, Śatabhiṣaj, and the three quarters of Pūrvabhādrapadā, who roam by day and by night; homage to all beings!
Homage to the deities of Mīna, Pūrvabhādrapadā, Uttarabhādrapadā, and Revatī, who roam by day and by night; homage to all beings!

Homage to the deities of the obstructions! Homage to the deities of Venus! Homage to the deities of Mercury! Homage to the deities of the Moon! Homage to the deities of the Sun! Homage to the deities of Jupiter! Homage to the deities of Saturn! Homage to the deities of the lion! Homage to the deities of the tiger! Homage to the deities of the boar! Homage to the deities of the donkey! Homage to the deities of the elephant! Homage to the deities of the bull!

Salutations to the dog-deities. Hara, Durgā, Guha, Viṣṇu, Brahmā, Lakṣmī, and the Lord of Wealth are the deities of the doorway. Having thus addressed them, the preceptor should offer the sacrificial oblation (bali) to them. This is declared to be the procedure for the bali, which destroys the entire multitude of obstacles.
One should discard the excess cow-tail hair and provide a covering of grass. One should prepare the fuel-wood, excluding the *jambīra* and the *kali* tree.
Smoke that is pure, vermilion-colored, or the hue of the rising sun is highly auspicious for fire; smoke with a deep sound like the beating of kettledrums (bherī) bestows good fortune upon the fire;
and smoke resembling the moon, sandalwood, or the kunda flower grants success in all undertakings.
A harsh sound accompanied by one's own chanting causes the total destruction of the fire;
a black color, due to the root *kṛṣ* (to scatter), destroys the kingdom as well.
Then, one who knows the ritual procedure should offer the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) and perform the reconnection (*sandhi*).

*Oṃ bhūr agnaye pṛthivyai mahate svāhā.* Then: *bhūvo vāyave cāntarikṣāya ca dive ca mahate ca svāhā.* Then: *svaś candramase digbhyaś ca nakṣatrebhyaḥ svāhā.* *Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaś candramase nakṣatrebhyaś ca digbhyaś ca mahate svāhā.* Having taken up the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles and filled them again with clarified butter, one should then place the oblation materials [into them].

Having again established [the fire] at the navel, one should offer the *brahmārpaṇa* oblation with honey. Then, once more, the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*): "Whatever was previously done by me through the authority of the vital breaths, the intellect, the body, and the faculties, in the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep—whether by mind, speech, action, the two hands, the feet, the belly, or the genitals;
whatever was remembered, spoken, or performed—let all that be an offering to Brahman, Svāhā! This is the mantra for the *brahmārpaṇa*; it is prescribed in the ritual of the *brahmārpaṇa*.
[Thus ends the twelfth chapter in the glorious Gautamīya. || 12 ||

Having thus performed the rite of the fire-oblation (homa), the preceptor should summon the deities residing in the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) and the leveled altar (sthaṇḍila), as well as the guardian deities of the directions (dikpāla) and the deities of the ritual sowing of seeds (aṅkurārpaṇa). The preceptor should also contemplate the unification within the water-pot (kalaśa). Having brought Kṛṣṇa accompanied by Svadhā, the knower of the Tantra should lead the disciple forward and diligently bind his eyes with a cloth using the Netra-mantra.
Having caused the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*)— which consists of the nectar of mantras—
to be offered, the knower of the tantras and mantras, having touched it, should purify the six paths (*adhvan*).
Having thoroughly purified the principles of Viṣṇu (*viṣṇutattva*), he should lead [the deity] to the consecration chamber.
The path of phonemes (varṇādhvan), the path of kalās, the path of padas, the path of principles (tattvādhvan), the path of mantras, and the path of worlds (bhuvanādhvan)—
these are declared by the sages who know the tantras to be the sixfold path.
The path of phonemes, the path of conch-shells (varṇa-śaṅkha), and the path of fruits (phalādhvan) are said to be comprised of these six.
The path of the feet (pādādhvan) is the collection of words; the path of the principles (tattvādhvan) consists of twenty-five principles.
Those who know the principles understand that there are thus thirty-six principles.
The path of mantras (maṃtrādhvan) is the aggregate of mantras, for they are indeed both Vedic and Tantric.

The path of the worlds (bhuvanādhvan) is said to consist of the fourteen worlds. "I purify this path of such-and-such a person; O Parvata!"—this is the mantra at the end for the purification of the path of the Vedagarbha.
The Guru should perform nine oblations for the purification of each individual path;
then, taking that disciple by the hand, he should lead him to the consecration hall.
Having seated him upon the Mātṛkā-yanttra, he should sprinkle him with the nectar from the ritual jars.
The preceptor, whose self is filled with the experience of Kṛṣṇa, should bring the water-pot;
touching the sprouts of *gorocanā* while perceiving them as the wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpavṛkṣa*),
he should place it upon the head of the child and recite the *mātṛkā* in reverse order.

Having likewise recited the root mantra, one should perform the consecration of the deity. If the practitioner consecrates [the deity] with that water which has Kṛṣṇa as its essence, beginning from the word "Śiva" and ending with "Ādi," he certainly becomes one whose self is Kṛṣṇa.

Through the application of various medicinal herbs, water becomes identical with Kṛṣṇa; by the mere contact with that [water], the child becomes Kṛṣṇa and not otherwise. Thus, he who performs this with devotion sanctifies his own self as Viṣṇu.
Having enjoyed [the fruits] here according to his desire, at the end of the body he shall go to that state—
his limbs anointed with sandalwood paste and endowed with the blessings of the twice-born,
having prostrated again and again before that preceptor who is identical with Kṛṣṇa.
Restrained and endowed with humility, he should sit near him;
the Guru, with a mind full of equanimity and effort, should place the entire net of mantras upon his body and whisper the mantra three times into his right ear.
Having recited the mantras of Gaṇeśa and the others, the Guru should explain the observances (samayas),

the meaning of the mantra, the seed-syllable (bīja) of the mantra, its power (śakti), and its digits (kalā). Then, he should reveal his own self directly as being identical with that [mantra], under his own name.

The mantra-possessing teacher should illuminate the single ultimate goal of the gods; out of compassion, the Guru should diligently refute non-Vaiṣṇava doctrines and instruct the disciple in that one [truth] so that he may attain absorption in it.
Just as a hundred village ponds, defiled by excrement, urine, and the like,
certainly become just like the Ganges when they merge with the Ganges;
and just as a child who has fallen into a pit of raw meat becomes satisfied by it.
The disciple, having recognized that [the initiation] is complete, should diligently please the guru.
Devoted to devotion, he should give the guru a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) equal to half his own wealth;
or he may give half of that, or whatever he can according to his ability and with devotion.

One should not practice stinginess regarding wealth; having accomplished one's purpose, one should collect the materials and present cows, land, gold, garments, and so forth to the preceptor. The disciple should likewise offer these to the preceptor’s son or his wife according to his own capacity.
One should give clothing, ornaments, and sweet food to eat according to one's preference;
one should give sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to the officiating priests adorned with garments and jewelry, and one should satisfy the Sātvatas with devotion according to the extent of one’s wealth.

From that time forward, O Sage, the knower of mantras, remaining established in the instructions of his Guru, should perceive through non-duality: as it is with the mantra, so it is with the deity; as it is with the deity, so it is with the Guru. Such is the sequence of devotion for the practitioner of mantra.
Causing lack of devotion in the world, such a deity brings about affliction;
for the sake of accomplishment, one should dwell with devotion in the presence of the Guru for three days. Otherwise, there is no doubt that his supernatural power will pass to the Guru.
[Thus ends the thirteenth chapter in the glorious Gautamīya. || 13 ||
Having performed the preparatory rites in the month of Caitra under an auspicious constellation according to the instruction of the Guru,

one should indeed commence the *puraścaryā* on the twelfth day (*dvādaśī*) of the bright fortnight in the month of Mādhava, on that specific lunar date, at Amalā for the sake of perfect accomplishment.
Recitation (japa), burnt offerings (homa), libations (tarpaṇa), sprinkling (seka), and feeding Brahmins—
this fivefold worship in this world is called *puraścaraṇa*.
At the outset, in order to perform the preliminary rite (*purasakriyā*), one should carry out the consecration of the ground (*bhūmi-parigraha*).
Thereafter, one should not overstep [the rules] for the sake of wandering according to one's own will;
for just as a body devoid of life is incapable of any action,
so too a rite lacking the *puraścaraṇa* does not bestow its fruit.
On a mountain peak, by a riverbank, in a cow-pen, or likewise in a temple; in a sacred forest, on the great shore of the ocean, in one's own home,
in a delightful grove of *tulasī*, or at the root of a *bilva* tree— it is highly commended.
In a sacred field of Viṣṇu, one should commence the recitation for the sake of accomplishment according to the prescribed rules.
A practitioner of mantras performing the *puraścaraṇa* rite should distinguish between what is fit and unfit to eat;
otherwise, from the fault of improper eating, a loss of accomplishment arises.

One should eat the food of those born of noble families and established in their stations, who are pure, illustrious, virtuous, householders, and generous; or the food of twice-born men who subsist on alms; or likewise, one may eat sacrificial oblation (haviṣya) or prescribed vegetables.
O Sage, one should avoid the fruit of the betel-nut palm and the *kendu* tree;
however, milk, curd, fruit, coconut as prescribed,
sacrificial food (*haviṣya*), or likewise barley-gruel (*śaktu*) produced from barley may be eaten according to the rules.
The rambhā fruit, the tamarind, the lotus, and the orange—these fruits may be eaten; one should avoid others among them.
A practitioner of mantra should avoid sugarcane products, except for sugar and sugarcane juice.

One should carefully avoid salt, alkaline substances, sour things, garlic, bell-metal, betel-leaf, and divided food when in the company of women. One should also avoid that which contradicts the Śruti and Smṛti, and refrain from reciting prayers at night.
Sleeping on the ground, practicing celibacy, maintaining silence, and being free from envy;
bathing daily at the three periods of the day, avoiding trivial activities,
performing constant worship, giving regular charity, and engaging in the praise and chanting of the deity.

Worship according to specific signs, faith in the Guru and the Deity, and steadfastness in recitation— these twelve are the duties that grant success in mantra. One should daily perform the ritual attendance upon the Sun and remain facing toward him.
Having worshipped the deity in an image and so forth, as well as in the fire, facing that [deity],
free from despondency and distraction, and observing the conduct prescribed in the scriptures,
one should be intent upon bathing, worship, recitation, meditation, fire-oblation, and libations.
Free from desire and offering all actions to the deity—one who observes such rules and the like is said to be performing the *puraścaraṇa*.
When possible, one should bathe at the three periods of the day (*trisavana*); otherwise, twice or once.
There is no fruit for one who does not bathe, nor for one who fails to satisfy the ancestors.
The body originates from impurities, yet through water there is purification of the senses;
therefore, bathing with water is considered by all sages to be the primary form of bathing.
One should not look upon a fallen person, a braggart, a slanderer, or one who reviles the Vedas;
likewise, one should not look upon a Brahmin who does not belong to an āśrama or one who reviles the nature of Viṣṇu.
Furthermore, a practitioner of mantras should not touch his own wife except during her fertile period.
One should completely avoid sexual intercourse, talk about it, or socializing regarding it.
Whether on a mountain, by the shore of a river, in a sacred forest, or on a riverbank,
if one performs the *puraścaraṇa* rite there, one need not worry about the tortoise [as a potential obstacle].
Whether in a village, a settlement, or a house, one should contemplate that [mantra];

for it is said that the face and the back of the minister [the mantra] are located at the place of the lamp. Success occurs at the place of the lamp, and not otherwise, even by ten million recitations.
One should lay down four lines according to the eastern and northern divisions;
this shall become a grid of nine squares, the unsurpassed body of the Tortoise (Kūrma).
Then, the knower of mantras, proceeding in a clockwise direction starting from the east, [should mark the points].
The wise one should write the five groups beginning with *ka* in five divisions;
he should likewise write the group beginning with *ya* and the group beginning with *śa* upon Lakṣmī and Īśa.
He should form the limbs and the body of the tortoise so that it becomes beautiful.
The vowels are arranged in pairs in the center and in the eight directions;
thus the Tortoise (Kūrma) possesses eight limbs and is the illuminator of the accomplishments (siddhi) for all.
One should write Dīpanātha in the center and worship him while meditating upon him.
In whichever direction the first letter of a village name is seen to fall,
one should know that to be the mouth of the Tortoise (Kūrma), where there is unsurpassed success.
Know that the two squares on either side of the mouth are indeed the two forefeet of the Tortoise.
The two sides of the belly are to be known as the middle, the two feet as the remainder, and the tail;
thus should one who discerns the lamp-circle understand the tortoise.
Success occurs at the mouth, and purification arises when it is deficient in the middle.
If [the mantra] is in the head (udāsīna), it remains in hand; if in the belly (kukṣistha), one experiences suffering;
if at the feet (pādastha), the practitioner is afflicted by imprisonment, eradication, and the like; if in the tail (puccha), death occurs. Such is the arrangement of the tortoise (kūrma).

If the mantra consists of the syllables of the mantra itself, or if it is [formed] from the name of the Tortoise (Kūrma), or even from the name of the practitioner— what is there that the reciter cannot accomplish?
For the Lords of the Field (Kṣetrapālas), whose forms are the universe, exist in the form of the fifty letters.
Therefore, a field endowed with these qualities leads to success, and not otherwise.
If it possesses even two of these qualities, one may attain success through the mouth or the stomach.
Thus, having thus examined the *cakra*, if it is a friend [to the practitioner], it bestows all accomplishments.

In whatever land the Lord of Lamps (Dīpapati) resides, known by the name Saguna, one should go there with great effort; for that sacred seat (pīṭha), along with its attendants, is considered difficult to attain.
One should worship with rudrākṣas, bhadra-akṣas, and excellent sandalwood.
And with crystals, corals, and likewise those made from knots of kuśa grass.
Likewise, a wise person should fashion a rosary for the Vaiṣṇava mantra from these materials produced at Malaka or made of Tulasī wood;
however, a rosary originating from Rudrākṣa is considered to bestow infinite fruit.
A garland made of lotuses bestows success in the Gopāla-mantra;
a garland made of Jīvaputra flowers grants a son after a long time;
and a garland made of red sandalwood bestows sovereignty, enjoyment, and liberation.
That rosary made of coral brings all beings under one's control;
a garland of beads made from *kuśa* grass knots is considered to increase righteousness (*dharma*);
and that which is produced from *tulasī* quickly bestows liberation.
A rosary made of one hundred and eight beads bestows sovereignty upon men and grants liberation at the end of the body's life.
One seeking liberation should recite it twenty-five times; one seeking a son should recite it thirty times.
Forty beads constitute [the rosary] solely for the purpose of malevolent rites (*abhicāra*).
A garland made of fifty beads accomplishes all ritual actions (*sarvakarmaprasādhikā*).
The rosary (*akṣamālā*) is proclaimed to consist of the letters beginning with *a* and ending with *kṣa*.
O best of sages, one should visualize Mount Meru at the mouth of the *kṣānti* [syllable];

by this, the recitation (*japa*) of all mantras bestows all prosperity. One should perform the daily recitation with the hands, but not the optional (*kāmya*) recitation, due to a lack of understanding.
Beginning from the base of the ring finger and proceeding in order by rotation until the tips of the index and middle fingers,
one should recite over the eight joints;
this is declared to be the "Garland of the Hand" for the mantras of the Gopāla-tantra.
The thread should be made of cotton produced by virtuous women,
or likewise from silk thread or gold thread;
for the attainment of the supernatural powers beginning with *aṇimā* and ending with liberation, the gold thread is used.
Silk thread brings progeny and increases wealth and sons;
thread made from cotton bestows dharma, kāma, artha, and mokṣa.
Having tripled it and then tripled it again, one should weave it according to the treatises on craftsmanship.
Joining mouth to mouth, one should likewise join tail to tail;
thus the garland should be shaped like a cow's tail or auspiciously like a serpent.
Having fashioned the garland in this manner, O best of sages, one should indeed purify it.
One should fashion a lotus shape using nine young leaves of the *aśvattha* tree.

In its center, one should place the rosary while reciting the root mantra of the *Mātṛkā*. Having performed the daily and occasional rites and having prepared the general *arghya* offering, [one should proceed].

The wise one should wash [the image] with the Īśasūkta and smear it with abundant perfumes while reciting the Tatpuruṣa hymn; he should fumigate it with the Aghora hymn and consecrate it with more than a hundred recitations of that very same Aghora Sūkta.
The wise practitioner should fashion the *śamī* [garland] with the *vāmadeva* hymn;
taking each individual string, he should fashion a *brahmagranthi* knot. At the beginning of the threading, he should recite the mantras for each individual letter of the *mātṛkā*.
One should fashion three beads of that same material, each consisting of a single eye;
having thus strung the rosary together, one should place it upon a lotus.
Therein, having invoked the deity, one should worship Him with extensive offerings according to one's means.

One who is learned in the mantras and tantras should consecrate [the object] with the root mantra, either in the regular order or by means of the method of transposition (kramayoga). Likewise, one should consecrate it with the letters of the Mātṛkā.
Then, one should wash it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and again with the Īśa-sūkta.
Having smeared [the body] again with cow products, one may recite the mantra at will;
however, the practitioner of mantra should not recite another mantra. One should neither shake nor tremble [the body];
from shaking comes the loss of accomplishment, and trembling causes great suffering.
If a sound occurs, disease will arise; if it falls from the hand, it brings destruction.
If the thread is broken, death will occur; therefore, one should be most careful. At the conclusion of the recitation, one should place it at the level of the ear or in a high location.
"O Mālā, you are considered the bestower of all accomplishments for all the gods;
by that truth, O Mother, grant me success—salutations to you!
Having spoken thus and performed worship, one should then conceal [the rosary] where there is water.
One should not bestow the rosary and the mantra upon the uninitiated (paśus);
it has been stated by those who know the Tantras that by revealing them, there is a loss of the efficacy of the rite.
Furthermore, recitation performed with the thumb and forefinger yields a hundredfold merit.
By joining the index finger with the thumb, one effects the eradication of enemies;
by placing the thumb in the middle [of the fingers], the accomplishment of the mantra is certain;
and by joining the thumb with the ring finger, it is considered effective for eradication and subjugation.
The destruction of enemies is considered to occur through the application of the *jyeṣṭhā-kaniṣṭhā* [finger] yoga.
Thus, O learned one, the definitive determination of the rosary has been told to you.
One should bathe three times a day according to one's capacity; otherwise, twice or even once.
One should recite the mantra at the three junctions of the day; that shall be equal to formal worship. Or, worship may be performed once; one should not perform recitation without worship.
Alternatively, one may worship Hari in the morning, or at the conclusion of the recitation.
One should perform japa beginning at dawn until midday;
for until midday, mantras remain in the state of a bound soul (paśu),
existing merely as forms of letters uttered through the sound of the suṣumṇā.
They attain sovereignty.
One should contemplate the syllables of the mantra as being declared within the power of consciousness (cicchakti),
which alone is nourished by the supreme nectar in the highest ether (paramavyoman).
"Show me the equipment for self-perfection even without worship, fire-offerings, and the like.
Withdrawing the mind from sense objects and fixing the consciousness upon the meaning of the mantra,
one should recite it neither too fast nor too slow, like a string of pearls."
Japa is the repetition of syllables; it is of three kinds: mental, whispered, and vocal.
When one mentally recites the sequence of syllables consisting of phonemes, vowels, and words while keeping the meaning in mind, that is known as mental japa.
One whose mind is fixed on the deity should move the tongue and lips slightly;
that whispered recitation which is barely audible is known as *upāṃśu-japa*.
One should utter the mantra with the voice; that is known as *vācika-japa*.
The characteristics of recitation (japa) have been described through three divisions: mental, whispered, and vocal.
Mental recitation is for those desiring spiritual accomplishments (siddhi); whispered recitation is for those seeking nourishment (puṣṭi);
and vocal recitation is recommended for the purpose of killing—thus has the characteristic of recitation been explained.

Having thus performed the recitation (japa) previously, one should offer it in the form of light into the right hand of the deity with water for the arghya offering, along with kuśa grass and flowers. Having meditated upon that [offering] as being accompanied by the recitation, one should perform three breath-control exercises (prāṇāyāma).
At the beginning and at the end of the recitation (japa), one should perform [the ancillary rites] three times each.
One should perform the recitation day after day neither deficient nor excessive;
if one should do so through negligence, then one will obtain an undesirable result.
If [the ritual] is deficient, there will be the defect of missing limbs; if it is excessive, there will be extra limbs.
Those [rites] performed here according to the rules bear fruit without effort.
At the end of the recitation (japa), the practitioner should daily perform a fire-oblation (homa) consisting of one-tenth of that [number].
O Sage, one should perform libations (tarpaṇa) and sprinkling (sekam) according to those respective tenth-parts;
every day, one should feed Brahmins to pacify any deficiency or excess.
By the mere act of feeding Brahmins, that which is deficient in its parts certainly becomes complete.
One should perform service to the cows, which bestows glory upon the deities;
for when the cows are pleased, this cowherd [Kṛṣṇa] is also gratified.
At the conclusion of one's work, one should remember Kṛṣṇa for the purification of the inner organ (antaḥkaraṇa).
The chanting of the names of Viṣṇu destroys all obstacles;
alternatively, one should perform rites such as the *homa* until a hundred thousand [recitations] are completed.
Once the vow is fulfilled, one should likewise perform the libation (*tarpaṇa*) and other such rituals.

If one eats at night food offered to Viṣṇu while disparaging it, the deities of that food will become his [enemies], and he himself shall become the food of those beings. He should sleep on a bed of kuśa grass, or on a woolen blanket spread over kuśa grass.
One should perform this every day until the vow is completed with all its constituent parts.
One should perform the fire-oblation (homa) as before, using milk-rice (pāyasa) or lotuses;
in the absence of a fire-oblation, one should perform recitation (japa), which should be four times the number of oblations.

O Brahmin, for a Śūdra who is supported by another, the recitation (japa) is sixfold and eightfold respectively; the recitation of his wife is equal to that. And whatever recitation belongs to a Brahmin who performs no fire-sacrifice (homa), that same recitation belongs to his wife.

For the sake of accomplishment, one should recite the ten-syllabled supreme mantra one million times; at the conclusion of that, one should perform the fire sacrifice according to the rules and carry out the ritual action. The practitioner of the mantra should recite the ten-syllabled mantra ten thousand times.
This is the primary ritual procedure for each day; another, inferior method has also been described.
Thereafter, one should mutter eighteen hundred thousand times this excellent mantra of eighteen syllables.
Thus the rite has been fully explained; other details are found in the compendium of rituals (Kalpasaṃgraha).
Then one should perform the libation (tarpaṇa) with water from sacred fords mixed with moonlight;

having invoked the Deity into the water, one should worship Him along with His retinue according to the prescribed rite and with devotion, using water-based offerings such as the water for the feet (pādya).
One should satisfy the attendants by offering water with each handful (añjali).
Then, one should satisfy Puruṣottama with a tenth part of the oblation (homa),
having first uttered the mantra preceded by "Śrī" and also the word "Kṛṣṇa."
"May I satisfy [the deity]"—this is the mantra for libation (tarpaṇa) ending with "namas.
One should likewise perform the consecration (abhiṣeka) with a tenth part of the libations.
Having performed the ritual placements (nyāsa) and the protective seals (mudrā), one should worship [the deity] through non-differentiation from that [mantra].
Having meditated upon one's own self as being of the nature of Kṛṣṇa and endowed with rays of light, the practitioner,
taking a handful of water mixed with a single flower and fragrant substances,
should recite the root mantra.

"I consecrate Śrī Kṛṣṇa; obeisance!"—with these words one should perform the consecration. One should satisfy the Brāhmaṇas with a tenth part of the materials used for the consecration, providing them with milk, sugar, and delicious foods, preceded by great honor.
By merely feeding a brāhmaṇa, one who is deficient in limbs will certainly become complete in all parts.
One should by all means feed brāhmaṇas, for they are the very body of Kṛṣṇa;
wherever a twice-born man eats with satisfaction, there Hari himself eats.
Wherever the Lord of Śrī eats, there he eats the three worlds.
One should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the Guru with food, clothing, and other necessities;
by the mere satisfaction of the Guru, the perfection of the mantra (mantrasiddhi) will certainly occur.
"Those who know the Tantras have said that the Guru is the root of all this;
one should prepare abundant sweet food and eat together with many.
In this way, the practitioner whose mantra has been perfected shall accomplish every desired object."

Having thus performed the daily rite (nitya-krama), one should then perform the occasional rite (naimittika). O Brahmin, when the occasional rite has been performed, the perfection of the daily rite is attained;
otherwise, there will be no success even through hundreds of ritual performances.

Dwelling in the great sacred field of Mathurā and worshipping Kṛṣṇa, one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times; then the desired maṇḍala and other goals will be attained. [This should be done] in the great forest of Mandara, in the grove of Sarala trees.

Subsisting on milk and subsisting on wild forest flowers, one who has conquered the senses and recites the mantra ten thousand times with devotion beholds Kṛṣṇa with his own eyes. Having gone to Vṛndāvana, the practitioner of mantra should take recourse in the thirty-two sacred sites.

Having made this the objective, one should recite [the mantra] with devotion; one shall obtain qualities such as *aṇimā* and others. Dwelling upon a paved floor in the midst of a river flowing to the ocean, a renunciant subsisting on milk should recite it a hundred thousand times; thus, the sin arising from ten million births is destroyed.

One shall destroy [all obstacles] hereof, there is no doubt, and one also attains the perfection of speech (*vāksiddhi*). One should worship Kṛṣṇa on a mountain peak, subsisting on vegetables, roots, and fruits; having recited the mantra a hundred thousand times there as well, the union with the *khecarī* (the sky-farer) occurs.
Dwelling in a grove of *tulasī* on the bank of a river flowing to the ocean,
one who recites [the mantra] one hundred thousand times there effects the destruction of the sins of ten million births.
By worshipping Kṛṣṇa for one month with lotuses (*puṇḍarīka*) and white water-lilies (*vakra*), [one attains the same].
One will certainly obtain dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa held within one's hand.
When the sun is situated in Libra, one should perform ten thousand oblations with lotuses;
for such a person, prosperity shall become stable, followed by sons and grandsons.
One should daily offer oblations of *śrīpuṣpa* flowers with milk in the month of Vaiśākha;
this causes the destruction of all sins and increases all spiritual perfections (*siddhis*).
All the gods bow with devotion to that bull among men.
One who is intent on devotion should satisfy Kṛṣṇa with auspicious waters mixed with sugar and camphor,
performing one hundred and eight repetitions at the conclusion of the worship;
through his own two-syllable mantra, he attains perfection from the maṇḍala.
Whatever the practitioner desires, he shall obtain that without effort.
By constantly performing libations one hundred and eight times with water perceived as milk,
satisfying all [deities], he obtains all his desires and attains liberation.
Having worshipped with *kuśa* flowers for one month, remaining free from disease,
celibate, and established in his vow, one shall obtain his desire through a white *hayāri* flower mandala for the sake of fame and the increase of dharma.
Likewise, by means of Rakta-aśvamāra, one shall attain immovable prosperity;
likewise, by worshipping both together, one finds worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Devotion to cows should always be practiced, as well as the scratching of their bodies.
When the cows are constantly pleased, the cowherd becomes fully gratified; this is remembered as the occasional [occasion for] devotion toward Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, those of other births,
and women as well, O mighty-armed one.
Having performed even one of these, however, one may then perform rites for the fulfillment of specific desires.
[Thus ends the fourteenth chapter in the glorious Gautamīya. || 14 ||
I shall describe the ritual worship of Govinda throughout the three periods of the day according to the rules;
this applies to both mantras, as well as to others and to one's own self.
[One should meditate on Him] who is dark like a blue lotus flower and has eyes like blue water-lilies.
And [he saw] the charming infant Vārṣika seated upon a lotus throne,
with hands, feet, and lips possessing the luster of coral and the bimba fruit,
his curly locks of hair like a swarm of bees surrounding his moon-like face.
Resembling a jasmine flower or the moon, with the quarters of the sky illuminated by his necklaces;
shining like two royal jasmine blossoms, surpassing many pearls;
strewn with heaps of great gems and adorned with numerous golden ornaments.
He was self-nourished, with limbs tinged by dust, rising with his cow amidst clouds of dust,
watched with great wonder by the cowherds, cowherd-maidens, and herds of cows,
and gazed upon with overflowing love even by Brahmā and Śaṅkara.
Having thus meditated upon the Supreme One, who is praised by the gods headed by Indra and by the sages, one should worship Kṛṣṇa, bowing down with the weight of devotion;
[one should worship Him] as surrounded by the threefold cycle of ignorance, the senses, and the like.

Having offered milk, sugar-candy, ghee, fresh milk, plantain, butter, *covā*, *rambhā* fruit, and whatever else is dear to Bāla, and having performed eight thousand recitations (*japa*), one should propitiate Kṛṣṇa.
With various kinds of hymns, devotees, knowing the mantras, should satisfy [the deity] one hundred and eight times with water conceived as milk, along with prostrations and circumambulations;
then, being ungraspable, they should offer themselves into that lotus of its digits.
Then, having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) with the mantra known as *brahmārpaṇa*, one should lead [the consciousness] to the heart.
Then, according to the previously mentioned sequence, one should complete the remainder otherwise.
Eating the remnants of the oblation at night, one should spend the night alone.
Whoever thus offers devotion to Kṛṣṇa for even a single month shall be honored by the world as a poet and an eloquent speaker; having attained Lakṣmī who follows him,
and being joined with sons, friends, and kinsmen, he goes at last to the supreme state.
At midday, he beheld that Vāsudeva situated in the midst of the circle of kings,
within a radiant palace in Dvāravatī,
which was filled with wish-fulfilling trees and resounded with the songs of auspicious birds.
In that delightful place with beautiful sandy banks, adorned with clusters of lotuses, blue lilies, and other flowers, and shaded by something [else],
it was further embellished with jeweled pillars, jewel-lamps, and strings of pearls.
One should meditate upon that arrangement of its sides, crowded with hundreds of various and diverse trees, together with *punnāga* and *keśara* trees,
as well as various other kinds of trees such as *pāṭala*, *campaka*, and so forth.
Surrounded by Vakula, Sarala, Vamya, and Kuruvaka trees, as well as by all-seasonal blossoming trees whose branches were bent low with flowers,
[he saw him] seated for a moment upon a jeweled lion-throne on a lotus petal.
Broad-chested, with limbs as beautiful as flowers, he enchants the hosts of kṣatriyas;
his navel resembles a lotus, and he is the imperishable one with eyes like lotuses;
with beautiful eyebrows, forehead, and face, he has a smile like a flower and lovely eyes.
With beautiful cheeks and lovely copper-hued lips, dark-complexioned and the abode of auspiciousness;
with the ends of his hair dark and curly, adorned with variegated garments and ornaments;
with a neck like a conch-shell and a broad chest resplendent with the Kaustubha gem.

Possessing great strength, with a broad chest and four mighty arms, he shone with a firm and well-proportioned waist; adorned by his lower lip, he was graced by the glorious marks that circle to the right and embellish the entire world.
With symmetrical knees and shanks, his pair of feet formed the svastika;
his toes were adorned with beautiful, high-set anklets, and his elevated feet were graced by finger-rings.
He was clothed in a pair of yellow garments and various kinds of ornaments and the like.
His four arms, adorned with armlets and gems, shone forth, beautified by a girdle of bells, a forest garland, and golden necklaces, and further embellished by a jeweled necklace.
Her feet were beautified by anklets joined with variegated bracelets;
she shone with golden finger-rings set with various gems;
her ears were adorned with shimmering makara-shaped earrings covered in endless jewels.
With a beautiful navel made of gold, adorned with various variegated and colorful flowers covered by hovering bees, his crown was radiant;
he held the conch, discus, mace, and lotus, with a peaceful face for a moment.
Endowed with divine marks, adorned with divine ornaments,
wearing divine garlands and garments, and anointed with divine perfumes;
[he is to be visualized] on the forehead, the heart, the belly, the throat, the arms, and the sides.
Adorned with a half-moon-shaped tilaka made of sandalwood paste that shone brilliantly,
he repeatedly threatened his enemies who had become a burden to the earth, and he consulted again and again with his chief ministers, such as Uddhava.
For the very purpose of their destruction, by means of the principles of Dharma, Artha, Nīti, and logic; thus,
when the time of midday had arrived, meditating upon the Teacher of the World,
he invoked him according to the rules and worshipped him with ritual offerings out of devotion.
The limbs are designated as before; one should worship them starting with Pūra.
[Then worship] Rukmiṇī, Satyabhāmā, Kālindī, Sulakṣaṇā, Nāgnajitī, Jāmbavatī, Mitravindā, and Suśīlikā.
Thus, these eight powers, the beloveds of the god Kṛṣṇa, are to be worshipped:
the Sudarśana discus in the southeast, the water-born conch in the southwest,
the divine mace in the northwest, and the radiant lotus in the northeast.
Then, on the outer petals, one should first worship Vasudeva and Devakī, as well as Nanda-gopa and Yaśodā;
one should worship them with water for the feet, respectful offerings, and flowers, starting from the eastern petal.
One should worship Balabhadra, Subhadrā, and Rohiṇī in the north;
likewise Sudāna, Dāna, Vasudāman, and Kiṅkiṇī.
On the left side of the deity, one should worship the sandals of the Guru.
Having worshipped there the Supreme Guru as well as the Parāpara Guru,
and having worshipped up to the sandals (pādukās), one should likewise sacrifice to the Pūrvasiddhas.
Having sacrificed to Gaṇapati in the east, one should worship him outside of that.
One should [install] Indra and the other world-protectors in their respective directions with their own mantras;
as well as Kumuda, the one named Kumuda, Puṇḍarīka, Vāmana, Śaṅkukarṇa, Sarvanetra, Sumukha, and Supratiṣṭhita.
One should worship these [deities] in clockwise order, starting from the eastern petal;
one should worship Viṣvaksena in the middle between the north and the northeast.
Having thus worshipped Hari with devotion, one should present the food offering (naivedya).
One should offer milk-rice, sugar, cakes, candied sugar and other sweets, plantain fruit, and white side-dishes within a golden vessel;
or alternatively, in a silver vessel, or again, in a copper vessel.
In the absence [of these], it may be offered on a lotus leaf; otherwise, one would go to hell.
Then, according to the ritual, [it may be placed] in a vessel of gold or silver.
Therein, one should offer boiled milk with sugar, along with side dishes and *pāyasa*.
One should present various kinds of offerings to Govinda;
having offered royal honors, and having praised and bowed down, one should dismiss Him.
He who, free from longing, thus meditates upon the divine Gopāla—
All the kings, along with their attendants, are his servants;
likewise, all the princes and queens follow him.
Having enjoyed excellent pleasures here, he shall go to the abode of Viṣṇu in the end.
One should perform one hundred and eight oblations (homa), observing that specific number;
by means of both oblation and libation (tarpaṇa), the practitioner shall accomplish all goals.
One should perform the oblation in the morning or likewise at midday.
One should perform the night oblation at midday; such is the prescribed rule.
Regarding the third period of worship, there is a conceptualization of time;
some learned scholars state that it may be performed either in the evening or at night.
If the enemy is present in the evening, one should use the eighteen-syllable mantra; otherwise, the ten-syllable one.

The exponents of Brahman declare that neither both [exist] nor both do not exist. At evening, in Dvāravatī, situated within the Citraka garden and surrounded by hundreds of ponds filled with fragrant blue lotuses—
In the midst of the Nandana garden, situated within a grove of *kadamba* trees,
it was adorned with pillars made of blazing jewels and pathways of exquisite gems;
it was beautified by walls and gates shimmering with various kinds of jewels.
A mansion made of great jewels was surrounded by sages—
by the best of sages such as Nārada and others, Śaunaka, Pippalāda, and the rest;
it was encircled by the sons of Brahmā, Sanaka and his brothers, as they deliberated upon the determination of ultimate truth.
To Nārada, Parvata, Jiṣṇu, Niśa, Uddhava, Dāruka,
Viśvaksena, and Śaileya— who were all marked by his compassionate glance—
he was bestowing his own supreme, imperishable abode upon those sages.
Resembling ten million moons, illuminating the space of the universe,
strewn with various multitudes of jewels, and adorned with a great crown;
with makara-earrings shining like the sun amidst heaps of many gems.
His chest shines with the Kaustubha gem as he moves, adorned with a garland of living beings;
his arms are encircled by eight bracelets and armlets studded with various clusters of jewels;
and he is clothed in a pair of yellow garments that possess the luster of molten gold.
With a charming and noble belly and a deep lotus-like navel,
with lofty lotus-feet adorned with shimmering golden rings,
and endowed with two pairs of brilliant jeweled bracelets and anklets;
With lips red as rabbit’s blood and lotus feet of a deep crimson hue,
bearing the conch, discus, mace, and lotus, and adorned with a forest garland;
because his intrinsic nature is pure knowledge, he is brilliantly white— that Supreme beyond the supreme.

Those who discourse on Brahman meditate upon the Supreme Self as being like a fresh lotus in its power to destroy ignorance, resembling ten million suns due to its dispelling of the darkness of avidyā.
Having meditated thus, one should worship according to the procedure for the central image;
one should recite the mantra one thousand times, perform libations (tarpaṇa) equal to one-tenth of the number of fire-oblations (homa),
and offer milk in a vessel adorned with silver and containing sugar-candy.

Having offered the preliminary services and then paid obeisance, one should dismiss [the deities]. Having meditated upon the householders, forest-dwellers, and renunciants within the lotus of the heart, and having worshipped them with mental offerings according to the sages' tradition.
Secluded and living as a householder, one should perform worship together with sages;
through Vāsudeva and the others, one shall attain the state of Nirvāṇa.
At the time of sunset, a person should worship Vāsudeva according to the prescribed rite.
All the gods pay homage to him, let alone humans and monkeys;
having crossed the terrible and shoreless ocean of saṃsāra, which is infested with crocodiles,
and having experienced the objects of the senses, the man of knowledge shall attain the supreme state.
Having abandoned the evil tendencies accumulated over ten million births,
one attains liberation in a single lifetime— the state of absolute isolation (kaivalya) fashioned by Viṣṇu. The heroes always behold that supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
At night, one should meditate on the son of Devakī, whose mind is overcome by love,
who is resting from the assembly of the rāsa dance, situated in the midst of the circle of gopīs,
and who has gone to Vṛndāvana in the shade of a wish-fulfilling tree.
He stands firm, playing the flute and singing, encircled by a forest garland;
dark-complexioned, wearing yellow garments, and surrounded by a multitude of gopīs; He is served by gods, asuras, gandharvas, and apsarases.
He was being praised by Yakṣas, hosts of Vidyādharas, and birds dwelling upon the earth,
as well as by Brahmarṣis and Devarṣis who were filled with great wonder;
and he was being gazed upon by various kinds of Apsarases who were likewise struck with amazement.
Being licked by hundreds of millions of Gandharvas and celestial women,
he was a jewel resembling a blue lotus, with a face like the beautiful moon,
a countenance like a full-blown lotus, and eyes like lotus petals.
Padmanābha, whose hands and feet are like lotuses, whose lips resemble lotuses,
the refuge of all beings, the beloved of the Gopī folk;
sometimes seated upon a lotus that has been crushed by his own weight.
Surrounded by hundreds of millions of women who had assumed various forms,
he was sporting and singing with divine melodies;
he shone resplendent in the midst of his beloveds, two by two.
Like a column of emerald encased in gold,
he was sometimes playfully stealing the garments of cowherd women;
at other times, he was dwelling among a multitude of women, laughing with them in jest.

Having thus meditated upon the enemy of Madhu— who is fashioned by hosts of gods, honored with showers of flowers, fanned by celestial women, and whose movements are characterized by longing for desire— the one firm in his vows should worship him.
It is surrounded by sixteen pairs beginning with Keśara,
likewise encompassed on all sides by Mahiṣīs and Goyīs;
having thus worshipped according to the rule in either a vessel of bell-metal or silver.
Having offered milk in the vessel, one should likewise gratify the couples;

then, having recited prayers, praised, and bowed down, one should dismiss Him into the lotus of the heart. Thus, with a pure mind and free from worldly ties, one should worship the Lord of the worlds.
He certainly becomes an heir to virtue, nobility, desire, and liberation;
the Brāhmaṇa shall become a master of the Vedas and an actual Indra upon earth;
the Kṣatriya shall be the best of kings, and the Vaiśya shall possess abundant wealth.
Having enjoyed all pleasures, the Śūdra shall go to the supreme state at the end.
Thus, O Brāhmaṇa, has been told to you that which destroys the fear of saṃsāra—
the threefold worship which cuts away the root-ignorance.
[Thus ends the fifteenth chapter in the glorious Gautamīya. || 15 ||
Gautama said: "O Omniscient One, tell me the cause of your state as Bālakṛṣṇa—
that which was previously declared by Brahmā when you were honored through service and austerity."
O best of sages, by your grace, nothing in the three worlds remains unknown to you; therefore,
with a composed mind, tell me everything in due order regarding the worship of Gopāla, for I am indeed eager to hear it.
Nārada said:
"O best among the knowers of the Vedas, today I shall tell you of the most wonderful childhood of the Lord;
there is nothing that should be hidden from you."
"O Kṛṣṇa, through austerity you have purified your mind; you are a devotee by certainty.
Tāra, Prajāpati, Śakra, Māyā, and Bindu—know this to be the supreme mantra, a most wonderful secret."
It produces great wonder and causes the agitation of enemies;
moreover, by the mere recitation of this, the fruits of the four aims of life are accomplished.
Furthermore, those mantras of Gopāla which will be spoken right here in this very tantra—
Let it be observed that this very [mantra], when illuminated, bestows the fruit;
this is declared to be the crest-jewel (cūḍāmaṇi) of the God in his form as a child.
I am known as the Sage (muni), and Gāyatrī is said to be the meter (chandas).
Kṛṣṇa, who bestows the fruits of all desires, has been described by the deity.
This [mantra] is uttered as a combination and is said to be in the middle pitch (madhyama-svara).
It is differentiated by the colors of time [corresponding to the numbers]: two, four, six, twelve, and eleven.
Having constructed the yantras of Manu, one should perform meditation with a concentrated mind;
one should meditate upon the Lord of the Universe, who has just been born, situated within the maternity chamber in the inner courtyard of Kaṃsa’s palace in the city of Mathurā.

It was surrounded on all sides by Siddhas, Cāraṇas, Gandharvas, Devas, Dānavas, and Kinnaras; by Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and Vetālas; and by sky-dwellers and those who roam the quarters, as well as by Vidyādharīs, goddesses, and Kinnarīs.
Hari was being gazed upon with joy by Brahmā together with his sons,
and by Indra and the other guardians of the quarters who were showering down showers of radiant flowers;
he was four-armed, bearing the conch, the discus, the mace, and the Śārṅga bow.
One should remember the discus in the upper right hand and the mace in the lower right hand;
the Śārṅga bow in the upper left hand and the conch in the lower left hand. He resembles a fresh rain-cloud and is clothed in yellow silk garments.
Upon his own head, which shines with the splendor of the coils of the serpent Śeṣa,
he wears a golden crown adorned with the finest jewels;
his remaining locks of hair are graced by fragrant pārijāta flowers.
Resplendent with a musk tilaka applied to the surface of his forehead,
shining upon the expanse of his brow like a crescent of the eighth-day moon,
and illuminated by a pair of eyes possessing the beauty of full-blown white lotuses.
Adorned with a bow resembling the rainbow of the god of love,
graced by a nose as beautiful as a victorious sesame flower,
and illuminated by a moon-like face that resembles the crescent of the new moon;
The Lord was enchanting with rows of teeth as brilliant as pomegranate seeds and jasmine buds;
his lips were radiant, shining like ripe bimba fruits;
and he wore shimmering makara-shaped earrings set with gold and many jewels.
His arms shone like great emerald pillars;
he was adorned with armlets, bracelets, and coils of jewels and gold; his neck was shaped like a conch shell, his chest was broad, and he was resplendent with a necklace of pearls.
He bears the Śrīvatsa mark, his chest is radiant with the brilliant Kaustubha gem,
he wears a garland of small bells set with gems and lapis lazuli,
and his waist is adorned and bound with a silk thread.
With His beautiful, jewel-encrusted anklets upon His lovely lotus-feet,
He was gazed upon by Devakī, Vasudeva, Śiva,
and Brahmā, who stood in the intermediate directions with palms joined in reverence and mouths chanting hymns of praise.
Having thus meditated upon the Supreme Self, the Guru, and one's own self as being like the peak of Mount Meru and seated upon Garuḍa,
and having perceived them as a single unity, one should then begin the worship.
On a surface smeared with camphor, saffron, and moist white sandalwood paste,
one should draw the diagram of the Son of Devakī with beautiful lines using either a rod made of coral or one made of gold.
First, a circle in the form of filaments (kiñjalka) should be drawn;
from that, a four-petalled [lotus] should be written, then a circle with eight petals, and then one with ten petals.
It should have equal lines, be quadrangular, and be beautifully adorned with four gates.
Adorned with seed-syllables at its four gates and graced by four corners,
one should worship the Lord of Gods in the center and then worship [the deities] on the four petals:
the god Īśvara in the northeast and Pitāmaha in the southeast.
In the southwest one should worship Vasudeva, and in the northwest Ambika;
likewise, on the eight petals, one should worship those beloved of the gods—
serene beings clad in red garments, holding lotuses in their lotus-like hands.
Resplendent with all ornaments and radiant with the charms of youth,
they are like honey-bees with their eyes fixed upon the lotus-face of the glorious Lord.
Then, outside of that, the world-protectors (lokapālas) are to be worshipped on the ten petals.
One should worship Garuḍa at the western gate and Jaya at the eastern;
likewise, Vijaya at the southern and Nārada at the northern. All of them have their hands joined in the añjali gesture and are vocal with beautiful hymns of praise.
Adorned with shimmering forest garlands and clad in yellow silk garments,
one should then worship the conch, the discus, the Kaumodakī mace, the Śārṅga bow,
and the cow; furthermore, one should worship them on the exterior of that [image].
Having worshipped Airāvata and the others, as well as the eight Gaṇas outside of that, one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times in the Kṛta age; likewise, double that in the Tretā age;
having recited three hundred thousand times in the Dvāpara age, one should recite four hundred thousand times in the Kali age.
Then the practitioner, longing for accomplishment, should perform the ritual applications.
One desiring unblemished prosperity should offer oblations with *lakṣmī* flowers;
one should offer this with clarified butter (*ājya*) for the abundance of food.
One brings Brahmins under control with wild flowers, kings with jasmine,
Vaishyas with fragrant blossoms, and Shudras even with blue lotuses;
one brings all people of the city under sway with *pūlavarṇa* flowers, and women with lotuses.
The cowherd Govinda, who is dear to the community of cows, quickly effects the pacification of cattle by performing a well-prepared oblation in the cowshed with milk-rice mixed with clarified butter;
he is the Lord who assumes the form of a child and is adorned with a network of tinkling bells.
Having remembered [the ancestors], the practitioner should offer libations with auspicious waters, perceiving them as milk.
Being pleased, he (the deity) bestows upon him wealth, grain, garments, and other such things.

One should fashion a six-syllabled [mantra] encircled by the root-mantra, shining in the corners of a pair of fire-triangles. One should fashion a ten-petalled lotus, vibrating with the ten-syllabled [mantra] and encircled by the seed-syllable of desire (Kāma-bīja).

A lotus situated upon its filaments, with petals shining with the forms of Murāri; the sixteen syllables dancing as consonants upon the filaments; the eight missing letters placed within the pairs of modified petals;
encircled by the noose and goad, and joined with the city of the earth and the pair of Yugas.
The yantra presided over by Lord Govinda, encircled by the eight-syllable mantra,
is remembered as bestowing the fruits of virtue, wealth, and desire, and providing protection from all [evils].
It consists of the letter 'Pa' (pakṣāntaka), situated upon the earth (dharā), and adorned with the seed-syllable and the bindu.

This is declared to be the supreme seed-mantra of the Piṇḍa, which bestows all accomplishments. One should recite it four hundred thousand times; thereafter, one should perform oblations amounting to a tenth part of that, offer libations amounting to a tenth part of that, and perform consecrations amounting to a tenth part of that.
One should also feed Brahmins in the sequence of one-tenth the number [of offerings],
and one should worship Gaṇeśa, Bhāskara, Rudra,
and Gaurī in the intermediate directions of the King of Yantras, preceded by their respective mantras.
By merely retaining this, a person shall become a knower of the three periods of time;
whatever he desires, he shall accomplish all of it—of this there is no doubt.
There exists neither a mantra nor a yantra equal to this.
O you of noble vows, this has been told to you solely out of a spirit of love.
[Thus ends the sixteenth chapter in the glorious Gautamīya. || 16 ||
Now I shall describe the applications common to both mantras,
by performing which the excellent practitioner is well-honored in both worlds;
and I shall also describe at various points the mantras that have those very [deities] as their essence.
I bow to that Son of Devakī, who possesses the luster of a freshly blossomed lotus,
who bears the conch, discus, mace, and lotus, and who wears a forest garland;
having thus meditated upon Him during the Brāhma-muhūrta, one should recite the excellent mantra one hundred thousand times.

Having recited [the mantra], one attains supreme intelligence and becomes a leader among poets. Alternatively, having meditated upon him as having the luster of crystal, with two arms, holding a pen and a book, then [reciting] one hundred thousand times during the Brāhmī Muhūrta;
Having recited this mantra, one who knows the three periods of time becomes equal to Bṛhaspati.
Now, indeed, the mantra equal to that is being proclaimed; listen to it according to its true nature. Having first uttered the word "Śrīmat," one should then say "Mukundacaraṇau."
With the utterance of "Sada," I take refuge in that dark-complexioned, tender infant playing upon his mother’s lap,
the two-armed one who drinks from her breast; by this, one shall become a possessor of the power of hearing and retaining all that is heard.
By reciting this one hundred thousand times, one obtains an equal fruit.
With the seed-syllable of desire (*kāma*) at its beginning, what mantra on this earth would not be accomplished?
Having withdrawn the divine limbs [of the visualization], one should offer them to the Mother, as to a Guru.
By meditating for a single *muhūrta* on the young calf moving about in the pasture and reciting these two excellent mantras,
the wise man becomes a knower of the meaning of all scriptures;
he certainly becomes proficient in the meaning of all the Vedas and possesses true knowledge.

Meditating thus upon the best of men— wandering in the courtyard of Nanda, grey with a mass of dust, radiant with a multitude of blazing jewels, and eager to behold Yaśodā— one should recite the mantra while established in the observance of the rules.
What on earth cannot be accomplished by one hundred thousand recitations of the *nāda*?
If one drinks water every morning while reciting it one hundred and eight times,
then even one who is mute, one whose speech is corrupted, the dull-witted, or as inert as a stone [shall attain eloquence].
By drinking this water, one becomes directly like the Lord of Speech;
there is no doubt here—this is the truth, the truth, and not otherwise.
Having set down the cart with his feet, he likewise wept like an ordinary man.
Having meditated thus, "One should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times," he will certainly be liberated from calamities;
he shall have no fear of enemies, nor of kings, nor even of bandits,
and he shall never experience any terror whatsoever, O observer of noble vows.
Now I shall further proclaim another secret honored by the gods;
having known this, O best of practitioners, the adept shall obtain the fruit of the ritual application.
One should worship Brahmā conjoined with Soma, adorned at the head by the vowels.
One should extract the King of Rituals (Kalparāja), pervaded by Bindu and Nāda;
likewise,
one should extract the second seed-syllable situated in Na-vī-ti-hotra, endowed with the vowels and pervaded by Bindu and Nāda.

One should extract the third seed-syllable, which is joined with the letter *va*, adorned with the fourth vowel, and endowed with the *nāda* and *bindu*. Then [one should take] the letter at the end of *tha* (the letter *śa*), joined with *Śambhu* (the letter *u*) and provided with the *indu* (*bindu*).
