Known as the *daurgabīja*, it wards off all calamities. The word for Śambhu joined with fire (*ra*), and endowed with *māyā* and the *bindu*, is the seed of the entire universe, renowned as *mahāmāyā*.
A practitioner joined with this [mantra] shall accomplish even that which is impossible to achieve.
The syllable *vāṃ*, conjoined with fire (*ra*) and adorned with the fourth vowel (*ī*),
is declared to be the seed-syllable of Śrī, bestowing all happiness upon men.
The seed-syllable that deludes the three worlds is joined with Viriñci (the letter *va*) and Indra (the letter *la*), adorned with the fourth vowel (*ī*), and marked by the Nāda, Bindu,
and Kalā; that syllable ending in a consonant is said to be endowed with the sixth vowel (*ū*).
The seed-syllable *kūrca* is traditionally known as being joined with the *nāda*, the *bindu*, and the *kalā*.
Having correctly understood the functions of these seed-syllables from a teacher and from the scriptures, the knower of mantras should accomplish all rites.

Otherwise, there would be no accomplishment whatsoever even in hundreds of kalpas. Meru, which is the fourteenth vowel (au), joined with fire (ra) below, is called the Nṛsiṃha-bīja; it destroys possession by spirits and epilepsy.
Having become composed in mind and having made a rosary of lotus seeds,
one who is devoted to the vow of celibacy should recite the mantra ten thousand times; thus,
desires will be attained with little effort, and one shall not be born poor.
All his desires are fulfilled; of this there is no doubt.
One who is constantly devoted to ritual action should worship Kṛṣṇa with *canya* flowers.
All [beings], including Brahmins, become submissive; of this there is no doubt.
One should mentally worship the one in the form of Gopāla with jasmine flowers;
kings become submissive—of this there is no doubt to be made.
Indeed, by means of red flowers, Vaiśyas likewise become submissive.
The Śūdras should worship with blue lotuses; one should offer black meat.
One should perform oblations with red flowers mixed with sesame seeds and rice.
Having recited the mantra eight thousand times, the ascetic (yati) should wear the sacred ash.
When this is worn upon the forehead, all indeed become submissive;
by means of this, kings come under one's control,
and women, sons, and ministers likewise become entirely subject to him.
One who desires marriage should recite the mantra eight thousand times for one month,
remaining established in the vow while meditating upon Kṛṣṇa situated in the center of the Rāsa-maṇḍala;
he shall thus marry an excellent, beautiful woman who illuminates her entire lineage.
One should meditate upon that Hari who, when entreated by a twice-born man saying, "Protect my son!
Protect him!", recovered the abducted son and gave him back;
such a person desiring a son shall obtain a beautiful son within one month.
Having propitiated Kṛṣṇa with jasmine flowers (*kundapuṣpa*), a maiden should meditate upon Him as being endowed with long life and unimpeded strength and vigor;
likewise, she should recite the mantra eight thousand times for two months.
Having obtained her husband as desired, she sports with him for a long time.
Having touched collyrium, flowers, garments, betel, sandalwood,
and various other objects of enjoyment, she should recite the mantra one hundred times.
O best of sages, by this very method, women quickly become submissive like slaves to whomever they are given;
indeed, by this very rite, a woman may bring a man under her control.

One desiring food and drink should offer one thousand and eight oblations with *śrī* flowers mixed with white rice; he shall become possessed of food. Having meditated upon the one who bears the universal form (*viśvarūpa*), one should recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times.
One shall become composed in mind, glorious, renowned, and famous.
Those afflicted by ghosts, spirits, piśācas, and grahas such as Skanda,
should meditate upon the one who drinks from the breast of Pūtanā and recite the mantra one hundred times.
Malevolent planets perish and flee hither and thither;
and those bitten by snakes, scorpions, fanged creatures, mice, and the like, should meditate upon Kṛṣṇa, the subduer of Kālīya, and recite [the mantra].
One should destroy the terrible poison of the one who threatens by means of the *huṃkāra*.
Here too, listen to another mantra, the pair of seeds beginning with *krūṃ*, according to its true nature.
And he performs a divine dance in the midst of the hoods of Kālīya.
I bow to the son of Devakī, Acyuta, the king of dancers;
one afflicted by fever should worship him with mantras and likewise recite them one hundred and eight times—
Kṛṣṇa, praised during the fever, together with Balarāma and Pradyumna.
By meditating on [the deity] standing upon Garuḍa, burning the city of Vāṇa and crushing it with his own fever, one destroys in an instant diseases such as Śītalā,
Kāmalā, and those arising from quartan fever (cāturthaka).

The mantra-practitioner destroys spleen-tumors, liver-tumors, wind-disorders, and epilepsy merely by his glance; of this there is no doubt. [He visualizes] the cowherd standing there, holding a staff and a rope, and accompanied by a cow.
Having meditated upon Kṛṣṇa, one who possesses devotion should mutter the mantra for a month;
he whose mind is set on becoming the domestic priest of a king shall obtain that position by offering oblations with white flowers sprinkled with honey from that maṇḍala.

Having attained great sovereignty, a man will certainly become renowned throughout the world; for when a terrible danger from wind, rain, and the like has fully arisen, a person should meditate upon Kṛṣṇa, the upholder of Govardhana, and recite the mantra.

Fear shall quickly perish; there is no need for deliberation on this point. One who desires rain should meditate upon Kṛṣṇa situated in Vṛndāvana and recite [the mantra] eight thousand times; he will obtain rain without a doubt.
Having meditated thus with the mind, one should cause rain to fall during the rainy season.
Likewise, having meditated upon a reservoir of water, one should recite [the mantra] eight thousand times;
then even at the wrong time, a great rain will occur—of this there is no doubt.
One who desires to sing should meditate upon Kṛṣṇa playing the flute while singing;
having offered eight hundred oblations of clarified butter, he is sung of along with the Kinnaras.
One who desires victory should mutter [the mantra] while [Kṛṣṇa] is taking away the wish-fulfilling tree (kalpakadruma).
Having meditated upon Acyuta, who is praised by the deities and mounted upon Garuḍa,
the practitioner of self-control should offer oblations with fuel-sticks of red karavīra;
after one thousand and eight offerings, the enemy will be defeated within a fortnight.
When one has encountered fear from kings and the like, or is beset by doubts in a difficult assembly,
by offering ten thousand oblations, one will certainly destroy that [fear] at that very moment;
likewise, with flowers such as blue lotuses, one should offer one thousand and eight.
Having meditated upon Hari, who dwells in the center of Dvārakā and is accompanied by the treasures such as the conch,
one should perform a rite for peace (śāntika) by offering oblations of rice grains and dūrvā grass;
[one should likewise meditate upon] Gopāla, wearing a forest garland, singing at the foot of a kadamba tree.
Having meditated upon Janārdana while touching *kadamba* flowers,
and having offered oblations with a hundred *apāmārga* plants, one should recite the mantra eight thousand times; thus,
having brought all desires under control, even a wise person quickly attains success.
At the royal gate, in the assembly hall, and during legal proceedings,
one who knows the mantra should first recite the mantra eight hundred times before uttering the initial statement.
By this very procedure, one shall be victorious everywhere.
A person desiring liberation who meditates upon the imperishable, supreme Kṛṣṇa— the lotus-eyed one praised by Sanaka and others, clad in white garments and bearing the conch and discus—
should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times.
Having encased [the mantra] with the two *tārās* (oṃ and svāhā) and having duly taken up his station,
one who worships Kṛṣṇa within the maṇḍala of the lotus-wheel while offering devotion is liberated from the ocean of saṃsāra; of this there is no doubt.

A Brahmin counselor who desires to bring the three worlds under his control should meditate upon Acyuta as he sings on a flute adorned with beautiful forest flowers; having worshipped him according to the prescribed rites, he should perform one hundred thousand recitations along with the accompanying fire-oblations.
Having recited [this], one becomes beloved by all the worlds; it is not otherwise.
Having enjoyed divine-like happiness, O twice-born one, he goes to Viṣṇu’s own body.
One should worship Kṛṣṇa mentally and recite [the mantra] a thousand times every day.

By knowing this sacrifice, one attains liberation within a year and does not return; this is the rule for those in the [other] stages of life, for householders, and even for renunciants. One desiring intelligence should offer oblations into the fire with palāśa wood and clarified butter mixed together.
Having meditated as before with fuel-sticks (*samidh*), one shall possess superhuman intelligence (*medhā*).
If one desires eloquence, one shall obtain speech by reciting the *Brāhma* [mantra] for a mere moment;
by reciting it a hundred times for six months, one shall become both eloquent and wise.
One who desires victory over enemies should meditate upon Hari, the remover of the *pārijāta* tree,
mounted upon Garuḍa, who has conquered all the inhabitants of heaven;
he should also offer oblations with sacrificial fuel-sticks produced from the *karavīra* plant.
Having recited the mantra one hundred thousand times, the best of those who know mantras should likewise offer oblations one hundred thousand times;
having conquered these hosts of enemies and not being overcome by them according to the rule, he who, meditating upon the Blessed One, should cause the consecration to be performed.
Having meditated upon Him dwelling in the city of Dvārakā, accompanied by the treasures Śaṅkha and Padma,
one should offer white rice grains with sesame seeds and clarified butter one thousand and eight times; thus, one certainly attains consecration.
Desiring to bring all the worlds under his control, O Lotus-seated One,
he constantly adorned the Blessed Lord with a garland of kadamba flowers—
the Lord who was dressed as a cowherd, who was being entreated by Sanaka and other yogis.
One should meditate upon the Leader of All, adorned with various flower garlands and a forest wreath, singing at the foot of a Kadamba tree;
one should also perform one thousand and eight oblations of clarified butter using sacrificial fuel sticks.
One should offer oblations mixed with honey and clarified butter; thus one shall become a subduer of all the worlds.
Those seeking liberation should meditate for a moment upon the Blessed One, who is being contemplated by Sanaka and others, as well as by other perfected beings and yogis, seated upon a lotus petal.

Upon a lofty divine lion-throne, its lotus-center invoked by hosts led by Brahmā, Indra, and Śaṅkara, as well as by the inhabitants of heaven, by Prahlāda and other foremost devotees, and by other great-souled ones;
Having thus meditated upon the Supreme Self, who increases the joy of Yaśodā,
one should worship Puruṣottama with leaves of Palāśa and Tulasī, auspicious golden flowers, or mentally, according to one's ability.
One should meditate upon oneself as the son of Devakī, who carries a staff as a mere plaything;
whatever the practitioner desires, he shall obtain that from every quarter.
By this method, one shall accomplish everything belonging to the Supreme Self.
The wise one should also join it with the fourth [vowel] of Viṣṇu;
one should know that the third and eighth [consonants], together with Brahmā and Viṣṇu, [are to be joined].
[Thus ends the seventeenth chapter in the glorious Gautamīya. || 17 ||
Now I shall describe other applications that are difficult to find on earth;
by performing these correctly, a human being immediately attains divinity. Whatever he seeks to accomplish exists for him on earth, in heaven, or in the subterranean realm.
Having seen Hari— who is like a cool autumn moon, dispelling the heat of Bhīṣma—
and gazing upon him with compassion as he showers nectar,
one should meditate thus; through this combined recitation, even an incurable fever is destroyed.

It quickly destroys fainting, burning sensations, diseases, eruptions, and those arising from poison or insects; it extinguishes the fire [of affliction] when one offers oblations of *amṛtā* and *śāṃśapa*.
That *kṛtyā* sent by the King of Kāśī toward the city of Dvārakā—
Having cut that [noose] with his own weapon, he [the enemy] burned those various cities with his splendor;
remembering Hari as he was thus burning them, one should recite [the mantra] ten thousand times with devotion,
and likewise offer ten thousand oblations at night with seven types of wood smeared with one's own fat.
Malevolent spells (*kṛtyā*) sent by others shall never devour them.

Through the worship of *ḍākinīs*, as well as through the application of recitation (*japa*) and fire-offerings (*homa*), [one subdues] malevolent spells, *yakṣas*, serpents (*pannaga*), *rākṣasas*, and other indeed cruel beings.
They travel from country to country, yet they are indeed unable to cause harm;
for they have meditated upon the Lord Viśveśvara, who pervades all space,
who resembles ten million suns and is as cool as ten million moons.
Having meditated thus, the wise one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times;
he should offer ten thousand oblations with devotion using *śatavīrya* grass—
known as *dūrvā* for the destruction of untimely death— for this is the supreme truth, the highest state.
By meditating upon Hari, the conqueror of death, one is liberated from all sins—
[Hari] who is seated in a divine hermitage adorned with groves of *badarī* trees.
Touching the body of Ghaṇṭākarṇa with his two large hands,
one should meditate thus and recite the mantra one thousand and eight times for a month,
in order to pacify all calamities and to attain tranquility.
Equanimity toward all beings, which swiftly bestows nirvāṇa;
mounted upon a chariot at dawn,
repeatedly threatening the host of enemies as they flee, he pursues them, O Acyuta.
By reciting the mantra one hundred thousand times, there shall be the immediate opening [of the door] from afar as he leads [the enemy] away with a multitude of discharged arrows;
[one visualizes] Hari situated between Rukmī and Pāṇḍya, causing them to hate one another.
Having meditated upon the excellent mantra one hundred thousand times, mixed with oil— this is the meaning— in a dreamless state,
at the conclusion of that, the practitioner of mantra should offer oblations of cow-dung pills.
Thus, by the mere application [of this mantra], mutual enmity arises;
through their mutual quarreling, one shall not even travel from one country to another. Hated everywhere, one shall wander the earth like a crow.
Having meditated upon Madhusūdana, who is seated in his chariot, teaching the meaning of the Gītā at his side,
standing in the midst of the circle of kings, and possessing a splendor equal to ten thousand moons,
the wise man should recite the excellent mantra a hundred times for the sake of tranquility.
By the mere recitation of this, what on earth cannot be accomplished?
It begins with "O Hṛṣīkeśa, in that place of yours," and so forth; it was spoken by Arjuna during the rainy season, is enveloped in the Gāyatrī meter, and has the Universal Soul as its deity.

The ritual service (*saparyā*) is declared to be as before; one should accomplish all desired objects by reciting the mantra preceded by the seed-syllable of Śrī (*śrī-bīja*), while meditating on the two excellent deities as previously described. By merely performing one hundred thousand recitations (*lakṣa-japa*), one rejoices like Kubera.
I shall describe another Gopāla, whose deity is food; listen to this according to the truth. [The mantra is:

*annarūpa rasarūpa tuṣṭirūpa padopari annādhipataye svāhā*. This is the mantra for the Lord of Food (*annādhipa*); it is said that this mantra, preceded by the seed-syllable of Śrī (*śrīṃ*), bestows an abundance of jewels here. The arrangement of the limbs (*aṅga*) begins with the discus (*ācakra*). Nārada is remembered as its sage (*muni*), the meter (*chandas*) is said to be Gāyatrī, and the deity is Hari, the giver of food.
One should perform all activities such as meditation and worship for him as previously described.
The practitioner who contemplates in this manner shall possess all prosperity.
Having fetched a golden vessel, it should be washed with pure water.
Having smeared [the ground] with fragrant mud, one should draw an eight-petalled lotus.
In the pericarp, one should draw two mandalas of fire joined together;
this means a hexagon encircled by two fires.
In the center of that, one should write the *kāma* (desire) mantra together with the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) and the ritual action (*karman*).
Then, the wise practitioner should surround that *kāma* with the letters of his desired mantra.
[One should place] Śrī in the corners of the hexagon, specifically in the directions of Indra, Nairṛta, and Vāyu.
One should draw the *māyā* (the syllable *hrīṃ*) within the fire, water, and trident [sections];
the knower of mantras should surround the filaments with the syllables of the *kāma-gāyatrī*.
Furthermore, he should place the syllables of the *māra-mālā-mantra* upon the eight petals.

One should write the Mātṛkā with excellent colors within the cavities; outside of that, one should draw the form of the earth (bhūbimba). Having thus written the mantra on a surface made of gold, one should also [place] Śrī and Māyā in the cardinal and intermediate directions.
Having installed the Wind-god upon a copper plate, or on birch bark, or even on silk, or on a cloth made of fine threads,
one effects the attraction of celestial women and the playful damsels of the Naga world.
The Piśācas, Yakṣas, and Rākṣasas, as well as those who abide as cruel planets,
and all wicked beings who roam upon the surface of the earth—
upon seeing the bearer of the King of Yantras, they flee and are utterly destroyed.
What is the use of saying more here? This [practice] brings happiness to all the world;
for kings, it brings subjugation of the people on earth;
for men, it grants the perfection of yoga and carries them across the ocean of worldly existence.

This yantra, which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, was proclaimed by Svayambhū. Mounted upon the syllables *vāṃ* and *yāṃ*, and adorned with the *māyā* (ī) and the *bindu* (ṃ), it is called the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of Śrī; it grants immediate happiness to men.
First, having uttered the syllable *klīṃ*, one should recite the word "Kāmadeva.
Then the word "Āyāntaṃ vidmahe," followed by the word "Puṣpabāṇāya.
Having spoken the word "Dhīmahī," one should then say "Tanno 'naṅga pracodayāt."

This is declared to be the Manmatha-gāyatrī, which kindles passion. Having meditated upon Kāma and the Nāḍī, one should then utter the word "Kāma. One should speak the word "Devāya," and likewise the word "Sarvajana."

One should say "priyāya" at the end of the word, and then again "sarvajanaṃ. One should say "sanmohanāya," and repeat the word "jvala. Likewise, one should say the word "prajvala" for "sarvajanasya hṛdayaṃ."
Having said "be under my control," one should afterwards utter the word and repeat it;
likewise, having uttered "so be it" (tathā), there is the mantra called Mālā.
The subterranean chamber (bhūgṛha) should be square and adorned with eight thunderbolts (vajras).

Having invoked Vāsudeva, the teacher of the world, into this mantra, what is there that the knower of mantras cannot accomplish? That which was to be told has been told to you. Thus the yantra has been described to you; now the ritual application (prayoga) is being stated here.
Having recited the mantra one hundred thousand times, one should offer an equal number of *palāśa* flowers as an oblation.
One becomes an expounder of all scriptures before long;
such a person is a yogi, a possessor of realized knowledge, a yogi of Viṣṇu, and likewise a knower of the Self.
For the sake of obtaining white clothing, one should offer white and other such flowers one hundred and eight times; then one shall obtain it from a king or from another source.
[The parents], tormented by the distress of being driven out of Mathurā, cried out to Kṛṣṇa, "Leave us!"
Having meditated, one should perform the recitation (*japa*) and at its conclusion offer oblations (*homa*) in that same number;
for whomever this rite is performed, that person is instantly released from fetters.
One should [meditate upon] Hari in Vṛndāvana, who stands there surrounded by the gods headed by Purandara.
Having consecrated the Lord of the Kings of Kings with the milk and waters of the Surabhī cow while offering hymns of praise, and having performed the auspicious rites,
he was attended by celestial nymphs led by Urvaśī.
Having meditated thus, one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times and perform ten thousand oblations with lotuses.
He by whom this rite is performed shall become a sovereign ruler of the whole earth,
while remembering himself as the slayer of Kaṃsa and his enemy as being of the nature of Kaṃsa.
At midnight, the practitioner, facing south, should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times. At the conclusion of the recitation, he should perform libations with *vāṇīra* twigs;
by performing ten thousand oblations alone, the enemy dies, and not otherwise.
If that [mixture] containing the leaves of the *ariṣṭa* tree is sprinkled with the dust from its roots,
an enemy will die upon being seized— even if he is protected by Śaṅkara himself. [Likewise,
one who is seized with] the leaves of the *ariṣṭa*, cotton, and fragments of bone from the sky [the *ākāśabhasman*], [shall perish].
If the enemy remains on the ground merely by being seized with a hundred thousand [units], even one who consumes nectar shall die, and not otherwise.
By the oblation of *haridrā* knots, one may paralyze the army of the enemy; by the oblation of *daridrā* knots, one may paralyze it.
In the Vaiṣṇava mantra, the rite of death (māraṇa) is never prescribed;
nor is it taught for one who is cruel, evil-minded, or deceitful, even toward the virtuous.
Upon encountering such a person, one should employ the rite of malevolent magic (abhicāra).
For expiation, the practitioner, having recited the Gāyatrī mantra one hundred thousand times, should at its conclusion perform ten thousand oblations (homa) with milk-rice (pāyasa).
Even for those who employ [the mantra] for harmful purposes, peace shall prevail; it cannot be otherwise.
[Thus ends the eighteenth chapter in the glorious Gautamīya. || 18 ||
Now I shall describe another ritual procedure; listen attentively, O sinless one!
By performing this, even one of meager fortune will indeed obtain the fruits of the mantra.
One should recite it a specific number of times, situated between two *praṇavas*.
By merely reciting it for three nights, one becomes equal to Bṛhaspati;
one becomes an expounder of all the scriptures and even of the Vedas.
On a Saturday, having touched the Aśvattha tree, [one should recite it] one hundred and eight times.
Peace shall arise again and again, and he shall live for one hundred and eight years.
Peace shall come to him for whom this rite was performed, even if it be incomplete. For one month, he should worship Kṛṣṇa with pure offerings brought quickly.
One is liberated from impure hardships and even the most terrible sins.
By worshipping with devotion using silk cloth, one shall attain prosperity and the mandala.
By honoring Kṛṣṇa with strides, one may bring the three worlds under one's control.
By worshipping with devotion using rubies (māṇikya), one becomes equal to Bhauma;
by worshipping Kṛṣṇa with rubies (padmarāga), one certainly becomes a king—
a Kṣatriya who becomes a sovereign ruler and shall conquer the entire earth.
By worshipping with gems made of emerald, one becomes possessed of knowledge;
even by worshipping with a diamond gem, what could one not accomplish?
By honoring [the deity] with flowers of gold, one who is devoted to the practice of offering for a month shall attain success.
Having attained prosperity equal to that of Kubera, he rejoices for a long time;
at the end of the body, having attained the state of Hari, he reaches the station of Nirvāṇa. On Sunday, with *arka* flowers, and on Monday, with white water-lilies (*kahlāra*).
On Tuesday, the ascetic should worship with red flowers; on Wednesday, with those produced from *tagara*;
on Thursday, with *campaka* flowers; on Friday, with those produced from *mukunda*;
and on Saturday, he should worship with devotion using *śamī* flowers.
On Sunday, one should offer food with ghee and anointed with milk;
on Monday, one should provide flour-cakes and the like mixed with sugar;
on Tuesday, food mixed with jaggery and endowed with many excellent qualities.
On Wednesday, one should offer barley-gruel to the Guru along with cakes;
on Friday, milk-rice; and on Saturday, milk-porridge with ghee.
In the month of Vaiśākha, one should duly perform the libation with Himalayan waters.
In the month of Jyeṣṭha, one should diligently worship Hari with fruits;
in the month of Āṣāḍha, one should worship the All-pervading Lord according to the rules with sacred threads (*pavitra*).
One should have each thread made of gold and provided with knots.
Alternatively, at the conclusion of the worship, one should present silk threads or lotus fibers to the God of gods and to his queens;
having likewise given them to the divine couples, one should celebrate a great festival.
One should gratify the Brahmins of firm vows with various kinds of food and edibles;
by performing this for a year, the practitioner of mantras shall attain his desired goal.
However, worship performed for only one year does not suffice for the propitiation of Vāstu.
In the month of Śrāvaṇa, one should worship that [deity] with black ketaka flowers,
well-perfumed with moon-scented sandalwood, musk, saffron, and other fragrances;
one should offer cardamom, cloves, kakkola berries, and many fruits.
In the month of Bhādrapada, one should worship Kṛṣṇa with foods endowed with many excellent qualities;
in the month of Āśvina, one should worship Him with devotion using abundant foods and delicacies,
along with garments made of cotton and various ornaments.
When the sun is situated in Libra (tulā), one should worship Kṛṣṇa for the duration of one month.
At night, during the fire-offerings with lamps,
one should offer a brilliantly shining lamp of ghee continuously for the entire month.
Having fasted on the eleventh day, on the twelfth day— the day of breaking the fast—
one should worship Viṣṇu with garments, ornaments, and other offerings during the bright fortnight;
and on this lunar day, the wise man should perform the annual festival.
One should offer various kinds of food and many delicacies to the Brahmins;
when this is done, the deities become pleased with him and grant his desires.
He attains the world of the Saṃtas, from which there is no return.
In the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, people should worship the Lord with auspicious offerings of fresh rice.
They should devotedly present to the God a preparation made from grated coconut mixed with jaggery and cumin, cooked in oil.
In the month of Pauṣa, one should indeed worship with *māṣa* beans and purified cakes (*pūpa*).
In the month of Māgha, one should worship Kṛṣṇa with very beautiful white unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*);
one should also offer sweet food mixed with sugar for the sake of milk.
On an auspicious day in this month, one should clothe the Lord with a garment;
in Phālguna, one should worship the Son of Devakī with golden flowers,
mango blossoms, fragrant flowers, and with incense and lamps in great abundance.
In the month of Caitra, one should worship Vāsudeva with all kinds of flowers;
on the full moon day, one should worship with devotion using *madana* flowers along with their clusters.
On this day, being intent on devotion, one should worship Rati and Kāma.
If the annual worship is not performed, it certainly becomes in vain.
Seeing Smara reduced to ashes, his faithful Rati wept.
Seeing her, Śiva himself, overcome with compassion, granted her a boon;
Rati replied, "May she attain good fortune."
O beautiful lady of Vraja, for the sake of sport in all the worlds,
there then arose from the blazing flame a beautiful flower called Madanaka.
By merely worshipping with it, one obtains the fruit of a full year.
He who performs one hundred thousand oblations with flour-cakes fried in ghee,
and having recited the mantra that same number of times, the knower of mantras beholds Kṛṣṇa.
Thus has the worship with seasonal offerings been correctly described to you.
What cannot be accomplished on this earth by performing according to this rite?
Both virtuous women and householders, as well as sages and celibate students,
and likewise forest-dwellers, shall attain their desires in an instant by performing it thus.
Women and Śūdras, having performed [the rite] according to the rules, shall obtain the fruit;
having enjoyed excellent pleasures here in this world, there shall be no further birth in saṃsāra.
Thus, by worshipping Kṛṣṇa with devotion, one attains that which was performed through ten million births.
That [mind] would not be defiled by evils, just as a lotus leaf is not wetted by water.
[Thus ends the nineteenth chapter in the glorious Gautamīya. || 19 ||
Gautama said: O Brahmin, tell me the mantras of Kṛṣṇa in detail;
I am your devotee, I am your disciple, and I am worthy to hear them, O Guru.
Nārada said:
Listen, O Brāhmaṇa, to the mantras of Kṛṣṇa, which are unanimously approved by all the gods;
by the mere knowledge of even one of them, rebirth no longer exists.
Having first extracted the *praṇava* (Om), one should then utter "namaḥ";
having pronounced "kaustubhāya," this is the supreme eight-syllabled mantra (*manu*).
Merely by knowing this, the ascetic (*yati*) becomes Viṣṇu himself.
The limbs of the Lord are considered to be composed of the six long vowels;
He is dark like a blue lotus flower, bearing the conch, discus, mace, and lotus;
His chest is covered with many jewels and illuminated by the Kaustubha gem.
Having thus meditated upon [the deity] seated upon Garuḍa, beautiful with a string of large pearls, one should recite the mantra a million times for supreme bliss;
one should then perform a fire sacrifice (homa) with one-tenth that number of prepared vegetable soups and milk-rice (pāyasa).
One should complete the remaining auxiliary rites, such as the *puraścaraṇa*.
The practitioner who worships this mantra— the sole cause of both worldly enjoyment and liberation—
will attain all goals through the hands [of practice] and, in the end, reach that supreme state.
Indeed, the worship consisting of ten syllables has been proclaimed as equal [to the previous].
Now I shall further proclaim another, the king of mantras with six syllables;
by the mere knowledge of which one may wander the earth liberated while living.

The six-syllable mantra is proclaimed as "Kṛṣṇā" joined with "namaḥ" in the dative case; it bestows both visible and invisible fruits. Nārada is said to be its sage (ṛṣi), and Gāyatrī is declared to be its meter (chandas).
Kṛṣṇa himself is the deity, the presiding deity of Durgā;
"Vi-mā-tra" is said to be the seed-syllable (bīja), and "Namaḥ" is declared to be the power (śakti).
"Kṛṣṇāya" is proclaimed as the peg (kīlaka) of this king of mantras.
The application (*viniyoga*) of this mantra is for the four aims of human life (*puruṣārtha*). The five limbs of this mantra are described by means of the wheels beginning with *ācakra* and so forth:
[one should meditate on the deity] resembling a dark blue cloud and wearing a garland of networks of small bells.
One should meditate upon the sky-clad Lord, resplendent with all ornaments, seated upon a red lotus,
praised by the foremost sages such as Sanaka and others,
and graced by a moon-like face shining with swinging earrings.

One should meditate upon the God, who bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation; his lips are red as rabbit's blood, his hands and feet are beautifully adorned with redness, and with his two hands he holds smooth milk-rice and fresh ghee.
Having thus meditated upon the Supreme Self, one should recite the mantra one million times.
At the conclusion of the recitation, one should perform the *homa* with pure milk-rice mixed with sugar.
One should then offer libations with water scented with camphor, amounting to one-tenth of the number of recitations.

One should perform the consecration (abhiṣeka) with a tenth part [of the total], and the feeding of Brahmins with tenth parts; at the conclusion of that, having given the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), one should accomplish one's own welfare. Subsisting on alms-food and remaining firm in the vow, one should recite the mantra for one year.
By meditating upon the God who consumes the oblation (Agni) and performing one hundred thousand recitations, the wise man certainly becomes a poet, an eloquent speaker, prosperous, and omniscient;
he attains divine knowledge and rejoices, having reached the three worlds.
Whoever, intent on devotion, worships this king of mantras in this manner,
having enjoyed excellent pleasures here in this world, shall enter the supreme state at the end of the body.
Now, I shall further proclaim the great mantra of sixteen syllables.
By the mere knowledge of which one enters the supreme self of Kṛṣṇa—
the Praṇava joined with the mind, as well as "Kṛṣṇa" and "Govindaka," preceded by "Śrī," ending in the feminine suffix "ṅi," and proclaimed as "huṃ phaṭ svāhā."

The sage of this [mantra] is declared to be Nārada; the meter is said to be Anuṣṭubh; the deity is the Supreme Self, Lord Hari, who bestows the fruits of worldly enjoyment and liberation. Recitation and fire-offerings (japa and homa) of this ten-syllabled mantra are highly praised.
The *prayoga* is said to be equal to that, and the seed-power (*bīja-śakti*) is likewise equal to it. He who meditates upon this mantra studies the four Vedas;
a mantra equal to this is not found even within the worlds.
By this [practice], Kṛṣṇa is propitiated and becomes pleased at that very moment.
Then, through the complete perfection of the lineage (*saṃtāna*), one obtains the leader of mantras (*mantranāyaka*),
by the mere knowledge of which the mantras of the practitioner (*mantrin*) become effective.
One should utter the word "Govinda" ending with "Devakīputra";
then, at the end of the word "Vāsudeva," one should say "O Teacher of the World" (jagadguro);
then "O God, grant me a son" (dehi me tanayaṃ deva), and finally one should utter the word "Thee" (tvām).
The imperishable Manu has declared that "I have gone for refuge" is in the Anuṣṭubh meter;
the wise state that Nārada is its seer (ṛṣi) and Gāyatrī is its meter (chandaḥ). Hari himself is proclaimed as the deity who bestows progeny.
Having formed the limbs with all the *vāstu* [elements], one should meditate upon the Lord:
dark-complexioned like the petal of a blue lotus, clothed in a pair of yellow garments,
four-armed, with a conch and a discus resting in his two upper hands.
With both hands held below, playing the flute with great joy,
his form radiant with a crown set with many jewels,
beautiful with various ornaments, and seated upon Garuḍa.
One should daily recite the Veda-stotra surrounded by sages;
having meditated thus, one should worship Kṛṣṇa with the five limbs as the supreme enclosure (paramāvṛtti).
The second enclosure consists of Indra and the other gods, while the third consists of their weapons.

Having thus worshipped the Lord of Devas, one should mutter the mantra ten thousand times (lakṣa). One should perform the fire-oblation (homa) ten thousand times with the fruits of the *putrajīva* tree upon a pyre of its wood. Immediately thereafter, one should perform the libation (*tarpaṇa*) and other rites for one-tenth of that number.

The practitioner who thus worships this great mantra known as Saṃtāna shall perish along with his sons and grandsons; yet at the end of the body, he shall go to the supreme Brahman. His lineage shall remain unbroken until the dissolution of all beings at the end of the kalpa.

On the tenth day of the bright fortnight, at midnight, having duly invoked Hari within a svastika-maṇḍala, one should worship Him with ritual offerings. By such mere worship, after a year, the householder shall possess a son.

Within a year, he obtains a son who is long-lived and endowed with unimpeded strength and vigor; this which I have spoken is the truth, the absolute truth. For whose sake the practitioner performs this rite, that man shall possess seven sons.

Even a barren woman obtains sons who live for a hundred years; a woman who has not yet borne a child, having recited the mantra one hundred and eight times over water at the foot of the Bodhi tree, should drink it, and she will certainly obtain a son.
One who aspires to such practice will certainly attain this method.
Ghee consecrated with this [mantra] is supreme for achieving the birth of a son;
by drinking water consecrated with this, even a barren woman shall obtain offspring within a year.
[Thus ends the twentieth chapter in the Gautama-dharma-sūtra. || 20 ||
Gautama said:
O wise one, O self-born Lord, I know all that you have spoken;
having heard your words, I am fulfilled, and not otherwise.
O Brahman, in former times, having performed austerities, the Lord prayed to Hari;
he replied, "If this is not told, it must be told in its entirety.
From that time on, O Brahman, he has been longing for a vision of you.
"O Gaṅgā, I wish to hear the mantra for propelling [the flow] in its true essence.
Nārada said:
"O best of sages, many mantras have been recounted by me to you."
I shall now declare that mantra by which knowledge becomes clear.
For whomsoever devotion characterized by love arises through mere consciousness alone,
and the fourfold scholarship is accomplished through mere knowledge alone— even for one who is dull-witted, emaciated, deceitful, foolish, or a great sinner— [liberation is attained].
By worshipping the King of Mantras, one attains mastery of speech and excellent intelligence.
O Sage, I shall relate to you exactly as it was previously asked of me by the Lotus-born One; I shall tell you that which is more secret than the secret.
This twenty-two-syllable mantra bestows the state of mastery over speech;
it is hidden in all tantras and must be kept secret by you, O Sage.
By means of this mantra, the Veda appeared to the Creator.
O Lord of Poets, you attained the status of Bhārgava; Vāgīśa became Bṛhaspati;
the gods, beginning with Mitra, obtained prosperity; Sanaka and the others attained knowledge;
the Moon attained good fortune; and even Kubera attained lordship over wealth.
Having known this supreme mantra, one certainly becomes omniscient;
even one who has not seen or heard the scriptures becomes an expounder of them and a master of the arts. Becoming a great poet and highly wise, one shall attain equality with the Lord of Speech.

But having attained the supreme knowledge of Viṣṇu, one goes to union with Him. Whatever desire a man contemplates while worshipping the Manu, he attains that very desire on earth, in heaven, or in the netherworld.
I shall declare its extraction, which is the cause of my omniscience:
*kṛṣṇā*, *govinda*, *kauṅenta*, and then *gopījana*;
followed by *vallabha*, *agnipriyā*, and *sargī*—this is the first [mantra], with the preceding vowel.
One should sequentially place Kāma (Klīm), Māyā (Hrīm), and Lakṣmī (Śrīm) at the beginning of the names.
This twenty-two-syllable mantra is proclaimed to begin with the Vāgbhava (Aiṃ). The sage of this mantra is Ahaṃ, the metre is Gāyatrī, and the deity of the mantra is [the Self].
Kṛṣṇa, who is saluted by all the gods, is Gaṅgāpravāhaṇa;
because his speech arises like the flow of the Gaṅgā, he is thus [named].
In the ultimate sense, he is celebrated by the name Gaṅgāpravāhaṇa.
The seed-syllable of Manmatha is proclaimed as the Śakti, the wife of the Fire-god (Havirbhuj).
The Heart-mantra is celebrated for Kṛṣṇa with the two Kāma-bījas;
likewise, the Head-mantra is for Govinda. Such is this great mantra beginning with Māyā.
Likewise, one should place the *śikhā* with "gopījana" preceded by the *śrī-bīja*;
"vallabhāya" is the *kavaca*, and "jāyā" is the *astra* of the Fire-god. These five limb-mantras are known to be accompanied by the remaining *bīja*.
On the crown of the head, the forehead, between the eyebrows, the eyes, the ears, and likewise the nose;
on the mouth, the throat, the roots of the arms, the heart, the abdomen, and the navel;
on the root of the penis, the anus, the thighs, the knees, and the ankles.
Having performed the pervasive placement (vyāpakanyāsa) with the entire mantra, one should contemplate the Lord:
dark as a kalāya flower, with a face resembling the full moon,
wearing a crest of peacock feathers and a garland of forest flowers.
Hari, adorned with a crown, necklaces, armlets, and jeweled earrings;
his chest radiant with the Śrīvatsa mark and illuminated by the Kaustubha gem;
his body beautiful with the youthful grace of a maiden.
Wearing divine yellow garments and adorned with beautiful necklaces, he has his flute placed upon his smiling, reddish lips; he is the Enchanter of the Three Worlds,
four-armed, playing a flute composed of the four Vedas.
He holds a crystal rosary in his two upper hands;
he is lotus-eyed and devoted to divine song. Possessing incomparable and abundant beauty, he infatuates the three worlds.
His feet were gazed upon by Śrī, who stood at his left side holding a blue lotus in her hand and possessing a shimmering luster like refined gold;
he sat upon a beautiful golden throne adorned with every kind of jewel.
Constantly attended by his queens, Rukmiṇī and the others;
adorned with a white parasol resembling the orb of the moon;
and worshipped by hosts of sages such as Nārada who seek the knowledge of reality.
Having meditated upon the Supreme Lord— the omniscient Sovereign of the universe— who is bowed to by the hosts of deities beginning with Indra, within the lotus of the heart,
one should recite this excellent mantra four hundred thousand times while maintaining that visualization.
One should perform the fire-oblation (homa) with sweet-smelling flowers born of the Brahma-tree;
this mantra becomes perfected through a tenth part [of the recitation], and not otherwise.
Worship is performed upon a ten-syllable pedestal, followed by the repetition of the limbs (aṅga).

The second [round] is performed with the queens, the third with the lords of the directions, and the fourth with their weapons; thus the fourfold repetition is described. Every morning, one should drink water consecrated with this mantra.

Becoming equal to Vāgīśvara, one shall become a great author of poetry. One who daily protects the vessel with this mantra consecrated by Brahmā shall become wise from the very mandala and a possessor of the great Vedas.

One should cook the paste of *brāhmī*, *kuṣṭha*, and *vacā* with double the amount of ghee and four times the amount of milk; this is the supreme ghee. Having removed it from the heat, one should diligently perform ten thousand recitations (*japa*) over it.
For one year, he should consume it every morning while observing silence.
By the mere consumption of this, one becomes equal to Bṛhaspati.
Placing it upon the tongue with the hand, one should recite the mantra ten thousand times with devotion.
Divine intuition arises, cultivated as the sole excellence in all the worlds,
if one should worship the God with pure offerings;
one attains divine knowledge, an intuition that conquers the universe.
When one has recited the Śrīvidyā, then Lakṣmī becomes unshakable;
by the mere recitation of [the mantra] beginning with Kāma, one brings all the worlds under one's control;
and by the mere recitation of [the mantra] beginning with Māyā, the perfection of speech arises without delay.
A mantra beginning with the seed-syllable of Śakti bestows liberation before long;
by enclosing it with the two Praṇavas, one certainly attains release.
Having thus recited this supreme mantra, what is there that the knower of mantras cannot accomplish?
Thus, whoever worships this supreme mantra, being intent on devotion,
shall enjoy excellent pleasures here in this world, endowed with all prosperity;
having attained the highest wealth, he shall reach the supreme state in the end.
The supreme Śakti, beginning with Kāma and Indra, joined with the *nadi* and the *bindu*—
this is declared to be the Kṛṣṇa-mantra, the leader of all mantras.
Brahmā is proclaimed as its seer (*ṛṣi*), and the Virāṭ meter is said to be its metre (*chandas*).
Śrī Kṛṣṇa is proclaimed as the deity who fascinates the three worlds;
his six limbs are proclaimed through the six long syllables of the seed-mantra.
He wears a left earring hanging from his ear, and the surface of his eyebrows is gently shimmering.

One should meditate upon the Enchanter of the World, who is gracefully posed in the triple-bend (tribhaṅga) at the foot of the Kalpa tree; his soft lips are slightly pursed, his eyes cast a sidelong glance with radiance, and he joyfully fills his flute with the sprout-like fingers of his trembling hands.
Having meditated thus, one should recite the mantra with faith ten lakhs of times;
one should then perform oblations with milk-rice or lotuses numbering one-tenth of that amount,
and worship according to the prescribed ritual upon the seat described for the ten-syllable mantra.
One should also perform all the ritual applications everywhere according to what has been taught therein;
or else, one may visualize Bālakṛṣṇa, who resembles a blue lotus,
blazing with jewel-ornaments, possessing two arms and dark locks of hair.
One should meditate upon [the deity] holding milk-rice (pāyasa) and fresh butter (navanīta) in his two hands;
one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times and perform oblations with auspicious milk-rice,
offering worship according to the rules with devotion ten times that amount, accompanied by the lords of the limbs and other deities.
The practitioner of mantras should perform ten thousand oblations with flour-cakes fried in ghee;
thus, barrenness is swiftly destroyed, and one attains luster and splendor.
By offering oblations with *palāśa* flowers, one certainly attains perfection of speech.
The mantra-practitioner should offer ten thousand oblations of lotuses and shall obtain prosperity;
by an oblation of fresh butter, he becomes a poet and an eloquent speaker.
Having uttered the word "Vāsudeva," [one should recite it] for the purpose of covering with a mace.
Having uttered "Vāsudeva dvayam" (the two Vāsudevas), one should say "svāhā"; this is considered its mantra.
Nārada is declared its sage (ṛṣi), and Aṣṭu is cited as its meter (chandas). Lakṣmī and Vāsudeva are its deities (devatā).
One should fashion the five limbs of the mind with the discus and other weapons;
having effortlessly cast Kaṃsa down into the midst of the royal assembly,
he himself brought his parents there, increasing the joy of his kinsmen.
Having been released from their shackles by her devotion, and having prostrated again and again,
they were stationed outside according to the rules while King Devakī was being watched by the kings;
thus meditating, one should mutter [the mantra] one hundred thousand times and perform oblations with a tenth part of that number.
All [the rites] beginning with the placement on the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*) have been declared by the foremost of speakers.
The mantra-practitioner who contemplates in this way becomes a treasury of perfect prosperity;
by mere recollection, he is liberated in an instant from fear of kings, fortresses, and other such dangers.
By the fire-oblation (*homa*) of *nirguṇḍī* root, one is released from bondage and other such misfortunes;
at the royal court or in the face of terrible fear, one is freed from that fear through mere remembrance.
[Thus ends the twenty-first chapter in the glorious Gautamīya. || 21 ||
O Sage, listen as I describe Gopāla and Piṇḍasaṃjña;
by hearing this with devotion to the Guru, one rejoices here and in the hereafter. A mantra equal to this is not found even throughout the worlds.
The five syllables, situated on the earth (the letter *la*), together with the bindu and the nasal vowel (*anusvāra*),
constitute this king of mantras, which bestows the fruits of worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Brahmā is its seer (*ṛṣi*), Gāyatrī its meter (*chandas*), and Śrī Kṛṣṇa its deity (*devatā*).
The seed-syllable (bīja) and the power (śakti) are placed on the two throat-veins, while the pin (kīlaka) is said to be the union [of the two].
One should perform the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅga) using the seed-syllable endowed with the six long vowels.
[One should meditate upon] Kṛṣṇa, situated in Vṛndāvana, seated upon a jeweled throne.

In the region at the foot of the Kadamba tree, the Lord who wears a forest garland was surrounded by the cowherd women and accompanied by the best of sages, such as Nārada, whose mouths were occupied with divine songs,
all approaching him with supreme devotion.

Having thus meditated upon the best of mantras— one blazing with jewel ornaments, with hands shining with the conch and discus, and holding a flute composed of the Brahman of Sound (Śabdabrahma) in his two lower hands— the self-controlled practitioner should recite it one hundred thousand times.
One should perform the fire-oblation (homa) combined with milk-rice (pāyasa) mixed with sugar;
for the practitioner who worships this [mantra], all accomplishments (siddhis) come into his hands.
By performing the oblation with white flowers, one obtains mastery over speech (vāk-siddhi) without delay.
Through the oblation of *karṇikāra* flowers, all forms of prosperity shall arise.
If one drinks water consecrated with this mantra every morning,
one soon becomes a poet, eloquent, possessed of a retentive memory, and omniscient.
What cannot be accomplished by the mere worship of this mantra?
Having enjoyed excellent pleasures here in this world together with sons and grandsons,
the practitioner of the mantra goes at the end to that supreme, stainless abode.
Now I shall proclaim the great mantra that bestows the fruits of all desires;
by the mere retention of which, what on this earth is not accomplished?
Having drawn a triangle as the seed-syllable, one should draw a hexagon outside of it.
One should write the six-syllabled mantra there within a circle and draw an eight-petaled lotus;
joined with the eight-syllabled mantra, outside of that is a sixteen-petaled [lotus];
the sixteen-syllabled mantra of Kṛṣṇa is placed on it, and it is endowed with an outer twelve-petaled [lotus].
Then, joined with the ten-syllable mantra, there is an eighteen-petalled lotus;
in its center is the eighteen-syllable mantra, and outside of that, one should draw a thirty-two-petalled lotus and write the verse beginning with "devakīsuta" (the son of Devakī) right there.
One should draw a circle surrounding the *piṇḍabīja*.
The *piṇḍabīja* should surround the yantra on all sides. Having produced a circle outside of that, one should encircle it with the *mātṛkā* [alphabet].
Having again drawn two circles, one should encircle them with the goad of the curse (*śāpāṅkuśa*). Outside of that, there should be one circle and a square containing a thunderbolt (*vajra*).
O best of sages, this great yantra has been described out of compassion.
He who, being ever well-composed, writes [this] on a golden leaf or on birch bark,
having prepared ink from the eight fragrances with a golden stylus— by the mere wearing of this, he becomes manifestly Indra upon the earth.
One is liberated from impurities and even the most terrible hardships and sufferings;
having attained eternal peace, one reaches that supreme state.
What is there that cannot be accomplished by constantly wearing [this] on the left arm of women?
Even a barren woman obtains a son who lives for a hundred years,
endowed with long life and unimpeded strength and valor;
having smeared the zodiacal circle (rāśicakra) and placed a water-pot as before.
Having cast the yantra into its center, one shall indeed accomplish everything through sprinkling [with water].
A Brahmin becomes a constant seer; a king rules the earth;
a Vaiśya becomes prosperous; and a Śūdra obtains his heart's desire.
This yantra, which is the sole means for achieving the goals of human life, has been described;
O Sage, you yourself must protect it with great effort and secrecy.
[Thus ends the twenty-second chapter in the glorious Gautamīya. || 22 ||
Now I shall declare the supreme mantra, which bestows all human goals:
from the knowledge of this sacrifice, all accomplishments (siddhis) come to rest in one's hand. [The mantra is:
Lakṣmī, Māyā, and the seed-syllable of Kāma, followed by the word "Kṛṣṇa" in the vocative case ending in -ṅe.
"SVĀHĀ"—this king of mantras bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Nārada is declared its sage (ṛṣi), and Anuṣṭubh is cited as its meter (chandas).
Kṛṣṇa is said to be its deity (devatā), the granter of all human goals (puruṣārtha).
One should perform the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅga) with the seed-syllable of Kāma (klīm), employing the six long vowels.
One should meditate upon Hari, who has gone to Vṛndāvana, who is dark as a kalāya flower,
surrounded by cowherds, cowherdesses, and cows, and clothed in a pair of yellow garments.
Beautifully adorned with various ornaments, his chest illuminated by the Kaustubha gem;
praised with supreme joy by the best of sages, beginning with Sanaka;
his arms resplendent with the conch and discus, playing the flute with both hands.
Having thus meditated upon the Supreme Self, one should recite the mantra four hundred thousand times;
the practitioner of the mantra should offer oblations with flowers born of the Brahma-tree (Ficus religiosa) for one-tenth of that number.
Then, with devotion, one should worship at the three junctions of the day with the limbs [of the deity] and with Indra and the other deities.
One should perform the practice in this manner for the sake of dharma, artha, kāma, and liberation.
By offering ten thousand oblations of milk-rice (pāyasa), one shall attain divine knowledge;
likewise, by offering salt, one will certainly attract people to oneself.
One should offer oblations with *palāśa* flowers; thus one becomes a poet and eloquent.

With the thought directed toward that [deity], the practitioner of mantras should satisfy [the deity] ten thousand times with molasses, plantain, milk, ghee, and milk-rice, using water from the Ganges.
Success sought through the mandala and other rites shall certainly come to pass; there is no doubt in this matter.
By means of the seed-syllable born of speech (*vāgbhava*), one attains equality with Vāgīśvara.
Having offered oblations with *brāhmī* flowers, one who observes the vow obtains a treasure.
By performing the fire-oblation (homa) with the fruit of the Śrīvṛkṣa tree, one shall attain royal sovereignty.
Thus, out of devotion, I have told you this leader of mantras, which is difficult to obtain;
having received this authentic tradition, what can a practitioner not accomplish?
This mantra, consisting of eighteen syllables and ending with the word "māra," bestows sons and wealth.
The wise have declared that Nārada is its sage (ṛṣi) and Gāyatrī its meter (chandas).
Bālakṛṣṇa is its deity, who grants the fruit of all desired objects.
The ritual action for the limbs is considered to be performed with the seed-syllable of Kāma, which possesses the six long vowels.
[One should meditate on] the Youthful One, who has the luster of a blue lotus, who deludes the three worlds,
and who is adorned with many brilliant ornaments made of shining jewels.
Resplendent with various jewels, his neck adorned with a Brahmanical cord and a goad, his hair shining at its ends, and his ears graced by shimmering makara-shaped earrings;
with hands like the trunks of elephants, he [offered] that ninth [portion of] milk-rice.
Having thus meditated upon the cowherd boy, who is surrounded by hosts of deities,
the practitioner of mantra should recite it thirty-two lakhs of times according to the prescribed measure.
At the conclusion of the recitation, one should offer oblations into the fire with milk-rice (pāyasa) in a tenth part of that number.
One should perform all the rites, such as the libations (tarpaṇa) and so forth, as previously described.
By means of this perfected mantra, the knower of mantras should accomplish all ritual actions.
Having offered ten thousand oblations of red lotuses, a twice-born man shall attain knowledge.
He shall be the sole teacher of all the world and a Kṣatriya; of this there is no doubt.
Whatever else may be desired by others, one should accomplish it with this mantra, having meditated upon [the deity] atop a jewel-lotus, using sugar and abundant parched rice.
Having gratified Keśava with water mixed with plantain and jaggery,
one obtains within a year a son who is honored by all the world. Furthermore, whatever else is desired may be accomplished through the mere recitation of this [mantra].

The thirteen-syllable mantra, enriched with *māyā* (hrīṃ), *ramā* (śrīṃ), and the seed-syllable of desire (klīṃ), bestows both seen and unseen fruits. Its seer is Brahmā himself, and its meter is said to be *anuṣṭubh*.

Śrī Kṛṣṇa is declared to be the deity, the bestower of great sovereignty. The practitioner of this mantra should perform the five-fold limb-assignment (aṅga-pañcaka) with the syllables beginning with *hrīṃ*.
[He should meditate on Him] whose hands shine with the conch, discus, mace, lotus, noose, and goad.
Holding a flute with both hands and blowing it, he who deludes all beings,
possessing a splendor equal to ten thousand suns, clothed in a pair of yellow garments,
beautiful with various ornaments, and seated within the solar disc.
Having meditated thus, one should recite the mantra four hundred thousand times with undistracted mind.
At the conclusion of the recitation, the twice-born should perform a fire-oblation (homa) with milk-rice (pāyasa) using a tenth part of that number.
He should worship the mantra according to the royal method to be described hereafter.

Having invoked Kṛṣṇa in the center, one should worship him according to the rite of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga). Having worshipped Vāsudeva, Saṃkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha on the petals of the cardinal directions, one should worship them on the intermediate petals outside of that.

Likewise, one should worship Sarasvatī, Lakṣmī, Rati, and Prīti; then the world-protectors (Lokapālas) in their respective directions, and outside of them, their weapons. Having thus worshipped according to the rules, one should accomplish one's desired goals.
A wise man should accomplish even the twenty applications taught in this ocean [of knowledge].
The practitioner who honors this and worships it with devotion shall attain royal sovereignty and, in the end, become that supreme light.

The ten-syllable mantra leader beginning with Kāma, Māyā, and Ramā is proclaimed; likewise, the ten-syllable mantra beginning with Ramā, Māyā, and Kāma is celebrated. For these two mantras, the practitioner [should perform] the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅga) starting with the Ācakra and the others.
Having properly performed meditation, worship, and other rites like Daśārṇava,
the wise one who is devoted to the ritual service of these two mantras shall enjoy excellent pleasures endowed with great sovereignty in this world.
Through sons, grandsons, and great-grandsons, a Brāhmaṇa attains the state of Hari.
Now I shall speak; listen, O Sage, to the ritual procedure of the Lord of the World,
which is performed by the gods headed by Indra for their own protection,
and which Kubera also performed while practicing austerities at the mouth of Brahmā.
Having attained friendship with Maheśa, he obtained the lordship of wealth without effort;
even Indra, by worshipping him alone, attained the sovereignty of the gods,
becoming the conqueror of the three worlds and the sole ruler of both gods and demons.
The eighteen-syllable mantra beginning with *māyā-ramā* and the twenty-syllable one—
mantras equal to these are difficult to find in the three worlds. Brahmā is declared to be the seer (*ṛṣi*), and the meter (*chandas*) is indeed Gāyatrī.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who is praised by the hosts of deities, has been proclaimed as the deity;
one should perform the five-fold limb-ritual (pañcāṅga) with the meanings of the mantra consisting of eighteen syllables.
[This is done] at Dvāravatī, the great seat of knowledge, adorned with hundreds of large ponds.
In the delightful Pārijāta grove, in the midst of a golden land,
within a variegated pavilion made of all kinds of jewels resembling Mount Sumeru,
he was seated upon a lion-throne, possessing a splendor equal to ten million suns.
One should visualize the lotus-like hands and feet as having a luster like that of a red lotus;
the right lotus-foot upon a vessel filled with jewels,
and the divine left lotus-foot formed in the shape of a svastika.
With four resplendent arms bearing the conch, discus, mace, and lotus,
the God is beautiful in every limb and adorned with all ornaments;
having been lifted up, He is illuminated by all kinds of jewels from the Jewel River.
Rukmiṇī and Satyabhāmā remain there, as does she known as Rādhikā;
with great joy, they sprinkle [the Lord] with gems from jeweled jars.
Kālindī and Ṛkṣajā stand at their sides, offering two jeweled water-pots.
Nāgnajitī, Sunandā, Mitravindā, and Sulakṣaṇā—
bringing a jewel-pitcher drawn from the Jewel River and bestowing all auspiciousness through their union, these queens shall carry him away.
Then, sixteen thousand beloved women surrounding him,
along with fifty deities, [should worship] with songs, dances, and musical instruments;
thus the practitioner of the mantra should meditate upon Hari and recite the mantra four hundred thousand times.
At the conclusion of the recitation, one should offer divine milk-rice oblations (pāyasa) in a tenth part of that number;
one should perform libations (tarpaṇa) with water mixed with bilva leaves in a tenth part of that;
having performed the ritual ablution (abhiṣeka) in a tenth part of that, one should worship even the Brahmins.
One should write the seed-syllable together with the name of the practitioner to be accomplished (sādhya) within the pericarp (karṇikā);
outside of that, one should write the remaining seventeen syllables, followed by a pair of fire-houses (vahnergeha-yuga).
Outside the circle, there should be an eight-petalled lotus and a square enclosure adorned with vajras.
This yantra, endowed with four gates and possessing auspicious characteristics,
has the syllable *māyā* written in the northeast, southeast, southwest,
and northwest corners; likewise, the six-syllabled *śrībīja* should be written in the other [intermediate] corners.
On the leaf, however, one should recite the Kāma-gāyatrī three times each according to its divisions:
"We know Kāmadeva; we meditate on the one with flower-arrows; may Anaṅga impel us.
Thus is declared the Kāma-gāyatrī, which deludes all people.
By reciting this [mantra] beginning with "Kāma," one shall accomplish all rites.
One should write the Kāma-mantra in the middle of the petals according to the sequence of the six syllables:
"Obeisance to Kāmadeva, who is dear to all people."
"O you who cause total delusion!"—thus [it is said]. One should kindle the pair of flames. At the end of the word "of all people," one should say "may my heart be in accord.
The mantra is declared to end with "svāhā," preceded by the pair of words "bring under control" (vaśaṃ kuru). Thus the mantra is proclaimed.
O Sage, this Gopāla-yantra, beginning with the syllable *Kāma*, has been declared as a means for accomplishment.
Having inscribed it upon a vessel made of gold or with foodstuffs,
one should wear the consecrated yantra through the power of recitation (*japa*), sprinkling (*seka*), and other rites.
By the mere wearing of this [amulet] on the earth, what is not accomplished?
Kings come under one's control like servants, and the world becomes crowded with parasols. This mantra, which deludes the three worlds, is uniquely honored by all people.
Having invoked Hari, the Lord of the Kings of Kings, into this yantra,
the practitioner should worship Him with devotion using all royal offerings.
One should perform the six-limbed worship (ṣaḍaṅga) in the six corners, and outside of that, on the petals in the intermediate directions.
One should worship Vāsudeva, Saṃkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha,
as well as Sarasvatī, Lakṣmī, Rati, and Prīti on the petals of the directions;
outside of that, one should worship the eight queens, beginning with Rukmiṇī.
Then, one should worship outside of that the treasures known as Indranīla and Mukunda, as well as Makarānanda, Kacchapa, Śaṅkha, and Padma; thereafter,
Indra and the other [guardians] in their respective directions, and immediately after that, the [weapons] such as the Vajra.
Thus, one should worship Acyuta with devotion using these sixfold repetitions;
having crossed the terrible ocean of saṃsāra, which is teeming with the crocodiles of latent impressions (vāsanā),
the practitioner reaches the supreme abode, and not otherwise.
One should recite the mantra four hundred thousand times and perform a fire sacrifice (homa) with milk-rice (pāyasa) ten times that number;
or else, with full-blown lotuses, and complete the remainder of the ritual as prescribed.
Then, one should [meditate upon] Viṣṇu in one's own heart and perform the mantra-depositions (nyāsa) as they have been taught.
Absorbed in that [mantra], the practitioner, having crossed the ocean of saṃsāra, should dwell [in this state].
By offering ten thousand red lotuses as oblations, he shall bring the entire universe under his control.
He should wear that ash upon his forehead; whomever he touches or whomever he gazes upon [shall be subdued].
What are the actions performed by those [deities] who abide in the wind? By means of reddish-brown horses and the like, kings come under one's control like slaves.
For the sake of obtaining white garments and the like, one should offer oblations with white flowers and the like.
Through oblations of rice-flour enriched with honey and reddish rice-ears,
or with *śrīvṛkṣa* flowers, Lakṣmī becomes pleased and remains constant.
One should offer oblations with *bilva* leaves to ensure that she follows after one’s sons and grandsons.
One obtains gracious Fortune (Lakṣmī) and through its fruits shall attain sovereignty;
by the offering of ghee alone, Brāhmaṇical splendor arises,
as well as the increase of longevity, fame, fortune, and the subjugation of all women.
One obtains happiness that surpasses all else; of this there is no doubt.
By offering oblations of ghee and rice, one becomes powerful before long.
By offering various kinds of food and edibles, one shall be an enjoyer of pleasures for as long as life lasts.
One should not perform the ritual application (*prayoga*) of the eighteen-syllable and ten-syllable mantras here;
rather, one who is intent on the practice should effect the single [result] by means of both.
Whosoever worships Gopāla with the jewel-consecration (*ratnābhiṣeka*) according to the prescribed rule—
"Though endowed with all sovereignty and prosperity, though the enjoyer of all and the doer of all,
she shall go to Hari upon the abandonment of the body"— thus have the sages sung.
[Thus ends the twenty-third chapter in the glorious Gautamīya. || 23 ||
Now, therefore, I shall fully proclaim the mantra of Rukmiṇīvallabha;
through knowledge of this sacrifice, one becomes beloved by all the worlds on earth.
At the end of "namas" is the word "bhagavān," followed by the feminine suffix "ṅīp," and then "rukmiṇīvallabha."
This great mantra (mahāmanu) consists of sixteen syllables, ending with *svāhā* and joined with the seed-syllable (*bhāva*).
By knowing this, the practitioner of mantra becomes wise without delay;
he certainly attains the fruit of the eightfold yoga (*aṣṭāṅgayoga*) through the practice of meditation (*dhānya*).
By remembering this mantra, one obtains the fruit of all sacred fords (tīrthas).
Nārada is declared to be its sage (muni), and the meter (chandas) is said to be Anuṣṭubh. Its deity (devatā) is Śrī Kṛṣṇa, known as the beloved of Rukmiṇī.
One who knows the six ancillaries (ṣaḍaṅga) should perform the ritual of the limbs with the words used individually and collectively.
[He should meditate on the Lord] dark as the flax flower, clothed in a pair of yellow garments,
beautiful with various ornaments, and with a chest adorned by the Kaustubha gem.
Adorned with the Śrīvatsa mark and graced with glorious jewel-ornaments,
seated upon a beautiful jeweled throne within the excellent palace of Dvārakā,
He is sweetly conversing with Rukmiṇī and bears the conch, discus, and mace.
Having thus meditated upon the Supreme Self, one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times.
At its conclusion, the practitioner of mantra should perform a fire oblation with sesame seeds soaked in sweet substances.
Then, one should worship [the deity] on a Vaiṣṇava pedestal according to the procedure for the ten-syllable mantra.
By offering oblations with *palāśa* flowers, one shall attain divine knowledge (*divyajñāna*).
One should perform the libation (*tarpaṇa*) as before and accomplish all desired goals. By offering oblations with white lotuses (*puṇḍarīka*), one attains prosperity (*śrī*) without effort.

"By the mere offering of oblations of clarified butter, one shall live happily for a hundred years. Thus, O Lord of Rukmiṇī, you too should diligently preserve before me this Vidyā, which is honored by sages and bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation."
One should utter the *praṇava* (oṃ) at the beginning and the word *bhavagate* at the end;
likewise, one should utter the word *nandaputra* ending in the dative case (*ṅe*), as well as *nandavapuḥ*.
This ten-syllable mantra, ending with *bhūti*, bestows the accomplishment of all goals.
The sage is declared to be Nārada; the meter is said to be Virāj;
and the deity here is Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who bestows the fruits of the four aims of human life. One should determine the five limbs of this mantra by means of the syllables beginning with "āca."
One should meditate upon the God in the beautiful Vṛndāvana, surrounded by hosts of cowherds and cowherd-maidens,
made lovely by various ornaments, clothed in a pair of yellow garments,
the deity who grants all that is dear, possessing a youthful and dark-complexioned form.
Having thus meditated upon the supreme sole teacher of the world, who is holding a flute with his two arms,
one should likewise recite the excellent mantra one hundred thousand times and perform oblations with sweetened sesame seeds ten times that number.
One should worship according to the prescribed rite upon the seat (pīṭha) described as having ten syllables.
The mantra-practitioner who contemplates in this manner shall be honored by both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Having offered ten thousand bilva leaves into the fire, one shall accomplish all desires.
Having recited it one hundred and eight times, one shall be victorious in the assembly;
becoming uniquely fortunate in all the worlds and endowed with every sovereignty,
at the end of the body one attains that state from which, having reached it, there is no return.
The word *nandaputra* ending in the dative case (*-āya*), likewise the word *śyāmalāṅga*,
*amṛta*, *mukhavṛtta*, and *māṃsavapuḥ*—
this ten-syllabled mantra is proclaimed as the bestower of all prosperity.
Nārada is declared to be its sage (ṛṣi), Anuṣṭubh is said to be its meter (chandas),
and Bālakṛṣṇa is proclaimed by the sages to be its deity (devatā).
The practitioner of mantra should, as before, perform the five-fold limb-assignment with the discus and other symbols.
[He should meditate on the Lord] dark as the flax flower, with hands shining with the conch and discus,
playing a flute with two arms, and clothed in a pair of yellow garments.

Having thus meditated upon the God, who is beautiful with various ornaments and resplendent with graceful gestures and laughter, one should worship Him with the five limbs and the lords of the directions;
having also worshipped Him with their respective weapons, one established in the vow should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times.
The practitioner of mantra should offer oblations ten times the number [of recitations] with milk-rice (pāyasa) soaked in sweet substances.
Having thus perfected the mantra, one may accomplish all rites.
By offering unbroken rice grains (akṣata) with sesame and clarified butter (ājya), one shall destroy planetary afflictions and diseases.
Having offered oblations with *palāśa* flowers, one shall attain equality with Vāgīśvara.
First, having uttered the *praṇava*, then the word *namo bhagavate*,
then the word *nandaputra* ending in the suffix *-ṅe*, followed by *bhūdhara* joined with the *mukhavṛtta*.
The word *vapuḥ* likewise ends in the feminine suffix *ṅīp* and consists of twenty syllables;
Nārada is declared its sage (*ṛṣi*), and the Virāṭ meter is said to be its metre (*chandas*).
Its deity is the son of Nanda, the sole delighter of all the worlds.
One should visualize the five limbs of the Mind (Mano-rāja) as being adorned with wheels and other ornaments;
he is dark-complexioned like a fresh rain-cloud, his eyes resemble lotus petals,
and he is decorated with necklaces, armlets, bracelets, and anklets shining like pearls and emeralds.
Adorned with many jewels, his hands shone with radiant earrings;
his chest was illuminated by the magnificent Kaustubha gem and marked with the Śrīvatsa sign;
he wore a crest of peacock feathers and was surrounded by cowherds, cowherdesses, and cattle.
Having thus meditated upon the Supreme Self, one should then mutter the mantra.

At the conclusion of four hundred thousand recitations, one should perform a fire-oblation (homa) with red lotuses numbering one-tenth of that amount; the remainder should be performed as previously prescribed.
Having invoked Viśveśa into the Daśārṇa yantra, one should worship Him.
The first circuit should be with the limbs (aṅgas), the second with the queens (mahiṣīs),
the third with the lords of the directions (digadhīśas), and the fourth with the thunderbolt and other [emblems] (vajrādyaiḥ).
Thus, whoever worships Kṛṣṇa joined with the fourfold repetition shall obtain the complete fruit of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa.
By offering ten thousand oblations of milk-rice (pāyasa), one becomes a lord of great wealth.
Through ten thousand oblations of ghee, the practitioner of mantra attains a full lifespan;
through a hundred thousand oblations of *dūrvā* grass, one shall live happily for a hundred years.
Thus has been described this mantra, which bestows all accomplishments upon everyone.
Now I shall further proclaim the mantra that bestows all prosperity;
by knowing this sacrifice, all sages become the sole ground for both enjoyment and liberation.
Having uttered "Līlā-daṇḍadhara," one should then say "Gopījana."
Having uttered "dorddaṇḍantu padaṃ," then the word "meghaśyāma," and finally "viṣṇoḥ svāhā"— this mantra bestows all human goals (puruṣārtha).
Nārada is declared its sage (ṛṣi), and the Anuṣṭubh is proclaimed as its meter (chandas).

The deity of this [mantra] is Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the instructor of the entire universe. The arrangement of its five limbs is performed with the words; thereafter, one should meditate upon Acyuta, who is dark like the Tāpiñja flower and eternally sixteen years of age.

Having meditated upon the Supreme One, the sole teacher of the world, who stands in the midst of the gopīs, embraced by those two whose hearts are filled with desire, beautiful with all ornaments and wearing yellow garments, one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times.
Having offered one-tenth of the portion with lotuses, one should complete the remainder of the rite.
One should daily propitiate the deity with milk and auspicious waters.
From the mandala, the desired perfection is attained, and one shall become a great lord of wealth.
He who constantly resorts to this [mantra], being intent upon recitation, fire-offerings, and so forth,
shall obtain his desired and beneficial goals and, at the end of the body, go to that supreme state.
One should then utter the seed-syllables of Māyā and Kāma, preceded by the Veda and so forth.
One should utter "Śrīkṛṣṇa" ending in the suffix -ṅ (ṅe), and likewise "Govinda.
At the end of the word "Gopījana," one should pronounce "Vallabha" ending in -ṅ. Ending with "Kāma," it is the seed-syllable of Ramā; thus is the leader of mantras proclaimed.
This mantra of Siddha Gopāla bestows all perfections upon men.
Having performed the five-limbed ritual (*pañcāṅga*) with seed-syllables (*bīja*) and words (*pada*), one should then meditate upon Acyuta,
who sits at the foot of the celestial tree (*suradruma*) under the shade provided by the King of Birds (*pakṣirāja*).
Shining like a conch or the moon, they subsisted on curd and milk-rice;
with many faces turned toward them, they were like the moon joined by the planets,
beautiful with various ornaments, and accompanied by the two Kandaravas who possessed the Kaustubha jewel.

One should meditate upon the two glorious boys, Rāma and Kṛṣṇa, who possess beautiful strings of pearls, who are composed of all wonders, and who are the refuge of the three worlds; while recollecting them,
one should mutter the excellent mantra one hundred thousand times and perform oblations with bilva fruits ten thousand times as a concluding portion.
At the conclusion of the *homa*, the mantra-practitioner should complete the remaining rites according to the rules.
He should worship [the deity] upon the seat described for the ten-syllable mantra, using the method to be explained hereafter;
or he may worship the six limbs in the filaments, or the lords of the directions, or even the watches of the day (*prahara*).
Having thus worshipped Puruṣottama, who consists of the three-fold repetition,
one should daily satisfy Him with water conceived as milk, which bestows the attainment of one's desires. By joining the hands at the mouth and reciting [the mantra], one becomes eloquent and wise.
Having offered oblations mixed with fresh butter, one shall become a lord of the earth.
On a Sunday, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times at the root of an Aśvattha tree;
endowed with sons and friends, one shall not die an untimely death.
Now I shall describe another mantra, which bestows prosperity:
one should sequentially fuse the seed-syllables of Lakṣmī (Śrīṃ), Māyā (Hrīṃ), and Kāma (Klīṃ) with the ten-syllable mantra.
This sixteen-syllable mantra directly grants Great Prosperity (Mahālakṣmī).
Brahmā is declared to be the seer (ṛṣi), the Gāyatrī is said to be the meter (chanda),
