and the glorious Kṛṣṇa is said to be the deity who bestows great prosperity.
O limb, with a mind focused on no other, one should meditate upon the Lord according to the ritual arrangement of the ten syllables.
Resembling a mass of dark clouds, with lotus-like hands and feet reddened [by lac], beautiful with rows of pearl necklaces, his chest adorned with the Kaustubha gem,
and resplendent with the waves of his crown, armlets, neck-ornaments, and bracelets.
One should meditate [on the deity] situated within a jeweled palace, seated in the center of a red lotus.
One should recite the mantra four hundred thousand times and perform ten thousand oblations with milk-rice (pāyasa).
All rites such as libations (tarpaṇa) and so forth should be performed according to the previously stated procedure.
The practitioner who worships this form of Gopāla,
having attained all prosperity along with Lakṣmī, shall diligently go to that supreme state.
[Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter in the glorious Gautamīya. || 24 ||
Now I shall further proclaim the King of Mantras, which is very difficult to obtain;
by the recitation of which, O lords of sages,
one attains divine knowledge and even the Lord of the Gods regained his lost kingdom through its worship.
Many other gods as well have attained their respective offices.
The mantra for the Blessed One, beginning with "O Govinda Mukunda," consisting of three morae (mātrās) in the heart,
is said to be the twelve-syllabled mantra that bestows all prosperity.
Nārada is declared to be its sage (ṛṣi); Virāṭ is proclaimed as its meter (chandas); Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who is saluted by all the gods, is declared to be its deity (devatā);
and the application (viniyoga) of this mantra is for the sake of the four aims of human life (puruṣārtha).
One should arrange the five limbs using the words both individually and collectively;
one should perform the purification of the hands through emanation, reabsorption, and maintenance,
as well as the ten principles ending with maintenance, and the encapsulation by the Mātṛkā-mantra.

Having thus performed the deposition of the principles (tattvanyāsa), preceded by Keśava and the others, [one should meditate on Him] who is uniquely skilled in the methods of creation, preservation, and dissolution;
who is dark as a blue lotus flower; and whose eyes are like blue water-lilies.
Adorned with many jewel-ornaments, illuminating all space with its radiance, likewise provided with excellent food and a favorable breeze, and clothed in a pair of yellow garments;
the Lord bears the Śrīvatsa mark and his chest is resplendent with the Kaustubha gem.
He was enchanting all that moves and is stationary with the sound of his flute-playing;
he was praised by hosts of sages, hosts of gods, and hosts of seers;
he was surrounded by throngs of queens and attended by the divine treasures.
Alternatively, having meditated upon the excellent mantra— [the deity] who has the luster of molten gold, who has pervaded the three worlds with his splendor,
and who sits upon a jeweled lion-throne amidst the creepers of the wish-fulfilling tree—
one should recite it twelve hundred thousand times with devotion.
Having made his ears the source of news regarding women, he remained steadfast in his vow; subsisting on water, roots, and fruits, the devotee, observing the aforementioned conduct,
should offer oblations ten times the number [of recitations] with flowers born from the *Brahmavṛkṣa* tree.

Then, one should complete the remaining rites according to the previously mentioned procedure. Having installed the deity in a cow-pen, in a sacred grove, or likewise in a temple, one who worships it becomes a partaker of worldly enjoyment and liberation.
One should meditate upon the great ruby pavilion situated in Vṛndāvana; then,
having purified the ordinary *arghya*,
one should worship the gatekeepers and worship the Lord of Birds (Garuḍa) on the earthen pedestal at the front of the door.
One should worship Japa, Vijaya, those known as Bala and Prabala,
Caṇḍa, Pracaṇḍa, Dhātṛ,
and Vidhātṛ at the doors starting from the east, proceeding in a clockwise direction.
One should worship Dvāraśrī above the door and Dehalī on the threshold;
likewise, one should worship Gaṅgā and Yamunā on the two sides of the door,
and Vighneśa and Kṣetrapāla at their sides.
Taking up *dūrvā* grass and unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), the knower of mantras should drive away obstacles from the exterior;
then, with his feet stamping, his hands clapping, and his faces filled with loud shouts,
he should dispel the threefold obstacle by means of the *astra-mantra*.
In the corners, one should worship Vighna, Durgā, and Vāṇī, as well as Kṣetreśa.
With a concentrated mind, one should worship Vāstupuruṣa in the center of the house. [The mantra is:
Tāra (Oṃ), followed by the word "Śārṅga," then "Ṅe" (Dative case), then "Astam" (Accusative case), and finally "Sa" along with the seat (Vāsana).
Having uttered "huṃ phaṭ namaḥ," one stands before Hari with devotion;
this should be performed everywhere, especially as prescribed for the installation. One who knows the ritual procedure should approach the seats with that mantra.
Having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) upon his own body from the head down to the end of the speech and self,
and having prepared the pedestal according to the procedure prescribed for the ten-syllable mantra, he should worship it;
likewise, having worshipped the gurus beginning with Nārada, he should sacrifice to the Bhāgavatas.
One should know that the syllable *gu* signifies death, while the syllable *ru* is its antidote;
by virtue of his union with Kṛṣṇa, he is called "Guru" (the Teacher) by the sages.
[Nārada spoke to] Parvata, Jiṣṇu, Niśaṭha, Uddhava, and Dāruka.
One should worship Viśvaksena and Śaileya, extending from the northwest (Vāyu) to the northeast (Īśāna);
likewise, the gurus, the supreme gurus (paragurus), the parameṣṭhi-gurus,
and similarly the higher and lower gurus, followed immediately by the ancient perfected ones (pūrvasiddhas).

One should offer salutations to the sandals (pādukā) by first mentioning the names of the Gurus— such as Sanaka, Sanatkumāra, Sanātana, and others who have attained the supreme state— and then saying "namas.
These protect one constantly from misfortune and ill omens.
The sandals are proclaimed as the bestowers of desired objects.
The root *car* is used in the sense of movement, and *tuṇa* is said to mean bliss (*ānanda*). Because they cause one to attain bliss, they are called *cāraṇa*.
Having performed the worship of the pedestal (pīṭhapūjā), one should then invoke Hari there and worship Him.
After performing all the ritual services (upacāras), one should worship the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) in succession. One should worship Rukmiṇī and Satyabhāmā on the right and left [of the Lord].
Vāsudeva, Saṃkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha— these are the [sons]. Kālindī, the one named Nāgnajitī, Suśīlā, Sanandakā, Ṛkṣajā, and Lakṣaṇā— these are remembered as the eight queens.
Having worshipped Kaumodakī, Pāñcajanya, Vasudeva, and Devakī,
and thereafter Nandagopa and Yaśodā,
and having likewise honored Kiṅkiṇī, one should worship Dāma and the others.
One should likewise worship eight elephants in their respective directions, possessing the hope of [removing] all obstacles:
Kumuda, the one named Kumuda, Puṇḍarīka, or Manaḥ, Śaṅkukarṇa, Sarvanetra, Sumukha, and Supratiṣṭhita.
Worshipping Kṛṣṇa once, twice, or thrice a day with devotion and a melodious voice, one becomes a vessel for both worldly enjoyment and liberation,
whether staying in a cow-pen, on a mountain peak, in a sacred forest, or on a riverbank.

By installing Kṛṣṇa in a temple, one obtains the fruit of ten million sacred fords (tīrthas). One obtains that same fruit by performing ten billion great gifts (mahādānas) or by wandering through ten million sacred fords;
yet by installing Keśava with devotion, one attains that very result.
Furthermore, whatever fruit one obtains from reciting ten million great mantras,
that same fruit one attains by installing Puruṣottama; and whatever merit comes from ten million sacrifices, that merit is gained by resorting to Puṇyāraṇya.
Whatever fruit a mortal obtains by installing Keśava,
and whatever fruit one may obtain by chanting the name of Hari throughout one's entire life—
that same fruit one attains by installing Puruṣottama.
Whatever fruit is obtained by the gift of ten thousand cows at Kurukṣetra during a solar eclipse,
that same fruit one obtains by devoutly installing Puruṣottama;
immediately joined with the Sārgī [vīṇā], Kāma is endowed with the five notes.
One should not say "mohāt" at the end of "māṃsāṃte nāthāya"; this is declared to be the mantra.
Nārada is said to be its sage (ṛṣi), Anuṣṭubh is stated to be its meter (chandas), and Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the beloved of the cowherds, is proclaimed as its deity (devatā).
One should visualize the five limbs of the mind, beginning with the wheel of speech (ā-cakra).
One should meditate upon Kṛṣṇa in Vṛndāvana, surrounded by hosts of cowherd boys,
dark-complexioned, enchanting the entire universe, holding a flute and a horn in his two hands.

Having thus meditated upon [the deity] adorned with many jewels, with tinkling bells, necklaces, and anklets, one should, with a concentrated mind, recite the mantra one hundred thousand times. One should then perform a fire sacrifice (homa) with ten parts of that number, using milk-rice (pāyasa) mixed with sweet substances.
The procedure for worship is recorded as being performed with the faces of Aṅga, Indra, Vajra, and the others.
The practitioner of mantra who thus attains Hari, the beloved of Śrī Gopāla,
becomes a sovereign lord over the foremost of the hosts of cows, endowed with the abundance of all sovereignty.
At the end of the body, one shall attain the abode of the Lord; there is no doubt in this matter.
It is endowed with upper teeth, has a void at its end, and likewise lacks an end; it possesses two "meats" (māṃsa) and is joined with the Vītihotra [fire] by means of the terrifying facial movement.
The eight-syllable mantra ending with "namaḥ" is declared to be the accomplisher of all goals.
One should place the seed-syllable of desire (klīm) at the beginning; it bestows all objects of desire.
Furthermore, there are certain mantras of Gopāla associated with Kuṇḍalīśa found here and there.
One should place the seed-syllable of desire (Kāma-bīja) at their beginning for the accomplishment of all aims.
Nārada is declared to be its sage (ṛṣi), Anuṣṭubh is said to be its meter (chandas), and Śrī Kṛṣṇa is its deity (devatā); it is the means for the welfare of all persons.
One should fashion the five limbs of the Mind-born One with the [mudrās] beginning with Ācakra;
he is dark like a kalāya flower, with eyes like blue lotuses,
beautiful with various ornaments, and appearing as a five-year-old child.

Meditating thus upon Hari, the Supreme Self, who causes the creation, preservation, and dissolution of the universe— who holds a vessel overflowing with curd in his two hands, who is beautiful with rows of bright pearl necklaces, and who is surrounded by cowherds, cowherdesses, and cattle— [one should worship].
One should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times and perform oblations with milk-rice (pāyasa) ten thousand times;
or alternatively, having performed oblations with lotuses, the mantra becomes perfected and one shall be happy.
One should worship [the deity] according to the prescribed rite upon the pedestal described for the ten-syllable mantra.
Alternatively, O Lord of Mountains, worship with vajras and other offerings is prescribed for him.
By offering clarified butter and unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), one becomes a master of all supernatural powers (*siddhi*).
By offering *syaka* flowers, one obtains a son; by offering *pāṭala* flowers, one gains the sight of a king.
By performing the fire-oblation (homa) here daily from the beginning, prosperity remains firm in his house;
indeed, by means of the previously mentioned libation (tarpaṇa), one shall accomplish all desired objects.
[Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter in the Gautamīya. || 25 ||
The leader of mantras, beginning with *kāma* (the syllable *klīṃ*), mounted upon the eight vowels and possessing the *sarga* (visarga),
is declared to be the two-syllabled mantra "Kṛṣṇa. With *kāma* preceding the vowel-quality syllables (*guṇākṣara*),
it consists of four syllables, beginning and ending with *kāma*, and bestows the fruits of the four aims of life.
The great mantra consists of five syllables, beginning with "Oṃ" and ending with "Namaḥ.

If that same mantra is preceded by the word "Kāma," it is known as the six-syllabled mantra (Ṣaḍakṣara Manu). Having thus chanted this, the lord of sages, Śātātapa, became a knower of the three periods of time.
By the mere recollection of this, one attains omniscience and the highest poetic skill;
there is no doubt in this matter. Truly, truly, my word is the truth: "Kṛṣṇa Govindau" (in the dative case) followed by the eight syllables beginning with "Kāma."
If the seed-syllable of desire (Kāma-bīja) is placed at the beginning and the end, it is considered a nine-syllabled mantra.
To the one whose self is perfectly tranquil, [is addressed] the seven-syllabled beloved of Fire (Vahni-vallabhā).
One should again extract the seed-syllable of desire, the seed-syllable of Earth (Dharā-bīja), and once more the seed-syllable of desire.
The ten-syllable mantra ending with *namaḥ* is: *śyāmalāṅgāya padaṃ ṅe'ntaṃ śivānto bālavapuṣe kṛṣṇāya*. Another mantra is considered as: *bālavapuḥ kāmaḥ kṛṣṇo ṅe'ntaḥ śivāntakaḥ*.
"Kṛṣṇāya" followed by two vowels (svaradvandva) constitutes another five-syllabled mantra;
the eleven-syllabled mantra grants the desired objects to those who worship it.
The six-syllabled mantra is declared to be "Gopālāya" joined with the two words for fire and wife (agnijāyā).
O Devakī, by the mere remembrance of whom nothing is unattainable in the three worlds—
of these excellent Manus, the sage Nārada is declared to be the seer;
the meter is said to be Gāyatrī, and Bālakṛṣṇa is the deity.
One who possesses the six long [vowels] should perform the six limbs through desire.
[He should meditate on the deity] whose eyes are like blue lotuses, a youth with a dark-complexioned body,
adorned with various jewels and endowed with diverse ornaments.
Seated upon a red lotus,
holding a vessel of curd and the *saṃvara* (skull-cup) in his two lotus-like hands, and surrounded by cowherd boys—
one should meditate thus and recite the mantra one hundred thousand times according to the prescribed rule.
At the conclusion, one should duly offer oblations with fresh bilva fruits (śrīphala) amounting to a tenth part [of the total recitation].
One should worship Hari according to the prescribed rite upon the seat (pīṭha) described for the ten-syllable mantra.
The first enclosure (āvṛtti) consists of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga), and the second consists of the lords of the directions (digadhīśvara).

The third [offering] is said to be performed during the watches of the night; when offered, it grants all desires. By performing an oblation with ten thousand bilva leaves, a man obtains splendor, seed-power, as well as beauty and Lakṣmī who dwells in all things.
By performing ten thousand oblations with red lotuses, kings become his servants;
likewise, by offering oblations with bilva leaves, one may obtain a kingdom free from thorns.
The wise person who devotes himself to even one of these excellent mantras [attains such results].
Having enjoyed the excellent pleasures described here, one shall go to that state at the end of the body.
Now, I shall likewise declare this supreme mantra which bestows all prosperity;
by the mere remembrance of which, the knower of mantras attains equality with the Lord of Speech.
Śakra is the lord of the gods, and Dhanada is the leader of wealth;
what on this earth cannot be accomplished by the mere recollection of this mantra?
[It begins with] Vāgbhava, Kāmabīja, Māyā, and immediately thereafter Lakṣmī.
The excellent mantra consists of ten syllables, and the mantra [of the goddess] consists of fourteen syllables;
beginning with the *vāgbhava* [syllable], the practitioner of this mantra becomes like the Lord of Speech himself,
possessing a brilliant intellect versed in the Vedas, Vedānta, Vedāṅgas, and the established doctrines.
Speech becomes a flow of nectar and poetry that conquers all;
one becomes a knower of all literature and a truly omniscient person before long,
provided the practitioner masters this mantra, which is the primordial consciousness itself.
Before long, the wise one becomes the sovereign lord of all accomplishments;
kings, along with their retinues and common subjects, come under his control;
and all the gods pay him homage—what more need be said of this supreme state?
When one recites the Lord of Mantras with devotion, preceded by the seed-syllable *Śrī*,
wealth shall come to his house that was previously unattainable;
and in his lineage, Fortune shall remain firm as long as the dissolution of all beings.
When a mantra preceded by the seed-syllable *kāma* is recited by the most excellent practitioners,
the three worlds come under their control through the actions of mind, speech, and body;
it becomes like Kandarpa to women, causing infatuation at the mere sight of him.
Causing wonder in the world, he shall live happily for a hundred years.
The seer (ṛṣi) of this mantra is Brahmā; Gāyatrī is declared to be its meter (chandas);
and Kṛṣṇa, the enchanter of all the worlds, is declared to be its deity (devatā).
One should assign the five limbs of the mind using the [syllables] beginning with Ā (ācakrādyaiḥ).

One should place the ten syllables upon the hands through the processes of emanation, dissolution, and maintenance; O Sage, having encased them within the *tāra* (Oṃ), one should place "namas" in their midst.
One should assign the ten syllables in the region of the Daśārṇāṅga-nyāsa;
likewise, one should assign the ten principles (tattvas) beginning with Keśava in successive order.
Having performed the assignment of the sages (ṛṣi-nyāsa) and so forth, one should then perform the six-limbed assignment (ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa).

The syllable *Kām* (Klim) is the supreme seed-syllable, and *Svāhā* is the sovereign Prakṛti; she is pure consciousness, the Supreme Power (*Parāśakti*), the deity presiding over the mantra. One should meditate upon her situated in the midst of the golden ground within the delightful Vṛndāvana.
In the noble Kalpāṭavī grove, which is strewn with various flowering creepers, adorned with clusters of trees, and graced by a magnificent pavilion of rubies,
frequented by gods, kinnaras, gandharvas, and sages.
When he has been approached with hymns of praise by Nārada and other eminent sages,
one should meditate upon him seated upon a jeweled throne atop a lotus;
dark as a water-laden cloud, with eyes like the petals of a red lotus.
His feet resemble red lotuses, adorned with hands;
he is decorated with ornaments set with the nine gems;
he blows a flute with his two hands and is clothed in a pair of yellow garments.
Upon his slightly reddened chest, his garment was illuminated by the glorious Kaustubha gem;
his breast was beautiful with rows of pearl necklaces and marked with the Śrīvatsa sign;
and at the edge of his gorocanā tilaka, his earrings appeared like hovering bees.
Adorned with a gemset *cillī* ornament resembling the bow of Kandarpa,
with shimmering anklets and earrings set with many jewels,
and wearing a crest of peacock feathers, he was beheld by all-knowing beings in every limb.
May it always attend the oblation, served by hosts of sages;

having thus meditated upon the excellent mantra, one established in the vow should recite it ten lakhs of times according to the procedure for the ten-syllable mantra, whereby the mantra becomes perfected.
With this perfected mantra, one should accomplish all desired objects;
one should worship on the seat described for the ten-syllable mantra according to its prescribed ritual.
The practitioner of the mantra should offer ten thousand oblations with flowers born from the *brahmavṛkṣa* tree.
The minister shall undoubtedly become a great poet and possessed of great wisdom. By offering oblations with *mālatī* flowers, one attains incomparable mastery of speech.
And by performing *homa* with *tagara* sprinkled with milk, one shall attain omniscience.
By performing oblations with *vakula* blossoms, one obtains desired prosperity;
by oblations of various kinds of food, both solid and soft, one attains incomparable abundance;
and by oblations of clarified butter alone, the splendor of Brahman is generated.
By offering oblations with the leaves of the *śrīphala* tree, one obtains a kingdom without effort;
by offering its fruits, there shall be mastery of mantras; and one should offer *dūrvā* grass for long life.
Having first performed the prescribed libation (*tarpaṇa*), one should propitiate everything.
One should perform every ritual application as prescribed for the ten-syllable mantra.
[Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter in the glorious Gautamīya. || 26 ||
Now I shall further proclaim another mantra that accomplishes all aims:
the three-syllabled mantra "Kṛṣṇa," situated between two seed-syllables of desire (Klīm).
This mantra, which bestows immediate fruit, has been told to you out of devotion.
Through focused attention upon this, Śakra attained the lordship of the gods.
The sage of this mantra is Brahmā; its meter is declared to be Gāyatrī;
and the deity is said by the sages to be Kṛṣṇa, the origin of the worlds.

One should practice with the six long vowels and the desire [element] according to the six-limbed rite. Having thus performed the ritual of the limbs, one should then meditate upon the Imperishable (Acyuta), who is dark like the *kalāya* flower, yet resembles molten gold on the earth.
Seated upon a jeweled lion-throne in the Pārijāta grove,
illuminating the quarters of the sky with the natural radiance arising from his own body,
he beheld the divine Vāsudeva, who pervades the universe and assumes the form of a child.
Adorned with various ornaments and beautiful, he was gazed upon by the cowherd girls;
he emerged from the wish-fulfilling tree (kalpavṛkṣa) and was sprinkled with streams of jewels;
he was lovely with rows of pearl necklaces and clothed in a pair of yellow garments.
The best of practitioners, established in the vow, should recite the mantra four hundred thousand times;
at the end, for the sake of all accomplishments, he should offer oblations with bilva fruits ten times that number.
Having invoked the deity into an eight-petaled lotus, he should worship him thoroughly.

One should worship the lords of the directions at the end of the enclosure of eight hexagons; these eight [deities] are also to be worshipped at the conclusion. This is declared to be the ritual of worship. Having offered oblations of fresh butter (navanīta) in accordance with the rules, one attains irreproachable prosperity.
By performing ten thousand oblations of *śrīphala* fruits, the practitioner shall attain men;
by offering an ear of grain, one becomes wealthy in no time;
by offering flowers, one becomes possessed of food; and from offerings of clarified butter, one obtains prosperity.
The practitioner who worships this, being intent upon recitation, fire-offerings, and other rites,
shall properly attain great fortune and, at the end of the body, go to that state.
Now I shall describe the Cūḍāmaṇi, the king of mantras, which is very difficult to obtain.
Through the knowledge of sacrifice, all the sages, including Bhṛgu who perceives the three worlds, [attain this].
By the application of fire to the desire of the mantra of the four castes,
this is declared to be the crest-jewel (śikhāmaṇi), capable of perceiving the three worlds.
Nārada is declared to be its seer (ṛṣi), and Virāṭ is cited as its metre (chandas);
Śrī Kṛṣṇa is proclaimed by the sages to be its deity (devatā).
The ritual application of the limbs (aṅgakriyā) is considered to be performed with the seed-syllable (bīja) of Kāma, conjoined with the six long vowels.
Having performed the placement of the phonemes (varṇanyāsa) encapsulated by the mantra, one should likewise perform the placement of the phonemes encapsulated [by the mantra].
Then, having placed the ten principles (daśatattva), and thereafter the placement of the hands and limbs (karāṅganyāsa),
one should meditate upon [the deity] situated in Vṛndāvana, standing in the midst of those bowing for tens of millions of kalpas.
Swinging on a golden swing with the gopīs,
possessing a splendor equal to ten thousand suns, adorned with shimmering crocodile-shaped earrings,
and decorated with various ornaments blazing with diverse jewels.
Meditating thus upon the child who is five years of age, whose face is radiant with curling locks of hair,
and who illumines the quarters of the sky with his noble smile and splendor—
one should recite the crest-jewel mantra four hundred thousand times.
One should perform the oblation with palāśa or lotus flowers using a tenth part of that [number].
Worship with women is prescribed according to the enclosures of the limbs and the thunderbolt (vajra). One should respectfully offer ten thousand oblations with flowers from the brahmavṛkṣa tree.
By offering even fresh butter (navanīta) into the fire, the practitioner of mantra becomes a knower of the three times;
by offering bilva fruits (śrīphala), he attains a kingdom free of thorns;
and by offering lotus flowers (lakṣmīpuṣpa), the practitioner of mantra shall indeed obtain prosperity (lakṣmī).
Visualizing the form of light within the center of the root triangle,
one will certainly become a knower of the three times after one hundred thousand recitations of this mantra; indeed,
one perceives the entire course of the universe as if it were an amalaka fruit held in the palm of one's hand.
One sees everything situated in the heart with the eye through the practice of recitation (japa).
On a Sunday, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times at the root of an Aśvattha tree. By performing this regularly, one does not die an untimely death.
Dwelling there, by reciting the mantra one hundred thousand times, one becomes omniscient before long.
[Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter in the glorious Gautamīya. || 27 ||
Gautama said: O Sage, if I am worthy to hear it, tell me in truth of that single-syllable mantra, the most excellent, which is Viṣṇu himself, the enchantment of the three worlds.
Nārada said:
O Sage, listen as I relate with great effort that single word which serves to kindle all the mantras of Kṛṣṇa.

The syllable of desire (KĀM), situated on the earth (L), adorned with the drop of peace (M), is said by you with effort to be Viṣṇu, the Enchanter of the Three Worlds. Nārada is its seer (ṛṣi), and Virāṭ is its metre (chandas). It is bliss itself.
The infallible deity Viṣṇu is declared to be Trailokyamohana;
among all Kṛṣṇa-mantras, this mantra is the leader of mantras. [One should employ] the ten principles of creation and maintenance, and the Mātṛkā, encapsulated by the mantra.

One should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) on the hands and limbs as well as on the head, forehead, heart, genitals, and feet, using the seed-syllable (bīja) consisting of six long vowels in due order.
Having performed the nyāsa with the seed-syllables of the Five Arrows (Pañcabāṇa), one should then meditate for ten thousand [recitations].
The two seed-syllables (bījas) ending in *thāṃ* and joined with *repha* (*ra*), adorned with *anaṃta* (*śa*) and *śānti* (*ha*),
and joined with *bindu* (*m*) and *nāda* (*ḥ*), are enchanters of the three worlds.
Following that is the Kāma-bīja, conjoined with Jalandhara.

Joined with the fifth vowel, endowed with the bindu and nāda, these are the seed-syllables (bījas); at the end is the moon (the letter *i*) joined with the creative emission (*sarga*). [These effect] purification, enchantment, inflaming, heating, and intoxication.
This five-syllable mantra also bestows fruits corresponding to its name.
[He beheld] a body consisting of all splendor, resembling coral and ruby,
adorned with a crown, earrings, armlets, and bracelets.
Adorned with strings of pearls, a connection of jewels, and a pair of *tulākoṭi* ornaments,
beautiful with various decorations and clothed in a pair of yellow garments,
he is seated upon Garuḍa in the center of a red lotus.
Resembling molten gold, Lakṣmī stood upon Rāma’s thigh;
beautiful with all her ornaments and clad in a pair of white garments,
she was full of desire and repeatedly enchanted the God with her playful gestures.
One should meditate for a moment upon the Lord of the World, who holds a conch, a discus, a mace, a lotus, a noose, a goad, a bow, and arrows, and who is as red as a crimson lotus;
he is embraced from the left by his consort Lakṣmī, who holds a lotus in her hand.
The practitioner of mantra should meditate upon the enchanting Bimbamātā as being firmly established;
having thus visualized the Lord of the World within the twenty-syllable pedestal,
the practitioner should invoke Him and worship with all ritual offerings without exception.

One who knows the ritual procedure should worship according to the rules with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, following the sequence of the *nyāsa*. To his left, Lakṣmī should be worshipped with the seed-syllable *Śrīṃ*.
One should also worship the Kaustubha gem on the region of the throat, as well as the crown and the pair of earrings.
One should duly worship the Śrīvatsa on the region of the chest, the forest garland above the throat,
and the crown, saying "Salutation to that which consists of all splendor," and then worship the Kaustubha and other [jewels] with their respective name-mantras according to the rules.
Having thus worshipped the limbs of dissolution (layāṅga), one should then worship the limbs of enjoyment (bhogāṅga).
Having first worshipped the fortnights and the moon with devotion while they offer praise,
one should worship the six limbs in the filaments, as well as in the intermediate corners and the cardinal directions.
One should worship Agni and the others at the base of the petals, and the five arrows in front of the Lord; then, starting from the eastern petal and proceeding clockwise,
one should worship Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī, Rati, Prīti, and Ananta in the intervening spaces.
One should place Kīrti, Kānti, Tuṣṭi, and Puṣṭi at the tips of the fingers;
outside are Indra and the other guardians of the directions starting from the east, and further outside are their weapons.
Thus, the practitioner who worships Śrī Puruṣottama with devotion [attains success].
One whose intellect is focused on the hands [the practitioner] shall attain that state at the conclusion of all his aims.
One should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times and perform oblations with a tenth part of that amount,
using milk-rice (pāyasa) consecrated with the three nectars according to the prescribed ritual.
Alternatively, one should perform a thousand oblations with *ravis* (sun-flowers) and an equal number of libations;
having offered oblations accompanied by red lotuses, one shall bring the three worlds under one's control.
By performing oblations with clarified butter alone, one shall live happily for a hundred years.
By performing one hundred thousand oblations with *palāśa* wood, one becomes equal to the Lord of Speech (*vākpati*).
One established in the vow, by reciting [the mantra] ten million times, certainly attains absolute liberation (*kaivalya*).
Furthermore, one may accomplish the rites prescribed for the ten and eighteen syllables by means of this [mantra].
A mantra equal to this Kṛṣṇa-mantra does not exist;
O Sage, it is said to be the very life-force of all mantras.
Indeed, those mantras that are devoid of this are powerless, weak, and blunted.
Those who stand on the side of the enemy and those who are merely possessed of physical form—
by the recitation of this and other [mantras], they are restored to life and purified.
The word *hṛṣīkeśa* in the dative case (*ṅe'-anta*), followed by *namaḥ*, preceded by the word *kāma*.

The eight-syllable mantra has been declared to bestow all human goals (puruṣārtha). For the sake of accomplishing all aims, one should perform everything— the seer (ṛṣi), meter (chandas), deity (daivata), ritual worship, and the application of the rite— just as in the case of the single-syllable Viṣṇu mantra.
"Trailokyamohana," thus it is said, and immediately after that, "vidmahe"; "kāmadevāya dhīmahi," and "tanno viṣṇuḥ pracodayāt.
This Viṣṇu-gāyatrī, which delights all people, has been declared.
By the mere recitation [of this], it brings the three worlds under control;
it pacifies all sins and liberates one from all calamities. It grants the accomplishment of mantras to men and purifies through expiation.
[Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter in the glorious Gautamīya. || 28 ||
Now I shall declare another supreme mantra that bestows all prosperity;
by worshipping which Indra became the protector of the gods.
It consists of the syllables *sadyaḥ*, *śauraḥ*, *śāntaḥ*, and *jātiḥ*, joined together in sequence.
The four seed-syllables are said to be mounted upon the *śānti-bindu*.
"Jaya Kṛṣṇa" is uttered twice, followed by "Nityānte krīḍāsaṃśaktaṃ. Then, indeed, it is said: "O you of delighted mind, O eternal beloved."

The word "Kṛṣṇa" ending in the dative case (ṅe), followed by the ten-syllable mantra ending with "kāma," and encapsulated by the seed-syllables of Vāk, Śakti, and Kamalā, is the sovereign of all mantras. This mantra is the crest-jewel (śikhāmaṇi) of all Kṛṣṇa-mantras.
It is the repository of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa according to the tradition;
those mantras which are devoid of tradition are considered fruitless.
Ānanda is the seer (ṛṣi), Nārada is the sage, and Virāṭ is declared to be the meter (chanda).
The deity of this [mantra] is Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who bestows the fruits of devotion and liberation.
The wise practitioner should perform the ritual assignment of the limbs (*aṅgakalpana*) using six lotuses preceded by the seed-syllables.
Having performed the entire network of ritual assignments (*nyāsajāla*) as before, one should then purify the hands and the limbs.
Then, the wise practitioner of mantra should perform the various nyāsas, enclosing the Mātṛkā and the mantra; he should place the Ṛṣi, Chandas, and Devatā upon his head, mouth, and heart.
With a tranquil mind, he should meditate upon Hari, the teacher of all moving and unmoving beings.
One should meditate upon the golden ground situated in the midst of the ocean of milk and in the center of the Golden Mountain (Meru); in its midst is a pavilion of jewels,
measuring many yojanas in extent and spreading over vast yojanas.
It was adorned with pillars made of various jewels and beautified by strings of pearls; it was decorated with shimmering garments resembling foam, variegated with moon-like patterns,
and filled with swans and ducks amidst blooming lotuses and water lilies.
Adorned with hundreds of oblong ponds and surrounded by great gardens,
it was fashioned with golden walls and variegated with jeweled archways;
there, the Supreme Lord was seated upon a beautiful jewel-throne.
Rukmiṇī, the daughter of Bhīṣmaka, holding chowries at His sides,
adorned with various ornaments and looking on with supreme joy;
and Kālindī, the daughter of Ṛkṣa, holding peacock feathers behind Him.
Dark blue like the luster of a great cloud, with eyes as red as lotus petals,
clad in shimmering yellow garments, endowed with the glorious Śrīvatsa mark and the Kaustubha gem,
beautiful with various ornaments and resplendent with necklaces of pearls.
He wore a crown of blazing jewels and shimmering makara-earrings;
his dark locks were adorned with a forehead mark glowing with the luster of yellow orpiment;
he was surrounded by hosts of sages such as Nārada and by affectionate people.
With vast cities crowded with joyful and well-nourished people,
adorned with palaces and houses graced by fluttering banners,
and filled with Brahmins, Kshatriyas, Vaishyas, Shudras, and rows of chariots;
The rows of chariots were adorned everywhere with excellent islands; it was graced on all sides by the dwellings of Brahmins, Kshatriyas, Vaishyas, and Shudras, which resembled mountains,
and by most beautiful women who adorned every place.
Adorned with various diverse and wonderful paintings, and endowed with all these [attributes],

having thus meditated, O best of sages, one should mutter the mantra one hundred thousand times. Thereafter, one should perform a fire sacrifice with Belva fruits smeared with the three sweets (honey, ghee, and sugar).
The knower of mantras should gratify the foremost of Brahmins with a tenth part of that [offering].
One should worship the Lord upon the Gopāla-pīṭha with the consecration of jewels;
one should worship the six-limbed enclosure externally, and the queens situated on the petals.

The auspicious primary goddesses, Rukmiṇī and the others, adorned with great jewels, [are placed] outside that; as well as Indra, Vajra, and the other lords of the classes of beings, together with their vehicles.
Having performed the worship in this manner, the best of the twice-born becomes one whose mantra has attained perfection.
He who accomplishes the ritual applications becomes everywhere both a creator and a destroyer.
By offering a hundred thousand oblations with *śrīpuṣpa* flowers, one becomes a lord of the earth;
by a hundred thousand oblations with *pālāśa* leaves, one attains equality with the Lord of Speech (*Vāgīśa*).
One who delights the world with red flowers becomes a lover of horses;
by the mere offering of ghee into the fire, one shall live happily for a hundred years.
By the offering of food, one becomes wealthy, and by the offering of milk, one becomes possessed of cattle.
By performing oblations with *kāraskara* fruits, one may instantly cause enemies to be eradicated.
By an oblation of black pepper (*marīca*), one may kill one's own enemy.
By offering ten thousand *puṇḍarīka* flowers as oblations, one is liberated from all sins.
By performing oblations with one’s own excrement (*anvakṣamātra*), one shall obtain royal sovereignty,
while meditating upon oneself as the slayer of Kaṃsa and the enemy as being composed of *kasa* (poison).
Facing the south, by reciting [the mantra] ten thousand times, one attains this.
Likewise, a minister with a wrathful disposition and impure conduct may slay the enemy;
even for one constantly seated upon the throne of immortality, O Śakra, there is always the day of Vaivasvata (the day of death).
Indeed, there is no one at all in the three worlds who is exempt from his mantras.
The act of killing is not recommended when reciting a Vaiṣṇava mantra;
O Brahmin, one should take up the Brahmāstra mantra and offer salutations (namaḥ) to a rabbit and the like.
If one should perform [the rite] out of negligence, it may occur in these very places.
(If one should perform [it] through negligence, it may occur in these places:
against a sinner, a rogue who causes distress to people,
or one who steals one's own wealth, house, field, or wife.
One may perform an act of exorcism through exorcism; then one is not tainted by fault.
The subduing of the wicked is praised; this has been told to you, O Gautama.
When the Unborn himself is born, it is for the restraint of those who follow wrong paths.
The preceptor should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times as an expiation;
by that, he shall be liberated from sins and become endowed with auspiciousness.
For the rite to be accomplished and the ritual performed, the Sādhya desires to enjoy the practitioner.
Therefore, the preceptor should always protect himself by means of this ritual;
he should also recite the Mṛtyuñjaya mantra at the beginning of the mantras according to the instruction of the Guru.
Indeed, in all rites, the Guru is always the primary cause.
Having obtained the permission of the guru, one should accomplish all rites.
[Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter in the Gautamīya; the twenty-ninth chapter. 29.
Now listen, I shall proclaim the mantra of Śrī Puruṣottama;
by worshipping it through knowledge, the excellent practitioner becomes a recipient of both enjoyment and liberation,
endowed with all perfections, and wanders the earth as one liberated while living.
At the end of the body, one attains that supreme state, the absolute abode.
Among all Kṛṣṇa-mantras, the Śrī Puruṣottama mantra is the most excellent;
it directly bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon men through mere remembrance.

Then, having uttered the Praṇava, the seed-syllable of Māra, and "Namaḥ" at the end of "Ramā," followed by the word "Puruṣottama" and likewise the form "Prahatarūpita," then [the words] "Lakṣmīnivāsa," "Sakala," and "Jagat" at the end.
Having uttered the word "Kṣobhaṇā" (the Agitator), one should become composed in mind;
likewise, [one should utter] the word "Vidāraṇa" (the Tearer) endowed with the hearts of all women,
followed by "Ulka," and then "Bhuvanama-donmādakara" (the one who causes intoxication and madness in the world).
At the end of the gods and demons, O beautiful woman, torment in your mind this pair who are beloved by the people; then kindle this dyad,
thereafter dry up this dyad, and finally slay this supreme dyad.
First, paralyze the pair; then, delude the pair again.
Afterwards, cause the pair to flee, and immediately thereafter [strike] with the sword.
Then, sever the pair with all the arrows, followed by the word "with the noose."
Having formed two *kaṭṭas*, strike twice with the *aṅkuśa*; then again, utter the word "turu" twice. After that, say "matha," then "oṃ," then "kiṃ tiṣṭhasi," and then "pada.
Continue this until the end of the *pada*, while keeping the mind concentrated in the interval.
Then, having addressed me with the word "Siddhi," let there be the pair of "Ṭha" at the end.
Jaimini is declared as the sage (ṛṣi), Anuṣṭubh is stated as the meter (chandas),
and Puruṣottama is the deity of all the worlds.
One should utter the word "Puruṣottama" followed by "tribhuvanam";
then "madonmādakara" followed by "huṃ," which is the entire heart-mantra;
then the word "jagatkṣobhaṇa" followed by "lakṣmīdayita huṃ śivaḥ."
Joined with the supreme *manmatha*, it bestows desire upon the body;
"Huṃ" is the head-mantra, endowed with the most excellent and auspicious syllables.
"Huṃ" is proclaimed as the armor-mantra (*kavaca*), which brings about all good fortune.
"Manāṃsi hara, yugmānte dāraya, dvitayaṃ ca me,
vaśamānaya huṃ, netraṃ tārābhyāṃ ṣaṭ namo'ntikāḥ"—
these are declared by the knowers of the Tantra to be the limb-mantras (aṅgamantras), ending with the eyes (netra) and concluding with "namaḥ."
After *trailokyamohana*, the word *hṛṣīkeśa* follows;
then *apratirūpa* and so forth, and again after *manmatha*,
the words *sarva* and *svī* are uttered, followed by *hṛdayākarṣaṇa*.
"Come, come!"— this mantra, preceded by *Tārā*, should be used. Having performed the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka*) upon the arms with this mantra,
one should meditate upon the eight types of mantras together with their respective deities.
In the midst of the ocean of milk stands a place where celestial trees grow without interval;
it surpasses in beauty the rising rays of the sun and moon, and having cast aside all other charms,
a multitude of peacock feathers dances upon its sight, O Lord.
The quarters of the sky were stirred by the fragrance of blossoming flowers, by the tumultuous joy of the limbs [of the gods],
and by the warbling of cuckoos;
they were graced by the wind carrying the scent of various flowers.
In groves of wish-fulfilling creepers,
it was adorned by throngs of Siddhas sporting there and by celestial Gandharva women singing;
the garden, endowed with many long ponds, was truly most wonderful.
In its center, within a jeweled pavilion adorned with arches,
upon a beautiful great lion-throne situated at the foot of the celestial tree— which possesses immense splendor and is incessantly served by the six seasons— [he sat].

One should meditate upon the Lord of the World, who is identical with the universe— the divine Śrī Puruṣottama together with Kamalā seated on his lap— residing upon Garuḍa in the center of a red lotus, accompanied by her who is difficult to attain.

One should meditate for a moment upon Him who holds a lotus entwined with the luster of a blooming water-lily, resting upon her; who is crimson-hued, whose face is a smiling lotus, and who bears in His hands the conch, lotus, mace, bow, discus, sword, mallet, and goad. Having thus meditated upon the Beloved of Śrī, one should recite the mantra four hundred thousand times.
Then, having prepared a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) shaped like a half-moon, the self-controlled practitioner should mutter [the mantra].
He should indeed offer oblations into the Vaiṣṇava fire with jasmine flowers;
he should also offer oblations with flowers and barley into the mouth of the Discus (Cakra), and he should feed the Brāhmaṇas as well.
Desiring to worship the Lord of the World, the Preceptor shall purify himself, the sacrificial materials, and the sacrificial ground with the Gāyatrī mantra;
then he should utter the words: "To the Enchanter of the Three Worlds, we know."
"Let us meditate upon Smara; may Viṣṇu impel us from behind.
This is declared to be the Gāyatrī of Viṣṇu, which bestows all accomplishments.
One should then prepare a seat upon the previously mentioned Vaiṣṇava pedestal.
The dual worship (dvandva) for the King of Birds (Garuḍa) is proclaimed as his mantra.

Having mentally conceived the deity within the form [of the image] by means of the root-mantra, the practitioner, with one-pointed mind, should invoke the god with that mantra and worship him using the pervasive (vyāpaka) mantra.
The seed-syllable of the Goddess is proclaimed to be the syllable *Bhṛgu* (B) joined with *Vāṃ* (Vaṃ) and the Moon (I).
First, one should worship this Vidyā in the pericarp (*karṇikā*), and then the deities of the limbs (*aṅgadevatās*) with their respective mantras.
At the bases of the petals, one should worship Lakṣmī and the others holding chowries.
With lovely, heavy breasts shimmering with strings of pearls,
languid from the weight of their full bosoms, resembling hibiscus flowers in hue, and moving slowly with the playful intoxication of youth—
they [sang] that which was beautified by the vowels excluding the three short ones and the neuter (visarga).
The wise say that the seed-syllables (bījas) of these goddesses are their respective mantras.
One should worship the conch, the Śārṅga bow, the discus, the sword, the mace, the goad, the pestle, and the noose— these weapons of the wielder of the Śārṅga— at the tips of the petals.
The mantras are declared in sequence by means of their respective mudrās and names:
the first is said by the Sage to end with two *ṭha*s;
the supreme mantra ends with *svāhā* and follows the word *śāṅgī* (for Śārṅginī), *yaśaḥ* (for Yaśasvinī), and *śavā* (for Śavā).
O Sudarśana Mahācakra, may you arise; burn the pair [of enemies], and thereafter sever the two parts of all the wicked ones individually.
Tear asunder the pair of feet and devour, devour the supreme mantras!
"Eat, O you two who cause terror! Protect each pair, Phaṭ twice!"—this is declared as the third mantra, "Salutation to the Discus" (Cakrāya Namaḥ).
At the end of the words "Sword, Sharp," there should be "Asura, Phaṭ" twice for each.
"Obeisance to the Discus"—this is declared as the second mantra.
At the end of the word "sharp-edged sword" (khaḍgatīkṣṇe), one should separately utter "cut, split" twice.
O high-minded one, this fourth mantra is proclaimed for the Kaumodakī mace.
The mantra ending in *svāhā*— *sarvāsurāntaka padaṃ prasīda yugavarma phaṭ svāhā*— is declared by the virtuous to be supreme for the Kaumodakī mace.
This sixth mantra is said to end with *kaṭṭa* twice after *aṅkuśa*.
Furthermore, at the time of dissolution, there is the pair beginning with *mūṣala*.
This seventh mantra is proclaimed as ending with *huṃ phaṭ* and *svāhā* (*dviṭhānta*). After that, there is the pair [of mantras] bound by nooses, followed by two words for attraction.
The eighth Manu, ending with the wife of Vahni (Svāhā), has been proclaimed by the virtuous.
Afterwards, one should worship the Lords of the Worlds (the Lokapālas) along with their garments and weapons.
In this manner, one should daily worship Puruṣottama correctly.

Having worshipped the Lord with *hayāri* flowers according to the prescribed rite, one attains great fortune, incomparable good luck, and fame; one finds long life, health, and other desired objects of the mind.
One should offer oblations with jasmine flowers one thousand and eight times;
within a single month, all kings shall become subject to his will.
By offering oblations with bilva fruits and leaves, one shall obtain irreproachable prosperity.

By offering a thousand oblations of *jyotiṣmatī* oil, a man obtains that very [result] through fully blossomed red lotuses; he becomes truly fortunate in the eyes of all—of this there is no doubt. This is known as the "Vasus" rite.
By this procedure, the practitioner is liberated from great disease;
an oblation of *aśvattha* fuel-sticks removes wealth that has been seized by others;
and by an oblation of *dūrvā* grass smeared with clarified butter, one is freed from the fear of death.

If one recites the mantra ten thousand times by way of number, he shall become like a servant to him; there is no need for further deliberation on this point. What is the use of saying more here? By means of this mantra, the practitioner becomes the most excellent of adepts.
One shall accomplish all desires, even those higher than Viṣṇu and Śiva.
Now I shall proclaim the mantra that bestows both visible and invisible fruits.
Having measured the ground from east to north, one should lay down nine new lines.
There, sixty-four compartments arise according to their divisions; from the northeast (Īśāna) to the southwest (Rākṣasa), and from the southwest to the northwest (Vāyu) corner,
one should write the mantra-syllables which consist of Anuṣṭubh verses.
This yantra is fully described as being named Sarvatobhadra;
it is the destroyer of all diseases and the bestower of all human goals (puruṣārtha).
When this yantra is inscribed according to the prescribed rules upon birch bark or similar materials, [it grants these results].
Constantly held in the hand, it bestows the fruits of all desires;
when fashioned from *khadira* wood and placed in a cow-pen,
it is a protector that swiftly destroys thieves and murderers, and is for the welfare of the cows along with their calves.
O observer of excellent vows, thus has this reality (tattva) been explained to you: *kṣīra-go-gokṣīra-rakṣamā-kṣa-kṣamākṣara-gonāmo-gagaṇo-nāgo-pakṣa-ga-kṣaya*.
This alone should be studied with diligence; what else do you wish to hear?
[Thus ends the thirtieth chapter in the glorious Gautamīya. || 30 ||
Gautama said:
O omniscient one, knower of all principles, you who have reached the further shore of the meaning of all truths;
salutations to you, O Self-born One! Have mercy, O merciful one.
There is nothing whatsoever unknown to you in the three worlds, including all that is mobile and immobile.
Now, O Brahmin, tell me the characteristics of the accomplishment of mantras;
out of compassion for me, tell me how many kinds of means for accomplishment there are.
Nārada said:
"The mental longings known as *manoratha* are a source of affliction, yet they are the supreme cause for success;
likewise, the sight of deities is the remover of deaths."

For practitioners, there is the accomplishment of the afflictions; but following the attainment [of stability], there is the entry into another's body and likewise the entry into cities. Furthermore, by means of the upward progression, there is indeed movement through the gods of the moving and the unmoving.
I shall describe the union with the Khecarī, the hearing of her stories and so forth,
the cavities of the earth, and the characteristics of the lowest [type].
There is the gain of horses, vehicles, ornaments, and the like, as well as long life.
It is the supreme means for subduing kings and their retinues;
it brings wonder to all places and all worlds, and bestows happiness. It removes diseases by its mere sight, and likewise neutralizes poison.
Through diligent effort, the practitioner attains fourfold wisdom:
freedom from enmity, the desire for liberation, renunciation, and mastery over all things;
as well as the practice of the eightfold yoga and the turning away from the desire for worldly enjoyment.
Compassion toward all beings and the arising of qualities such as omniscience—
such a perfection of virtues is the characteristic of attainment (*siddhi*).
Furthermore, there is renown, the acquisition of ornaments, vehicles, and the like, and a very long life.
Affection for kings and women, influence over the world,
great sovereignty, wealth, and the prosperity of sons, wives, and so forth—
these are declared to be the inferior accomplishments (siddhis), which constitute the first stage for a practitioner of mantra.
He who possesses a perfected mantra is Śiva himself; there is no doubt about this.
Thus has the characteristic of perfection been described; now its means is explained here:
those who are pure by birth from both father and mother, who are of pure conduct, and who have conquered their senses.
For those who are instructed according to the tradition, success will come swiftly. But those who are impure, shrouded in defilement, sinful, fickle-minded,
averse to the worship of the deity and so forth, and who behave deceitfully toward the guru— [for them, it does not].

For them, those mantras which were previously shrouded in impurity, consisting merely of the forms of syllables— those that were lifeless, devoid of essence, blunted, and suppressed— are perfected by him through the recitation of mantras, fire offerings, and other such rites.
Those who stand on the side of the enemy, those joined with groups of sinners and the like,
those mantras that have not attained the prescribed ritual, and those devoid of the established conclusions (siddhānta)—
those corrupted by such defects grant success only through limited application.
"Mantras that remain in the state of mere cattle (paśu), consisting solely of the form of phonemes,
may they attain sovereignty when uttered as sound within the Suṣumṇā.
O sinless one, I shall explain that means to you in the final chapter."
Now, I shall explain in truth and according to the rules those accomplishments of mantra which arise from ritual refinement at the end of a kalpa through even a slight application of yoga: first,
birth (janana), then life-giving (jīvana), followed by striking (tāḍana) and awakening (bodhana).
Now, consecration (abhiṣeka), purification (vimalīkaraṇa), nourishment (āpyāyana),
satiation (tarpaṇa), illumination (dīpana), and protection (gopti)— these ten are the purificatory rites for mantras.
Having inscribed the supreme Mātṛkā-yantra upon a vessel made of gold or other precious materials, [one should perform these rites].
O observer of noble vows, one should then use saffron, or ash, or sandalwood paste.
Saffron is prescribed for the consecration of Śakti, sandalwood for Vaiṣṇava mantras,
and ash is declared for the drawing of the Mātṛkā-yantra in the Śaiva tradition.
The extraction of mantras from the midst of the Mātṛkā is known as their "birth.
According to the determination of the Tantras, the sages have prescribed this method in sequential order.
A wise person should recite the syllables of the mantra, placing the Praṇava (Oṃ) between each one, according to the ritual rule.
It is taught that one should recite [the mantra] one hundred times for each [syllable];
having written down the letters of the mantra, one should strike them with sandalwood water.
It is held that the striking of each [letter] with the seed-syllable of air (Yam) is to be performed as previously described.
Whether with ashes, flowers, or again with sandalwood—
these three auspicious substances are prescribed according to the various divisions of the Śaiva and other Tantras.
Having written the mantra-piṇḍa, one should [worship] it with karavīra flowers.
Awakening [the deity] with the letter *ra* repeated as many times as there are syllables in that mantra,
followed by consecration (*abhiṣeka*) according to the procedure prescribed for that specific mantra, is thus proclaimed.
The practitioner of mantras should sprinkle [the deity] with the sprouts of the *aśvattha* tree, reciting the mantra as many times as there are syllables in it.

Having mentally contemplated the mantra at the base and center of the *suṣumṇā*, the Lord should duly burn away the three impurities with the light-mantra (*jyotirmantra*). The mantra of the Lord is considered to be:
*Tāraṃ* (Om), followed by *vyoma* (H), *agni* (Ra), and a pair of *marut* (Ya), ending with *daṇḍīte*. Thus: *Oṃ Hrāṃ Hrīṃ Hruṃ Phaṭ*.
The ritual sprinkling (*mārjana*) is performed with water from *kuśa* grass or likewise with water containing flowers;
by means of that mantra, the procedure for nourishment (*āpyāyana*) is prescribed according to rule.
One should then kindle all mantras through the application of the two [mantras] of desire.

One should guard the blazing mantra that bestows all accomplishments. Now, regarding the libations (tarpaṇa) in the Śākta and Vaiṣṇava Tantras, it is properly declared that they should be performed with water mixed with camphor; in the Śaiva [Tantras], with ghee and milk.
These ten ritual preparations of mantras have been described to you;
by performing them according to the tradition, the practitioner of mantra attains his desired goal.

Now I shall further explain the characteristics of the accomplishment of mantras, by performing which correctly and with effort, a knower of mantras attains purity; and into those mantras that are devoid of potency, one should join the seed-syllables (bījas).
Whether it be the seed-mantra of desire or the seed-mantra of poison, a mantra bestows success through its recitation.
Now, O Sage, listen as I shall explain another means of attaining success:
mantras that grant fruit when established in their proper place and when established in meditation.
Those who are devoid of the proper posture and meditation do not obtain the fruit even from ten million recitations.
Now, therefore, I shall explain another characteristic of mantra-siddhi:
the wise practitioner should recite his own mantra after having encased it within the *mātṛkā*.
Indeed, the commentary on the *Varṇagrantha* concludes with two hundred thousand recitations;
it has been stated by those who know the Tantras that the accomplishment of mantras will certainly be achieved thereby.
Now, I shall briefly describe the supreme *puraścaraṇa*.
During an eclipse of the moon or the sun, being pure and having previously fasted,
one should stand waist-deep in the water of a river flowing toward the ocean and,
with a concentrated mind, recite the mantra from the moment of the first swallow until its release.
One should perform the fire-oblation (homa) with a tenth part of that [number], the libation (tarpaṇa) with a tenth part of that,
the ritual sprinkling (abhiṣeka) with a tenth part of that, and the feeding of Brahmins (viprabhojana) with a tenth part of that;
by performing these five acts in this manner, a person becomes one whose mantra is perfected (siddhamantra).
Alternatively, having meditated upon the Guru at the crown of his head and remaining silent,
the practitioner of mantra should dwell facing east and perform the recitation of the mantra as prescribed.
Thereafter, he should perform the fire-oblation (homa) and other rites in sequence, using one-tenth of the total number.
By acting thus, the practitioner becomes one whose mantra is perfected, and not otherwise.
Through the mere satisfaction of the Guru, success that grants liberation shall arise;
a mantra is never perfected through recitation alone, nor ever through burnt offerings alone.

If [the deity] has not been worshipped according to the rules, nor satisfied, nor fed, there is no fixed limit to the number of times the mantra—consisting of the five principles—is to be recited. It is said that in the Kṛta age, success comes from the prescribed recitation; in the Tretā age, the recitation must be doubled.
In the Dvāpara age, it is threefold, and in the Kali age, the count is fourfold;
however, O divine sage, by means of the Kṛṣṇa-mantra, no such calculation of ages applies.
Success is achieved through recitation, fire-offerings, libations, and so forth, according to the count prescribed for the Kṛta age.
Because this mantra is already perfected, there is no need for the exertion of service over many ages.
[Thus ends the thirty-first chapter in the glorious Gautamīya. || 31 ||
Now I shall further declare another most wonderful means for attaining accomplishment (siddhi),
by which the knower of the mantra, once accomplished, becomes the agent of creation, maintenance, and dissolution;
he should employ the respective yoga in accordance with each specific action.
The various types of mantra application, such as *grathana* and so forth, shall now be explained:
*grathita*, *saṃpuṭa*, *grasta*, *samasta*, *vidarbhit*, as well as *ākānta*, *ādyaṃta*, *garbhastha*, and *sarvatovṛta*.
Likewise, *mukti*, *vidarbha*, and *vidarbha-grathita*— thus,
when mantras are employed in these eleven ways, they grant the accomplishment of one's purpose.
When a single syllable of the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) is joined at the end of the mantra, [it is known as *mukti*].
That is declared to be "grathita" (strung together), which is supreme for bringing others under control and attracting them.
One should utter the entire mantra at the beginning, followed immediately by the name of the person to be accomplished (sādhya);
then, the mantra is repeated in reverse order at the end—that is known as "saṃpuṭa" (encased).
It should be known as bestowing peace and nourishment, and granting sovereignty over the three worlds.
A wise practitioner should place half [of the mantra] at the beginning and half at the end;
the object of accomplishment (*sādhya*) should be placed in the middle—this is called "the swallowed" (*grasta*).
When seized by mantras used for killing or expulsion,
one should first utter the name and then likewise utter the mantra;
this entire procedure is said to effect the expulsion of enemies.

Where two mantra-syllables enclose each syllable of the name of the target (*sādhya*), it is declared to be "interlaced" (*vidarbhitam*); this destroys the wicked and has the characteristic of subjugation (*vaśya*). If every syllable of the mantra is interspersed [with the name], that mantra remains effective.
One should recognize that as "conquered" (ākānta), which immediately bestows all desired objects.
In rites of agitation, paralysis, possession, subjugation, and eradication,
one should first recite the mantra once, and likewise again at the end.
And its center should contain the object to be accomplished (sādhya) at both the beginning and the end; so the experts know it.
For those who are mutually engaged [in conflict], one should employ this supreme mantra for inciting enmity; one should apply it twice, both at the beginning and at the end.
The name of the person to be acted upon (*sādhya*) is placed once in the middle; that is then said to be "situated within the womb" (*garbhastha*).

One should employ the rites of killing (māraṇa), expulsion (uccāṭana), and subjugation (vaśya) for men; likewise, with a gentle mind, one should paralyze the weapon (hetinī) within the womb when it has gone there. One should utter the mantra three times at the beginning and likewise three times again at the end.
The middling [mandala] should be made circular on all sides; by its performance, the goal is accomplished in a single instance.
It pacifies all malevolent magic (*abhicāra*), wards off great death, generates all good fortune, and bestows immortality upon the dead.
First one should write the mantra, then the name, and then the syllables of the object to be accomplished (sādhya).
Having performed this three times in this manner, it becomes "interlaced" (vidarbhitam),
which is said to remove all diseases and crush spirits and epilepsy.
Having placed each syllable in the middle, the mantra should be interlaced (vidarbha). Another method previously described should be applied at its beginning and end;
this is called the "interlaced" (vidarbha) arrangement, the most excellent among the kings of mantras.
It is declared to accomplish all rites and bestow the fruit of all sovereign powers.
Thus, these applications grant success to one whose mantra is perfected.
Now, I shall further describe the characteristics of the perfection of a mantra.

Having known which, the best of practitioners will certainly attain success in mantra. If, despite being properly performed, success does not arise, it must be performed again by that same person; thereafter, success will certainly be achieved.

If the mantra is practiced again and yet accomplishment (siddhi) does not arise, it must be performed once more by that same person; then it will undoubtedly be accomplished. If that mantra is practiced yet again and accomplishment still does not arise—
In that regard, the seven expedients spoken by Śaṅkara should be employed:
causing it to wander, awakening, subjugation, pressing, drying, nourishing, and ending with burning; one should perform these in sequence, and then one will certainly become accomplished.
One should perform the rotation within the *vāruṇa* seed-syllable and the threading according to the sequential method.
Having mixed yellow pigment (*rocanā*) with *guru*, along with cardamom, camphor, saffron,
*uśīra*, and sandalwood, one should write the mantra as it has been strung together.
One should cast that which has been written into the midst of milk, clarified butter, honey, and water.
Through worship, recitation, and fire-offerings, once it has been rotated, it becomes a bestower of success.
If, when rotated, it does not achieve success, one should perform its awakening.
One should perform the recitation while encasing the rotation [of the mantra] with the seed-syllable of desire (Kāma-bīja).
Thus, the perfected one becomes restrained; if not, then bring him under control.
Take lac-dye, sandalwood, costus, turmeric, realgar, and mica.

Having written this mantra on a very beautiful birch-bark leaf (bhūrjapatra), it should be worn around the neck; one will then become a perfected master (siddha) or may even inflict torment [upon others].
Indeed, having recited the mantra with the feet in the inverted order (adharottara-yoga), one attains success.
Having written the Vidyā of the goddess Dhyāpītā, who likewise possesses an upper and lower form,
with the milk of the sun, and having stepped over it with one’s foot,
one should perform a fire sacrifice (homa) day after day with the mantra "tathā bhūta."
If [the disciple] is overcome by shame, he should always nourish him;
one should join the third seed-syllable of the young girl (Vālā) at the beginning and end of that [mantra].
Having smeared [the hand] with cow’s milk and honey, one should cause him to hold the vidyā in his hand.
If this [mantra] has been nourished and perfected, one should not perform the rite of withering;
rather, with both hands, one should hold the seed-syllable at the heart and the throat.
This lore, endowed with strength and virility, should be maintained during the act of sexual union.

If, even after being withered, success is not attained, one should burn [the obstacle] by means of the fire-seed syllable (*agnibīja*). That first syllable of the mantra which is used for the initial action is placed in the middle and above, like the milking of a cow during the ritual act.

Then, having fashioned a [seat] made of darbha grass from the root of a Brahma-tree, the mantra will become perfected upon a consecrated site; this was declared by Śaṅkara. Thus has it been fully related to you solely out of devotion.

One who is firm in his vows achieves his purpose with but a single [mantra]; what need is there for many? Now I shall proclaim another most wonderful mantra-remedy, by the performance of which one will certainly attain success immediately.
By rubbing the root of the *karavīra* plant with honey in one's hand and smearing it upon one's limbs, and placing [the mantra] around the neck, Kṛṣṇa becomes instantly pleased;
freed from the entire flood of sins, one beholds Kṛṣṇa with one's own eyes.
The practitioner shall become liberated while living; this is the truth, the truth that I have spoken.
Whether he desires to go to any place whatsoever on earth, or even out of curiosity to the netherworld (pātāla), the practitioner [shall attain his goal].

At that very moment, one indeed departs [from this world] and becomes a lord of all supernatural powers (*sarvasiddhiśvara*). Thus, O Brahmin, the characteristics of mantra-perfection have been correctly described; and its means has likewise been revealed solely through your good fortune.
This has been proclaimed in many tantras and is approved by many sages;
now, O Brahmin, what more do you wish to hear?
[Thus ends the thirty-second chapter in the glorious Gaudapāda-mahātantra, the best of all tantras. || 32 ||
[It is finished; may there be auspiciousness.]
This book was written in the middle of Jambūdvīpa in the month of Bhādrapada, [Saṃvat] 1944.
